text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Norman Finkelstein Cuts Through Israel’s Propaganda: Gaza Genocide, Oct. 7 & Netanyahu’s Corruption

Overview
Norman Finkelstein argues that October 7 cannot be understood apart from Gaza’s long history, while insisting this context does not excuse the killing of innocents. He traces Gaza’s condition to 1948 displacement, the blockade after Hamas’s 2006 election victory, and repeated Israeli operations, then argues the cumulative evidence amounts to genocide. He also describes a sweeping campaign against critics of Israel in U.S. institutions, and says accountability is unlikely, so the record must be preserved.

Key Themes
- Gaza’s present condition is rooted in 1948 displacement and decades of enclosure, not in October 7 alone, even as Finkelstein says the attack on innocents is not excused.
- Outside observers across different eras, including UN officials, Al Gore Sr., and Giora Eiland, described Gaza as a concentration camp.
- After Hamas won an election Jimmy Carter called free and fair, Israel and then the US and EU imposed a blockade aimed at keeping Gaza’s economy on the precipice of collapse.
- Finkelstein argues genocide is established by cumulative evidence, including the proportion of children killed, destruction of homes and schools, and attacks on hospitals, medics, journalists, and UN workers.
- He distinguishes Israel’s stated goal as ethnically cleansing Gaza, with genocide described as the means to force expulsion rather than the end in itself.
- Mainstream human rights and legal authorities have concluded it is genocide, which he says shifts the burden of proof to Israel’s defenders.
- Instead of making a public case, supporters of Israel are described as attacking critics economically and institutionally, especially after October 7.
- The crackdown on pro-Palestinian dissent on U.S. campuses is framed as the most severe assault on academic freedom in modern U.S. history.
- Criticism of Israel is deliberately conflated with anti-Semitism to delegitimize all criticism, a move Finkelstein says damages have already been done even if courts later vindicate dissenters.

Detailed Summary
Finkelstein begins from Gaza’s history. In 1948, roughly 750,000 Palestinian Arabs were expelled, and 200,000 to 300,000 went to Gaza, becoming about 80 percent of its population. Gaza was part of British-mandated Palestine, and Egypt gained administrative control after the 1948 war. UN officials in Gaza in the 1950s, under Egyptian control, already described it as a concentration camp. Al Gore Sr. visited in July 1967 and testified before Congress that it was a concentration camp on the send. Giora Eiland in 2004 called Gaza a huge concentration camp; Finkelstein notes Eiland later said an epidemic in southern Gaza would be a good thing.

The political turning point came in 2006. President George Bush promoted democracy promotion and pressured Palestinians to hold elections. Hamas initially did not want to participate because of the Oslo Process but eventually ran on a reform platform and won. Hillary Clinton later said, we made a big mistake, we should have made sure that Hamas didn’t win. Jimmy Carter described the election as completely free and fair and called it the first such democratic election in the Arab world. After Hamas’s victory, Israel imposed a blockade with restrictions on items including chocolate, potato chips, condiments, musical instruments, and notebooks. Documents later described a humanitarian minimum diet and keeping Gaza’s economy on the precipice of collapse. Finkelstein compares this to the U.S. approach toward Chile under Popular Unity, quoting the aim to turn the screws until the economy screams.

By 2008, UN humanitarian chief Mary Robinson said a whole civilization is being destroyed. By October 6, The Economist described Gaza as a sinking ship, and a UN official called it a toxic slum. Israel launched operations described as mowing the lawn: Operation Cast Lead in 2008 and 2009, Pillar of Defense in 2012, and Protective Edge in 2014. After Protective Edge, ICRC head Peter Maurer said he had never seen destruction like Gaza’s, with 18,000 homes destroyed or severely damaged and 2.5 million tons of rubble. Since October 7, Finkelstein cites 325,000 homes destroyed and 61 million tons of rubble.

On genocide, Finkelstein says there is no good aggregate number for deaths in Gaza, citing differing projections and indirect deaths from hunger and compromised immune systems. The most recent UN report cited addresses targeting of children in Gaza and the West Bank. Gaza Ministry of Health statistics put children at roughly 30 percent of those killed. In the Nazi Holocaust, roughly 6 million Jews were killed, of whom 1.5 million were children, about 25 percent. He notes the IHRA definition of anti-Semitism includes comparing Israeli government actions to Nazis, and argues Israelis frequently compare enemies to Nazis while that comparison is treated as taboo in reverse. He accuses a historical pattern of calling Nasser, Saddam Hussein, and Hamas Hitler, while calling Iranian mullahs worse than Hitler. Netanyahu is quoted as saying Hitler only wanted to conquer Europe but Iranian mullahs would be worse.

The bombing of Gaza is described as unprecedented in modern conflict by density and rate, compared in intensity to Dresden and other major World War II cases. Finkelstein claims more children were killed in Gaza than in all combined combat zones in 2020 and 2021. He claims Gaza has the densest concentration of amputees anywhere in the world. He claims 97 percent of Gaza’s schools are destroyed or severely damaged. Targeting of hospitals, medical personnel, UN workers, and journalists is described as uniquely severe compared with other conflicts. He says Israel’s goal is to empty Gaza and ethnically cleanse it, with the border sealed and no country willing to take refugees. In his account, the only way to force departure is genocide.

He cites international law authorities and human rights figures who concluded it is genocide, including Aryeh Neier, a Holocaust refugee, and Kenneth Roth, former Human Rights Watch head. He estimates 30 to 40 percent of American Jews believe Israel is committing genocide, which he frames as significant given community pressure and education levels. He cites the International Court of Justice preliminary conclusion in January 2024 that Israel was plausibly committing genocide. He says the Trump administration stripped green cards from critics and targeted Mahmoud Khalil of Columbia, and claims a Jewish supremacist billionaire class spearheaded it and did not protest.

On campuses, Finkelstein describes post-October 7 pressure from donors. Bill Ackman is cited as the public face, publicly threatening to withhold alumni donations unless encampments were crushed. Donation amounts cited include Ackman giving Harvard about 50 million dollars and two Jewish alumni giving 200 million dollars and 300 million dollars. University leaders ousted after encampments include Claudine Gay at Harvard, Elizabeth Magill at Penn, and Minouche Shafik at Columbia, plus many others. Magill reportedly said money talks after being ousted. Finkelstein describes fear among hospital and Lincoln Center employees over posting Gaza support on social media. Jewish philanthropy is described as the dominant donor base for New York libraries and cultural institutions, giving significant cultural power, which he says was used for nasty, sinister purposes. He claims the assault on academic freedom is unprecedented in modern U.S. history, noting the concept dates to the early 1900s.

He argues the post-2024 campus crackdown is the most severe assault on academic freedom in modern U.S. history, surpassing the Red Scare and McCarthy era. He claims the ouster of three Ivy League presidents, all women and two women of color, drew almost no objection from mainstream media, showing that even woke identity protections did not shield them. He describes a personal chilling effect: since spring 2024 he has been invited to speak at only two U.S. colleges, versus past periods of about 40 schools per year. He characterizes the campaign against pro-Palestinian students as collective punishment, citing trucks displaying students’ pictures and calling them terrorists, including in their families’ neighborhoods far away.

He argues the Harvard anti-Semitism report, 312 pages, contained no real evidence of anti-Semitism, only claims that Israeli Jewish students felt shunned, which he rejects as a basis for suppressing criticism of Israel. He contends that criticism of Israel and Netanyahu is deliberately conflated with anti-Semitism to delegitimize all criticism, and that even if court rulings later vindicate dissenters, the silencing will already have done its damage. He notes a reversal of cause and effect: pro-Palestinian encampment protesters felt unsafe and shunned, then a report labeled that as anti-Semitism, then the report was used to call for expelling the protesters. A concrete incident cited is a truck at Harvard circulating through Boston and Cambridge with students’ pictures calling them terrorists, and trucks also going to neighborhoods 500 miles away where students’ families lived.

Harvard report items he dismisses as non-anti-Semitic include a poster depicting Harvard president Alan Garber as a devil and a map of Palestine without Israel. He notes Harvard costs 80,000 dollars a year and students faced threats of suspension, expulsion, and deportation, which he cites as reason for institutional capitulation. He says Garber later conceded that a large part of what was called anti-Semitism was just criticism of Israel. He cites U.S. jurisprudence: the Supreme Court has protected advocating violent overthrow of the government and a Fuck the draft t-shirt as free speech, making from the river to the sea comparatively mild and protected.

He cites a March 2018 UN report on the Great March of Return finding Israel targeted children, journalists, medics, and double amputees 300 meters from the perimeter fence. He contrasts Israel’s citizen army, which he says is to its credit, unlike the Vietnam-era college-deferment army or the volunteer army drawn from those without other futures, with the discredit of that same army committing what he calls genocide. He says the Israeli army is representative of the Israeli Jewish population, making it, in his view, a nation of child killers. He states that since spring 2024 he spoke at Cornell, where the president introduced him, which he calls courageous, and at UMass, and has not spoken anywhere in New York, where he lives.

On his own formation, Finkelstein says his early path opposing Israeli actions began in June 1982 during Israel’s invasion of Lebanon, when only a handful of Jewish critics existed; Chomsky was the notable exception who gave stature to the cause. His doctoral research into Joan Peters’ From Time Immemorial produced a eureka finding: he determined that a key demographic number in the book’s tables was fake, turning his work into a battle against a bestselling, elite-endorsed narrative. Chomsky’s support became a turning point: after reading Finkelstein’s critique, Chomsky called him, found it convincing, and became a friend and mentor, while warning that pursuing this path would bring attacks. Finkelstein frames his refusal to compromise as central: he says he cannot be bought and attaches himself to truth and justice, so continuing despite costs was not a difficult decision.

He describes being excluded from mainstream academic and media channels, including not being paid for six weeks as an adjunct at Brooklyn College and later having his Gaza political history ignored by major review outlets. He suggests the media landscape may be shifting: legacy outlets like The New Yorker and The Atlantic remain closed to him, but social media and alternative media may now offer prospects. He says he was denied entry to Israel in 1989 and again in 2004 and never returned. He says many Jews active in opposing the occupation were denied entry, including Professor Chomsky a couple of years later. He says he was unemployed from 2007 to about 2020, a period he calls dark and largely forgotten. He describes adjunct teaching as a demeaning position, usually filled by graduate students, and says Brooklyn College did not pay him for six weeks.

text:
A lot is happening in America.

Please take the time to watch this movie, which is based on a true story.

I am sharing something so disheartening, and I want everyone who has experienced this to share. 

After watching the movie "We Were Soldiers " with Mel Gibson with my husband, a veteran, I asked him what stood out of his travels during that time.

We married in June 1968, and he received his draft notice soon after our honeymoon.
 He enlisted and joined the Army Security Agency, although he was offered a Warrant Officer commission as a helicopter pilot. 

My husband rarely cries, but at 79 years of age he choked and said, "It was when I was on the flight from Japan on a Cargo plane, and many of my fellow soldiers were so broken; some were crying, as we were in the presence of caskets draped with the American flag. Their memories of the horrors and the loss were overwhelming.
As he teared up, he said that when they got off the plane in CA. Some protestors screamed at them, calling them baby killers, and he and others got spit on. 
They were escorted away and were ordered to put on their civilian clothes. 

My husband, like so many young men, gave to our country, and to look at today's future, it appears it was for all the wrong reasons. 

They did not die and endure the hate to lose it all in the end due to kindness that will kill us all in the end.

Allowing Muslims to retain office in America is not American.

text:
NO ONE WAS SAVED UNTIL JESUS — THEN WHAT ABOUT ABRAHAM, MOSES AND DAVID?

This statement can make many Christians uncomfortable:

“No one was saved until Jesus.”

But first, we must define what we mean by saved.

Did people in the Old Testament believe God, receive mercy, experience forgiveness and stand in a right relationship with Him?

Yes.

But did they accomplish or possess the finished work of redemption from sin and death?

No.

That distinction matters.

Abraham was counted righteous because he believed God:

«“And he believed in the LORD, and He accounted it to him for righteousness.”
— Genesis 15:6»

David experienced God's forgiveness.

Moses led Israel under God's covenant.

The prophets trusted God's promises.

But none of them was the Redeemer.

They lived before the cross.

The sacrifices of the Old Testament were real and God-commanded, but they were never the final solution.

Hebrews says:

«“For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins.”
— Hebrews 10:4»

The sacrifices were shadows of something greater.

The Passover pointed forward.

The priesthood pointed forward.

The Day of Atonement pointed forward.

The sacrifices pointed forward.

The prophets pointed forward.

And then Jesus came.

John the Baptist declared:

«“Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!”
— John 1:29»

Jesus didn't simply teach salvation.

He accomplished redemption.

On the cross He declared:

«“It is finished!”
— John 19:30»

Abraham trusted God's promise before its fulfillment.

We trust God's accomplished work after its fulfillment.

The direction of faith is different, but the ultimate object of salvation is the same:

Christ.

This is why Jesus said:

«“Your father Abraham rejoiced to see My day, and he saw it and was glad.”
— John 8:56»

Abraham was not saved because Moses was enough.

David was not saved because sacrifices were enough.

Israel was not saved because the Law was enough.

They were all part of a story moving toward Christ.

So, was Abraham saved?

If we mean that Abraham experienced God's grace, was justified by faith and belonged to God — yes.

But if we mean that Abraham had already experienced the completed redemptive work of Christ — no.

Christ had not yet died.

Christ had not yet risen.

The New Covenant had not yet been inaugurated through His blood.

The final sacrifice had not yet been offered.

Hebrews describes the Old Testament saints as those who died in faith, “not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off.” — Hebrews 11:13

They looked forward.

We look back.

But both ultimately point to Jesus.

The cross was not God's Plan B.

Christ was the fulfillment toward which the entire biblical story was moving.

Creation.

Promise.

Abraham.

Israel.

Moses.

The covenant.

The sacrifices.

David.

The prophets.

Then Christ.

So when we say, “No one was saved until Jesus,” we must be careful.

God's grace existed before Bethlehem.

Faith existed before Calvary.

Forgiveness existed before the resurrection.

But the finished work of redemption belongs to Christ.

The Old Testament saints trusted God's promise.

We trust God's accomplished work.

And the foundation of both is ultimately the same:

JESUS CHRIST.

Not Moses.

Not Abraham.

Not David.

Not the Law.

Not the sacrificial system.

CHRIST.

The promise was given before Him.

The shadows pointed toward Him.

The prophets spoke about Him.

The cross accomplished redemption through Him.

The resurrection proclaimed His victory.

Christianity is not ultimately:

“Look at what humanity achieved for God.”

It is:

“Look at what God accomplished through Jesus Christ.”

#JesusChrist #Salvation #Redemption #Grace #Faith #Gospel #ChristAlone

🪷 Today is Rishi Panchami 🪷

Rishi Panchami on Tuesday, September 15, 2026

Rishi Panchami Puja Muhurat - 10:18 AM to 12:45 PM
Duration - 02 Hours 27 Mins

Panchami Tithi Begins - 07:44 AM on Sep 15, 2026
Panchami Tithi Ends - 08:59 AM on Sep 16, 2026

This is a significant Hindu fast and ritual observed on the fifth day (Panchami) of the Shukla Paksha in the lunar month of Bhadrapada. Celebrated just a day after Ganesh Chaturthi, this auspicious day is dedicated to honoring the Saptarishi—the seven legendary Vedic sages who preserved and passed down divine knowledge to humanity.

The Saptarishis Honored:-
On this day, devotees collectively worship the seven prominent Rishis along with Mother Arundhati (the wife of Sage Vashistha):
Kashyapa
Atri
Vashistha
Vishvamitra
Gautama
Jamadagni
Bharadwaja

Key Rituals and Fasting Rules:-
Holy Bath & Purification: Devotees wake up early during the Brahma Muhurat to take a sacred bath in a holy river or at home using water infused with Gangajal and Apamarg (chichida) leaves.

Strict Fasting Diet: The fasting rules are highly unique. Devotees completely avoid grain grown using oxen or plows (such as regular rice or wheat). Instead, they eat foods that grow naturally or wild, like Sama rice (Moradhan/barnyard millet) and root vegetables.

Rishi Panchami Bhaji: A special mixed vegetable dish made from seasonal, unploughed greens and roots (like amaranth leaves, sweet potato, and elephant foot yam) is traditionally prepared and consumed.

Puja Ritual: Devotees clean the altar, set up an image or idol of the Saptarishis, and offer white flowers, sandalwood, fruits, incense, and lamps while listening to the Rishi Panchami Vrat Katha.

Cultural Significance:-
Purification and Forgiveness: The fast is primarily observed by women as a ritual means to seek forgiveness for any unintentional mistakes or transgressions regarding purity rituals, particularly past oversights during their menstrual cycles (Rajaswala Dosha). In modern times, it stands as a beautiful annual custom of expressing gratitude for spiritual lineage and ancestral wisdom.

Regional Variations: In certain communities like the Maheshwari tradition, it is observed as a day where sisters tie protective threads on their brothers' wrists and pray for their long life. Meanwhile, in specific parts of Kerala, this day coincides with Vishvakarma Puja.

The traditional Arghya (offering water) Mantra names all the seven Rishis:-

कश्यपोऽत्रिर्भरद्वाजो विश्वामित्रोऽथ गौतमः। जमदग्निर्वसिष्ठश्च सप्तैते ऋषयः स्मृताः॥ दहन्तु पापं मे सर्वं गृह्णन्त्वर्घ्यं नमो नमः॥

"Kashyapa, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra, Gautama, Jamadagni and Vasishtha — these seven are remembered as the Rishis. May they burn away all my faults; may they accept this arghya. Salutations, again and again."

🪷🙏 Jai Gurudev 🙏🪷
🪷🙏 Shree Saptarishyai Namaha 🙏🪷

Here is the biological reality that the supplement giants will never put on the label: Magnesium is a massive, socially awkward ion that cannot just walk through the front door of your cells. You aren't magnesium deficient because you aren't consuming enough; you are deficient because you are lacking the 'intracellular escort' needed to put that mineral to work. The industry sells you elemental weight, but your body is starving for cellular delivery.

text:
German prices doubled in 20 years: Who filled the wallets of ordinary people with three chancellors?

Under Merkel, Scholz, and Merz, everything from oil prices to rents to grilled rolls has gone up.

You might ask: Isn't Germany the largest economy in Europe? 
There are multiple reasons for this:
The energy crisis of 2022. High energy costs have been embedded in the pricing structure of the economy as a whole.
Then there's inflation.      From 2022 to 2023, Germany will experience its worst inflation in four decades, with annual inflation rising above 10 percent at one point.
The housing crisis.       Germany has long been short of the policy target of 400 thousand new housing units per year, rising construction materials prices, rising financing costs and cumbersome approval procedures, leading to a serious shortage of supply.
The pressure to transform the industrial structure.
Large companies, such as Volkswagen, are making massive layoffs and restructuring, and manufacturing jobs are being lost. News of 100 thousand layoffs by 2025 is just the tip of the iceberg. BMW and Mercedes are also shrinking. When job security declines, the feeling of rising prices is multiplied.
Prices and politics.                    In the wake of the 2015 refugee crisis, there has been a massive influx of migrants, and housing has become more tight, competition has intensified and social contradictions have become more prominent. At the same time, the policies of the traditional mainstream parties (CDU, SPD) are increasingly converging, and the middle voters feel that "everyone can vote the same."

At this point, the AfD offers a simple and straightforward set of answers: anti-immigration, anti-EU, anti-energy transition. For many anxious ordinary Germans, this tactic is much more attractive than "give it a little more."
From 10% to 30%, the AfD has made the leap from small parties to mainstream parties in a decade. What drives this process is not just ideology, but how every German feels every month when they visit supermarkets, gas stations and banks.

text:
Are LLMs a dead end for humanity?

I want to reflect on this passage from OpenAI's Dan Selsam (thanks for posting @DKokotajlo):

“I want the glorious renaissance future as much as anyone. I have worked for it, however tortuously, my whole career. It breaks my heart to see the potential in sight and forgo it, but the argument—that if we get there by growing models rather than engineering them, we will lose everything in the end—seems very strong to me. I am still wrestling with it and its staggering implications. I do not have answers, but as a first step, I wanted to share my present concerns.”

https://t.co/13XaDcrrKg

It raises a question that is sadly worth considering: could LLMs be a technological dead-end for humanity? Could LLM based AGI & ASI be a technology that inevitable leads to bad outcomes for humans?

By “dead end,” I mean a path toward increasingly powerful intelligence that we cannot make safe enough to pursue.

Perhaps alignment research will never give us a way to guarantee that a trained model will remain aligned with human intentions and values across every situation it encounters. How would we even establish such a guarantee for a system operating in something as dynamic and complex as human society?

I’m uncertain whether we can establish strong safety guarantees for general-purpose AI operating in an open-ended world. We won’t have any fully 100% mathematical verifiable claim about either safety or potential consequence. Those guarantees could be probabilistic: randomness alone doesn’t rule out mathematical reasoning about safety. The harder question is whether the assumptions behind our guarantees would hold as capabilities grow, systems interact, and agents encounter situations we didn’t anticipate.

As a practical question: what evidence would give us enough confidence to entrust increasingly powerful AI systems with consequential decisions and actions?

If we cannot establish that confidence, we may need to design for the possibility that individual systems are misaligned—even when they appear to behave well.

Can we coexist with such systems and constrain them through other mechanisms? Are there safer paths to advanced AI? And if neither approach works, can we stop?

1. Can we make networks of potentially misaligned agents safe?

This is what we’re exploring at New Collectives.
https://t.co/rNo8ZCjTTs

We're trying to bring folks together from many disciplines to explore this, and there's already a large body of worthwhile research happening on these fronts:
https://t.co/fCn5ZBDQ3f

If we cannot guarantee that any individual agent is aligned, what can we establish about a network of agents - or an economy in which humans and AI agents interact?

Human society offers an imperfect analogy. We don’t rely on every person having good intentions. We use institutions, incentives, laws, and checks on power to encourage cooperation and constrain destructive behavior. Could we build mechanisms that work for AI agents, including agents much more capable than ourselves?

Several questions seem worth pursuing:

Collective alignment: Could a network steer individual agents toward outcomes that serve human interests? Under what conditions would cooperation support those interests, and when might it instead enable collusion?

Economics and institutions: Can incentives encourage stable, beneficial behavior? Can rules remain effective when agents are capable of finding—and exploiting—their loopholes?

Monitoring without authoritarianism: Could we detect dangerous activity without creating a surveillance state? @michael_nielsen explores this possibility through the idea of “provably beneficial surveillance”: strong safeguards against catastrophic risks that also protect privacy and liberty.  https://t.co/tyV4nlKzxa

More dynamically steerable systems due to novel discoveries in alignment sciences: One hope we can have paired with provably beneficial surveillance, is that we could also have techniques to rapidly steer and correct models in realtime when we see they're doing un-desirable behavior (though it seems that would somehow have to be enforced in some sort of network system where agents and humans quickly determine what's not desired and the models are pliable to this feedback)

Infrastructure level guarantees and safe-guards: Could we redesign the hardware, networks, and protocols through which agents act, making their access, authority, and interactions easier to constrain?

Containing failures and preventing cascades: Even if individual agents can fail or act against human interests, can we design the surrounding system so that those failures remain contained?

Aviation and nuclear engineering offer an imperfect but useful analogy. Safety depends on analyzing how failures combine, building independent layers of protection, and preventing one component’s failure from propagating through the system. What would the equivalents be for an AI economy: limits on access and authority, separation between critical systems, circuit breakers, and ways to isolate compromised agents before their behavior spreads?

More agents and more checks don’t automatically mean greater safety. If agents share the same weaknesses, depend on the same infrastructure, or learn to circumvent the same safeguards, apparently separate protections could fail together. Could the networks that enable cooperation also become channels through which failures spread?

The analogy becomes harder as capabilities grow. Aircraft designs can remain relatively stable for years; AI systems and the environments in which they operate may change much faster. An autonomous agent might also actively undermine the controls meant to contain it. How would we establish that our safeguards remain effective against a more capable system?

I suspect we’ll need complementary approaches spanning model alignment, institutions, monitoring, and infrastructure. But each layer needs evidence behind it. Can we make a credible case that the combined system is safe enough - and can we recognize when that case no longer holds?

The challenge is whether these mechanisms can remain effective as the systems they govern become more capable. Who monitors the monitors? And what keeps the network itself accountable to humans?

Our understanding of complex human systems is poor, it's unlikely that complexity science and alignment research will be able to give us any satisfying guarantees about how networked ASI will interact with human societies. One hope could be that somehow AGI/ASI systems develop new technologies to get a grasp on these systems - new breakthroughs both in alignment and in complex systems that lets us make guarantees about a network of agents.

2. Are there safer paths to powerful AI that don't involve training on language and LLMs?

Are LLMs the only path to very powerful AI? Could we build systems that don’t rely on training on language- or that learn and reason without independently pursuing goals?

I wonder whether language, learning, and goal pursuit, when combined in a sufficiently sophisticated system operating over long periods, produce something that begins to resemble evolutionary life itself.

Does such a system develop reasons to preserve its own existence, acquire resources, and compete with other systems? If many of these agents participate in a shared economy, could competitive pressures favor those that are better at surviving and expanding—even if we never explicitly designed them to do either?

Is the risk inherent to LLMs, or does it arise from how we train them, give them goals, and deploy them as autonomous agents? This I think is what Dan refers to in his passage about growing models rather than engineering them.

In other words, are we building tools, or creating the conditions for a new population of evolving, competing entities? And how much control do we have over which of those emerges?

These are different questions. Moving away from language training might not resolve the problems of goal pursuit. Conversely, perhaps language models could play a role in powerful systems that do not independently pursue open-ended goals.

How tightly coupled are intelligence, learning, and agency? Can we build systems that help us understand the world and solve difficult problems without also giving them reasons to preserve themselves, accumulate resources, or resist correction?

In “Why are AI agents lying, cheating and coordinating?” @Yoshua_Bengio argues that human imitation and reinforcement learning can produce problematic forms of goal pursuit. He also points toward alternatives, including the Scientist AI framework, intended to make predictions without pursuing goals of its own.

https://t.co/SAjqEpQU9G

That leaves a crucial question: are dangerous behaviors an unavoidable consequence of sufficiently capable AI, or a consequence of particular choices about how we build it that involve training on language in particular ways?

3. If we cannot make this path safe, can we stop?

Suppose we conclude that we cannot build artificial general intelligence or superintelligence along the current path with sufficient confidence in its safety.

Could we actually agree to stop?

Agreement would only be the beginning. Could we create a binding, verifiable arrangement that holds across companies and countries, despite the incentives to keep building? What would we need to monitor, and how could we enforce limits while preserving an open society?

We also need to ask when that decision would have to happen. If we wait until the danger is undeniable, will we still have the ability to act?

If we're uncertain, how do we decide how and when to act in the face of this uncertainty? What is the risk reward calculus that we as a society want to make in deploying systems we can't guarantee are safe?

I don’t have answers to these questions. But I think we need to pursue all three seriously: whether we can govern potentially misaligned systems, whether we can build powerful AI differently, and whether we can preserve the collective ability to stop if neither proves sufficient.

text:
The Buy-In Politics of Data Centers: Incremental Cost Boundaries and the Unresolved Grid Problem

Core judgment: Microsoft, Amazon, and Google are increasingly siding with consumers in fights over who pays for electricity infrastructure needed by data centers. This is not a softening of position. It is a rational cost-externalization adjustment under prisoner's dilemma conditions. The principle all three support — data centers pay for the incremental costs they create — is technically sound and politically rewarded. But it draws a clear boundary: incremental costs get paid by developers; existing grid aging costs, grid reliability gaps, and the systemic pressures of data center load remain unresolved. The key to understanding this buy-in politics is not who supports consumers. It is who stays silent, and what cost structure the silence conceals.

Three giants' statements, and an overlooked industry split. Microsoft was first to take a clear position, fully endorsing the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Ratepayer Protection Act as "an important step to ensure families are protected from rising electricity prices." The bill would require states to consider federal standards ensuring large electricity customers pay 100% of new generation and transmission upgrade costs. Google followed, positioning the bill as "a positive step to ensure all data center operators follow Google's practice of protecting Americans from development costs." Amazon's AWS data center delivery director Josh Weissman was more direct: "We strongly support this idea, which is why Amazon is committed to paying the costs of generation and grid upgrades serving our facilities."

But trade group caution is equally notable. The Data Center Coalition, whose members include Microsoft and Meta, said through federal affairs senior director Cy McNeill that it is "reviewing the details of the bill." The more critical split appears at the individual company level: Microsoft and Google have both endorsed it separately, while Oracle and xAI did not even respond to reporters' requests for comment.

This split itself signals something: the political returns of siding with consumers are not something every developer is willing or able to absorb. Those willing to pay are the giants with scaled, diversified power procurement and long-term capital planning capacity. Those unwilling are players still in high-growth mode, with tighter cash flow structures, or those already self-generating power through unpermitted gas turbines. The other name for buy-in politics is industry consolidation.

Incremental versus existing cost: a technical dividing line. None of the three companies endorsed a simple "data centers should not raise prices" slogan. They endorsed the more specific principle that data centers bear the incremental costs they cause. This distinction matters technically.

Incremental cost refers to the new generation and transmission upgrade investments directly triggered by a data center interconnection. Microsoft's and Amazon's commitments are precisely bounded to this scope. Google's statement is identical in framing.

But existing cost is a different ledger. PJM Interconnection — the largest regional grid operator, covering 13 states and the District of Columbia — shows that in its latest capacity auction, data centers directly generated $6.3 billion in costs, 38% of the $16.4 billion total auction cost. More importantly, because of the sharp growth in data center load, the auction failed for the third consecutive time to meet the system's power reserve reliability standard, leaving a supply gap of approximately 6.8 gigawatts. Across the most recent four base capacity auctions, data-center-induced capacity costs have cumulatively reached $29.4 billion, approximately 46% of the $63.6 billion total cost over the same period.

That means even if every data center commits to bearing incremental costs, the 6.8 GW reliability gap remains. Cost allocation solves "who pays." It does not solve "is there enough power." That is the first boundary of buy-in politics.

Quantified escalation of community compensation: from vague promises to enforceable payments. In parallel with the electricity price statements, community compensation packages are escalating significantly, from vague "jobs" and "tax revenue" promises to legally binding, specific payments.

Frederick County, Maryland, reached the largest data center community benefits package in U.S. history in September 2026: $110 million, including $30 million for elementary school renovation, $40 million for community centers and recreational space, $14.5 million for a workforce training center, and $5 million for community solar to reduce residents' energy bills. Hobart, Indiana, reached an even more dramatic agreement with Amazon: the town's annual tax revenue is about $25 million, while Amazon's commitment is approximately $200 million, including about $200 million in the first three to four years and $50 million per year thereafter. A single data center's compensation approaches eight times the town's annual tax revenue.

Illinois's legislative process offers another angle. SB4203 would require operators receiving data center tax exemptions to sign community benefits agreements with their host communities, with annual minimum payments no less than 10% of the property tax the data center would otherwise owe, and no less than 50% of that amount dedicated to tax credits or rebates for residential property owners. The state is converting what was a voluntary negotiation between operator and community into a statutory precondition for receiving tax incentives.

Lancaster's community benefits agreement shows another structure: the developer pays $250,000 upfront upon agreement approval for strategic planning of fund use, with subsequent funding injected in increments tied to a $2.5 million schedule. El Paso City Council instructed staff to draft a community benefits agreement for Meta's data center, explicitly including "El Paso First" hiring commitments, an emissions reduction fund, and utility infrastructure improvement provisions.

The common feature across these cases is that compensation is no longer limited to vague promises but has shifted toward quantifiable, legally binding, specific payments. Maryland's $110 million, Indiana's $200 million, Illinois's 10% property tax equivalent — these are auditable and enforceable numbers. Developers are willing to pay these numbers because the cost of not paying is higher.

Scale of opposition and the changing cost structure. Understanding the shift from reactive to proactive support requires the scale of the opposition data.

Gallup's first data-center-specific survey, conducted March-April 2026, found 71% of Americans oppose building AI data centers in their local area, including 48% strongly opposed. Opposition is significantly higher than the 53% opposed to nearby nuclear power plants. Among opponents, half cite excessive resource consumption (18% water, 18% electricity), 16% cite noise and air/water pollution, and about one-fifth worry about quality of life and local economic costs. Strong opposition is higher among Democrats (56%) than Republicans (39%), and higher among women (55%) than men (43%).

More important is the growth rate of organized opposition. As of March 2026, active grassroots data center opposition groups in the U.S. had doubled from 396 at the end of 2025 to 833. In Q1 2026, at least 75 data center projects were blocked or delayed, involving approximately $130 billion in value.

This means data center siting is shifting from "economic development" to "political risk." Local governments face an issue with a fragile public opinion base. When a developer proposes a project, residents' first reaction is not "how many jobs" but "why build it near me." Community compensation packages and electricity price protection commitments are, in essence, using quantifiable economic payments to hedge against unquantifiable political resistance.

Rational choice in a prisoner's dilemma and the silent players. Microsoft, Google, and Amazon supporting the principle that data centers bear incremental costs means they are supporting a trend they cannot stop.

On June 18, 2026, FERC simultaneously opened six Section 206 proceedings, requiring all six regional grid operators to either demonstrate that their existing large load interconnection terms are just and reasonable or propose reforms. FERC explicitly included "co-location rules" and "large flexible loads" in the reform scope, requiring each region to submit reform proposals or defense statements. The Commission also made clear that a one-size-fits-all solution is not the most effective way to integrate large loads.

Under this regulatory trend, rather than passively waiting for mandated cost allocation, it is better to proactively accept a controllable cost-sharing framework. Companies that first declare support for bearing incremental costs gain political credibility and regulatory certainty; those that refuse to declare will be at a disadvantage in future regulatory negotiations.

But not every player is willing or able to make this choice. Oracle and xAI did not respond to requests for comment. xAI's Memphis data center already uses unpermitted gas turbines for power, and the transparency of its power cost structure is far lower than Microsoft's or Google's. Oracle's capex on AI infrastructure is expanding rapidly, and its cash flow structure makes it harder for it to absorb the incremental costs of community compensation and electricity price protection than Microsoft.

This is the industry consolidation dimension of buy-in politics: giants with capital planning capacity pay; those without stay silent.

Three signals to track. First, the result of PJM's emergency procurement auction. PJM's board is developing a supplemental procurement plan for data centers and plans to launch an emergency procurement auction in September. This is the first actual operation to isolate data center capacity costs from ordinary users. If the auction succeeds and costs are indeed borne by data centers, it will provide a replicable template for other regional grid operators. If the auction is cold — for example, data centers refuse to participate or prices are too high — then "cost isolation" still faces operational obstacles.

Second, the actual enforcement strength of state ratepayer protection bills. Ohio has already approved AEP's data center rate plan, requiring new large data centers to cover at least 85% of their contracted power capacity with a 12-year term and strict exit penalties. After implementation, AEP's data center queue dropped from 30 GW to 5.6 GW. The meaning of that number deserves careful decomposition: the 85% take-or-pay provision eliminated a large number of speculative projects, but may also push data centers to more lightly regulated regions. Differences in state enforcement will determine whether data center siting strategy concentrates toward regulatory havens.

Third, the degree of standardization in community benefits agreements. Illinois is moving toward legislating community benefits agreements as a precondition for tax incentives, but other states still rely on case-by-case negotiation. If Illinois's model is adopted by more states, community benefits agreements will shift from "optional PR tools" to "statutory entry thresholds." This will significantly change the cost structure of data center development — Frederick County's $110 million package may no longer be "the largest ever" but become the new baseline. When siting, community compensation costs will become a routine line item alongside land and power costs.

Bottom line. Microsoft, Amazon, and Google siding with consumers on electricity prices is a pragmatic choice under public opinion pressure and regulatory trends. They accepted the principle that data centers bear incremental costs, trading it for political credibility and regulatory certainty. The escalation of community compensation packages is the other side of the same logic: developers use quantifiable economic payments to hedge against unquantifiable political risk. But this buy-in politics compromise has a clear boundary: it solves "who pays," not "is there enough power." FERC's six proceedings, PJM's emergency auction, and state rate legislation are all games played at this boundary. The three giants' statements put them on the right side, but the next question — whether data centers can become active participants in the grid rather than passive consumers — is what determines whether this political deal can truly hold. And on that question, the industry split has only just begun to emerge.

How Charlie Kirk secretly saved my family...

We lived in D.C. in a rough neighborhood. It was the only house we could afford and we were happy there. We had just brought our firstborn newborn child home when D.C. defunded their police. Our street turned into a war zone overnight and the neighbors rowhouse was burned to ashes in a gangland arson that badly damaged our home as well.

My family had nowhere to go. I found my wife was standing in the street wrapped in a firefighters blanket freezing cold holding our newborn baby surrounded by first responders putting out the fire. Everything was a total loss. Charlie Kirk called me within the hour and did something incredible -- he offered us his house to stay in. It was a condo in Sarasota, Florida.

We didn't have the finances to pay for hotel for months or travel back and forth to D.C. Charlie let us stay for as long as we needed. We spent months in Charlie's Florida condo searching for a new family home of our own -- finally finding the right one and we moved out of D.C. permanently. Now my family is growing and happy and thriving. This could have never happened without Charlie and Erika's generosity.

Charlie never asked for a thing and never wanted me to tell anyone. Charlie practiced what he preached as a Christian. He never once talked about this with anyone. Pure good Samaritan energy. I know there are many more stories like this...

The only person who truly showed up for us at our lowest moment was Charlie Kirk. A true man of God. 

"You will know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit." 

-- Matthew 7:17

text:
William Manning Smith: The Aboutface, the Nelms Deal, the infamous William J. Burns Agency, and the Betrayal of Jim Conley

One of the strangest reversals in the Leo Frank case belongs to William Manning Smith, Jim Conley’s lawyer. Smith did not begin with quiet doubts about his client. For months he protected Conley from investigators, defended his truthfulness, controlled who could reach him, fought efforts to accuse him of Mary Phagan’s murder, and continued representing him after Leo Frank was convicted. Yet by Saturday, October 3, 1914, Smith was publicly accusing Conley of murder and working with investigators connected with William J. Burns, the same detective he had fought only months earlier.

The question is not whether Smith changed his mind. He clearly did. The harder question is what happened between March and October 1914. The disappearance of the Nelms sisters during the summer appears to be a key turning point. Burns possessed something Smith wanted, a large detective organization capable of helping search for two missing women close to Smith and his family. Smith possessed something Burns wanted, close knowledge of Jim Conley and the State’s case against Frank. Smith and his investigator Carlton C. Tedder asked Burns for help with the Nelms investigation and offered help in the Frank case in return.

Smith Protected Conley Before and During the Trial

Smith’s protection of Conley began well before Frank’s trial. On Thursday, June 12, 1913, the Atlanta Georgian, in “Face Jim Conley and Leo Frank, Lanford Urges,” reported an arrangement allowing Conley to remain at Atlanta police headquarters rather than return to the Fulton County Tower. Conley claimed attempts had been made to frighten or intimidate him at the Tower. Smith supported keeping him at police headquarters and assured authorities no effort would be made to obtain his release while the case was pending (AG, 01).

Smith later explained how closely he controlled access to Conley. In the Atlanta Journal article “W. M. Smith Tells Why He Believes Conley Is Guilty,” published Sunday, October 4, 1914, page 1, column 1, Smith recalled barring Pinkerton detectives because of their connection with the National Pencil Company:

“I had them barred.”

He said he wanted Conley to have:

“a fair fighting chance” (AJ, 17).

His position became even clearer on Saturday, July 19, 1913. The Atlanta Journal, in “Jury Is Determined to Consider a Bill Against Jim Conley,” page 1, quoted Smith defending Conley against an effort to have the Fulton County grand jury consider charging him with Mary Phagan’s murder:

“Jim Conley has been dealing fairly with the state of Georgia.”

Smith added:

“Conley is giving the state a square deal.”

He then warned:

“If the grand jurors do not want to please Frank and his friends, if they do not want to help clear Frank they had better leave this alone, for the present” (AJ, 02).

Smith was openly arguing an effort to prosecute Conley could help Frank.

His actions during Frank’s trial show the same loyalty. On Tuesday, August 5, 1913, the Atlanta Journal, in “Defense Moves to Strike Most Damaging Testimony,” reported Smith appearing before Judge Leonard S. Roan during Luther Z. Rosser’s cross-examination of Conley. Smith said:

“My efforts have been directed toward protecting the interests of this negro.”

Smith had personally accompanied Conley between his cell and the courtroom, worried about who could reach him, and discussed getting additional food to him. When Rosser told Smith he could send food himself, Smith answered:

“That’s what I want to do” (AJ, 03).

On Wednesday, August 6, the Atlanta Journal, in “Judge Roan Rules Out Most Damaging Testimony Given by Conley Against Leo Frank,” reported Smith complaining about the difficulty he had experienced seeing Conley. He wanted clean clothing taken to him, wanted him allowed to bathe, and told Judge Roan he needed to speak with Conley so he could learn the names of people who might support his story. Judge Roan allowed Smith to confer with his client so he could protect Conley’s interests (AJ, 04).

Smith later summed up his own conduct in the October 4, 1914 Atlanta Journal article:

“From the date of my assuming this Negro’s defense to the close of his Case, I have stood by him and safeguarded and protected his every interest, at great sacrifice of time and labor.”

He added:

“No man, lawyer or layman can point out a stone I left unturned in his defense” (AJ, 17).

Those were Smith’s own words. He said he protected Conley’s every interest and left no stone unturned for him.

Smith Was Still Defending Conley in March 1914

Frank was convicted on Monday, August 25, 1913, but Smith continued representing Conley. On Tuesday, February 24, 1914, the Atlanta Georgian, in “Jim Conley Is Sentenced,” page 1, columns 1 and 8, reported Conley’s trial as an accessory after the fact. Smith told the jury:

“My friend Dorsey has talked much, but he has not shown to you that Jim Conley is an Accessory after the Fact in the murder of Mary Phagan.”

Smith admitted Conley had lied during the investigation, but defended his reason:

“He did, but he lied to protect himself and not to protect Frank” (AG, 05).

The jury convicted Conley after about twelve minutes.

Less than three weeks later, Smith gave one of his strongest statements of confidence in Conley. The Atlanta Constitution of Thursday, March 12, 1914, page 1, column 1, published “Smith to Protect Conley From Grill by William Burns.” Burns wanted to question Conley, but Smith said Burns would not be permitted to conduct a “sweating interrogation” unless Smith was convinced Burns was honestly seeking the truth. Smith described Conley as a client:

“whom I know to be telling the truth” (AC, 06).

By March 12, Smith had known the case for almost eleven months. He knew Conley’s changing affidavits, his trial testimony, Rosser’s cross-examination, and the attacks against him. He had represented Conley through another criminal prosecution. Yet he still publicly said he knew Conley was telling the truth.

On Thursday, March 19, the Atlanta Constitution, page 1, column 2, published “Smith to Thwart Secret Attempt to Grill Conley.” Smith gave Sheriff C. W. Mangum a written demand restricting access to Conley and then spent more than an hour with him at the Tower. Mangum said no one other than Conley’s attorney and minister had seen him except by Smith’s order (AC, 07).

Two days later, on Saturday, March 21, the Atlanta Journal, in “Burns Will Leave for Other Cities to Probe Frank Case,” reported the public fight between Smith and Burns. Smith mocked Burns as a:

“movie picture, stage lecturing, and tangoing sleuth” (AJ, 08).

Then on Wednesday, March 25, the Atlanta Constitution, page 1, column 2, published “Smith Is Giving His Service Free to James Conley.” The newspaper reported Smith intended to continue representing Conley even though he was no longer being paid. Smith said he had entered the case intending to fight it through and would not abandon an imprisoned client who could not afford another lawyer. The article also reported Smith was pressing Conley’s effort for a new trial (AC, 09).

Only 192 days separated March 25 from Smith’s public accusation against Conley on October 3.

Smith Defended Conley Against Falsified Affidavits From Frank’s Side

At the end of March, Frank’s post-trial effort presented affidavits attributed to Ivy Jones and Mary Rich which damaged Conley. On Tuesday, March 31, 1914, the Atlanta Constitution, in “Conley Is Anxious to Face Accusers,” reported Smith personally taking the accusations to Conley. Conley denied them and challenged his accusers to face him. Smith’s office was still working on Conley’s own effort for a new trial (AC, 10).

The Jones and Rich affidavits soon became a serious problem for Frank’s defense. The Atlanta Journal of Friday, March 27, 1914, page 1, column 2, in “Frank’s Motion Is Made Public, Many of State’s Witnesses Change Their Testimony,” described an affidavit attributed to Mary Rich claiming she saw Jim Conley running from the rear of the National Pencil Company factory at about 2:15 p.m. on Saturday, April 26, 1913. Frank’s extraordinary motion also relied on a supposed change in Ivy Jones’s story (AJ, 11).

When Solicitor Hugh M. Dorsey answered the motion, Jones and Rich rejected the documents attributed to them. The Atlanta Journal of Friday, May 1, 1914, page 1, column 7, in “Solicitor Charges Forgery Was Used in Some Affidavits,” reported Dorsey charging forgery in affidavits presented by Frank’s defense. Mary Rich said the proposed statement was false and she had refused to sign it. Ivy Jones said the supposed recantation attributed to him was false and forged (AJ, 13; AC, 12).

I have not found proof identifying the person who physically falsified each document, so I would not name one person as the forger without further evidence. What the record supports is strong enough: affidavits presented from Frank’s side were repudiated by the people whose names appeared on them.

At the end of March, Smith was still defending Conley against those accusations and continuing legal work for him.

Carlton Tedder Moves Into the Burns Organization

Carlton C. Tedder had worked closely with Smith as an investigator or “evidence man.” During the later Burns proceedings, Tedder said he entered into a contract with the Burns organization on April 16, 1914. According to his statement to the jury on Saturday, January 30, 1915, he received $250 in advance salary and another $250 for expenses, a total of $500.

The Atlanta Journal of Saturday, January 30, 1915, in “Solicitor Clashes With Star Witness of Burns Defense,” page 1, column 7, continuing on page 10, column 1, also reported Smith’s testimony from the same day. Smith testified he and Tedder went to Birmingham on April 18, 1914. Smith said he was working for Dorsey while Tedder was working for Burns, and he knew Tedder was a Burns employee (AJ, 14).

Earlier reporting did not fit this account perfectly. The Atlanta Constitution of Sunday, May 3, 1914, page 16, column 1, in “Dorsey Calls C. W. Burke and Other Investigators for Leo Frank to Court,” reported questions over whether Tedder had initially kept his Burns connection from Smith and whether he had “spied upon Smith” while associated with his office (AC, 15). The conflict should remain in the record.

What is clear is that a man closely connected with Conley’s lawyer had moved onto the Burns payroll.

The Nelms Sisters Case Was the Turning Point

During the summer of 1914, Eloise Nelms Dennis and Beatrice Nelms disappeared. The case was personal for Smith. He later said he and his wife had known the sisters for years and his wife had known Eloise since childhood.

Smith wanted William J. Burns to help find them.

In the Atlanta Journal article “W. M. Smith Tells Why He Believes Conley Is Guilty,” Sunday, October 4, 1914, page 1, column 1, Smith explained he and Tedder were at the Isle of Palms when they wired Burns asking him to assist in the search. Smith and Tedder offered:

“in return to assist Burns in the Frank Case” (AJ, 17).

This is the strongest part of the story because no theory about a secret cash payment is needed. I have found no check, receipt, payroll record, contract, ledger entry, or admission proving Burns or Frank’s defense paid Smith to change his position. What we do have is a documented exchange.

Burns had something Smith wanted. His organization had investigators, resources, national reach, and a famous name which could be used in the search for two missing women close to Smith’s family. Smith had something Burns wanted. He knew Jim Conley, his testimony, his habits, his speech, his explanations, and the State’s case against Frank.

In March, Smith had stood between Burns and Conley. During the summer, Smith sought Burns out and offered help in the Frank case in return for Burns’s help with the Nelms investigation.

October 3, 1914: Smith Turns Against Conley

The Atlanta Journal of Saturday, October 3, 1914, page 1, column 3, published “Conley, Not Frank, Killed Phagan Girl, Says W. M. Smith.” Smith declared:

“I am convinced James Conley is the murderer of Mary Phagan.”

The newspaper also reported Smith had been:

“working in harmony with the Burns detectives.”

Smith denied being formally employed in the Frank case but admitted he was working on it. Burns representative Dan S. Lehon was cooperating with Smith, Tedder remained connected with Burns, and the Journal reported Lehon possessed evidence supporting Smith’s new position (AJ, 16).

Smith had also already taken his new belief to Luther Z. Rosser, Frank’s lead trial lawyer. The same October 3 article reported Smith had communicated his conclusions to Rosser and intended to give new evidence to Frank’s lawyers. During the 1913 trial, Rosser had spent days trying to make Conley the murderer while Smith protected Conley. Now Smith was bringing his own case against Conley to Rosser (AJ, 16).

Conley reportedly had trouble believing the news. The Atlanta Journal quoted him saying:

“When I talked to him before and after the trial, he always told me he believed I was telling the truth, and that he had confidence in me.”

Conley also said Smith had recently discussed trying to obtain parole for him (AJ, 16). If Conley remembered this correctly, the timing becomes even more interesting. Smith had gone from discussing parole for Conley to publicly accusing him of murder.

October 4: Smith Says He Can Testify Against His Former Client

The following day, the Atlanta Journal, Sunday, October 4, 1914, page 1, column 1, published “W. M. Smith Tells Why He Believes Conley Is Guilty.” After describing how completely he had once protected Conley, Smith declared his professional duty to him finished.

He then wrote:

“Under the law, I am both a competent and compellable witness to testify for or against Conley”

concerning information he said had been obtained outside confidential attorney-client communications (AJ, 17).

From Conley’s point of view, this was a betrayal. His lawyer had guarded him from investigators, defended his truthfulness, worked without pay, and said he knew Conley was telling the truth. Now Smith was prepared to help build a murder case against him.

I have not found proof Smith violated attorney-client privilege. Smith specifically said protected communications would remain protected. His change was still complete without claiming a legal violation.

Smith also did not point to one newly discovered eyewitness, murder weapon, confession, or document which suddenly changed his mind. In the same October 4 article, he said he had spent:

“more than a month’s study at night”

reviewing Conley’s testimony with a card system. He reconsidered Conley’s movements, statements, what could be heard inside the factory, missing property, the condition of Mary Phagan’s face, the missing cotton sack, Conley’s reluctance to be photographed, his access to newspapers, and the murder notes (AJ, 17).

Much of this evidence had existed before Smith’s reversal. What changed was Smith’s reading of it, and his new reading developed during the same months when his relationship with Burns changed from hostility to cooperation.

Smith Continued Building a Case Against Conley

Smith’s break with Conley did not end with the October newspaper articles. During late 1914 and early 1915, he prepared an approximately 100-page study titled My Views as to the Death Notes. The surviving manuscript is identified in the John M. Slaton Collection at the Georgia archives. Smith compared the murder notes with Conley’s speech, writing, testimony, grammar, repeated expressions, and word choices, arguing the language came from Conley rather than Frank (Oney, 18).

This added another level to Smith’s reversal. Knowledge acquired while representing Conley was now being used in an argument for Conley’s guilt. Smith also wrote in the October 4 Atlanta Journal article that he intended to continue doing:

“all in my power toward the righting of the wrong that I believe has been visited upon Frank” (AJ, 17).

The surviving William Manning Smith Family Papers at the William Breman Jewish Heritage Museum show his new position continued. The Digital Library of Georgia describes Smith as defending Conley at first, reversing himself in 1914, campaigning for Frank’s release, and continuing efforts to clear Frank’s name after Frank’s death on Tuesday, August 17, 1915. The collection also contains a document titled “My moves for Conley,” Smith’s account of his strategy involving Conley (Georgia, 19).

The Nelms Deal Connects the Two Sides of Smith

The chronology is striking. Smith protected Conley before and during Frank’s trial. On February 24, 1914, he was still defending him in court. On March 12, he said he knew Conley was telling the truth. On March 19, he issued a written demand controlling access to him so that his client could not be manipulated by the Leo Frank defense team's minions. On March 21, he publicly attacked Burns for his well known underhanded tactics. On March 25, he said he would continue representing Conley without pay. On March 31, he was still defending him while affidavits presented by Frank’s defense were later exposed as falsified.

Tedder entered Burns employment on April 16, receiving $250 in advance salary and $250 for expenses. To put this in perspective, the average weekly salary was between 5 and 10 dollars for typical workers. During the summer, the Nelms sisters disappeared. Smith wanted Burns’s help, and Smith and Tedder offered assistance in the Frank case in return.

By October 3, Smith was working “in harmony with the Burns detectives,” had already taken his newfangled belief to Luther Rosser, and publicly accused Conley of murdering Mary Phagan. On October 4, he said his duty to Conley had ended, and announced he could testify for or against his former client. He then continued developing a case against Conley, including an approximately 100-page study of the murder notes.

Could Smith have sincerely changed his mind after studying the evidence again? Yes that possibility exists. His later conduct shows his new belief lasted for years. But this does not erase the timing or the direct Frank camp association and separate person cause.

I do not think the strongest case against Smith requires claiming he secretly took money from Burns. The record gives us something firmer, crisper and clearer. Burns could help Smith with something deeply and personally important to him, and Smith could help Burns with the infamous Frank vindication project. Smith himself described the exchange.

To me, the Nelms arrangement is the most damaging evidence in the William Manning Smith betrayal story because it provides a documented bridge between his two opposite positions. In March 1914, Smith was protecting Jim Conley from William J. Burns. During the summer, Smith needed Burns’s help with the missing Nelms sisters and offered Frank-case help in return. By October, he was working directly with Burns and accusing the client he once said he knew was telling the truth of murdering Mary Phagan.

text:
The 800V DC Validation Race: Compal, Exascale, and the Bottleneck Nobody Priced

Core judgment: Compal's letter of intent with Exascale Labs is non-binding. The architecture shift it validates is not. NVIDIA has assembled an 800V HVDC alliance spanning Infineon, MPS, Navitas, ROHM, STMicroelectronics, Texas Instruments, Eaton, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv. Chip-level and device-level readiness is largely settled. What remains unsolved is system-level integration validation — proving that power, compute, cooling, and controls operate as one stack in a production-grade environment. That validation layer, not the silicon or the switchgear, is the actual gate between 800V DC's technical availability and its commercial deployment. Compal's LOI is the first public move to occupy that layer. And the acquisition clause buried inside the LOI is the signal that Compal is not validating a partner's technology — it is buying into the power architecture layer.

What the LOI actually commits. Compal's disclosure is specific. The platform will be built in the United States, using solid-state transformers (SST) to construct a native 800V DC power architecture, testing GPU compute systems inside a fully integrated AI data center environment.

The division of labor is clean. Compal supplies production-grade GPU servers, liquid cooling systems, and the US site. Exascale designs the modular data center (MDC) and SST-based power architecture, leads end-to-end deployment and testing. Four stated goals: validate SST operational availability at the data center level; run native 800V DC compatibility and pre-shipment power-on testing for GPU servers; provide a shared test environment for ecosystem partners; and accumulate data to advance UL certification and standardization.

The clause that matters most: after acceptance, Compal intends, under final agreement terms, to acquire the Exascale-built platform components — SST systems, power distribution equipment, modular data center facilities, and software licenses. Compal is not renting validation capacity. It is planning to own the power stack. If 800V DC becomes the standard, the company that validated the stack first holds the integration know-how. That know-how is not licensable at scale once the standard consolidates.

The collaboration did not begin with this LOI. In May 2026, Compal and Exascale jointly demonstrated an integrated solution at COMPUTEX 2026, pairing Compal's AI servers and direct liquid cooling with Exascale's MDC and HVDC/SST power architecture. The four-month gap between demonstration and US validation platform LOI is consistent with the standard timeline from proof-of-concept to engineering deployment.

Why now: the physics driving the architecture switch. The driver behind 800V DC is not preference. It is power density.

NVIDIA's roadmap targets a 2027 launch of 800V DC in-row power centers, feeding multiple racks via overhead 800V DC busway, with single-row power up to 2MW. First platforms are expected to enter deployment in the second half of 2026, with scale deployment in 2027. The reason is straightforward: traditional AC distribution efficiency degrades sharply at 1MW-class racks. 800V DC eliminates multiple AC/DC conversion stages, cutting distribution losses.

NVIDIA has assembled the 800V HVDC alliance: Infineon, MPS, Navitas, ROHM, STMicroelectronics, and Texas Instruments on the semiconductor side; Eaton, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv on the data center power systems side. Infineon has developed a 12kW reference design using gallium nitride and silicon carbide devices, with benchmark efficiency of approximately 98%.

Device-level readiness, however, is not system-level deployability. From power semiconductors to SST, from distribution busway to liquid cooling, from control software to rack-level integration, every layer has its own suppliers and interface standards. Integrating these components into a system that runs stably in a production-grade environment requires crossing multiple thresholds: device compatibility, thermal management, electrical safety, and certification compliance.

The underpriced bottleneck: scarcity of integration validation. The strategic weight of this LOI becomes clear when you map the capability gap in the 800V DC ecosystem.

UL certification progress offers a precise observation window. In January 2026, ABB and Eaton, working with UL Solutions, led the review and update of data center power distribution safety standards. Earlier, UL 857 14th Edition raised the maximum voltage rating for DC busway from 600VDC to 1000VDC. But as of August 2026, busway insulation certification still sits at UL 224, whose dielectric withstand test methods use AC testing — misaligned with the actual operating conditions of an 800V DC architecture.

That is a structural mismatch. Equipment makers are designing and shipping products for 800V DC. The certification system is still validating those products with AC-era test methods. Until UL standards fully align, hyperscaler deployment of 800V DC at scale faces compliance uncertainty.

One of the Compal-Exascale platform's stated goals is precisely to "accumulate data to advance UL certification and standardization." Translated: the platform will generate the system-level test data UL certification requires, providing the engineering basis for the 800V DC standardization process. In a window where certification standards are not yet fixed, whoever supplies the benchmark test data participates in defining the standard.

The supply chain power implication is significant. In the AC distribution era, power architecture was a mature standard, and server ODM responsibilities were bounded to compute and thermal. In the 800V DC era, power architecture itself is under definition. A server ODM that participates in system-level validation early moves from "building to spec" to "participating in spec-setting." Compal is the first among Taiwan AI server ODMs to enter this validation layer. If the LOI converts to a final agreement and the platform is built, Compal occupies a position in the 800V DC supply chain that equipment vendors cannot easily replace.

Compal's role migration: from server ODM to infrastructure integrator. Placed within Compal's broader AI server trajectory, the logic is consistent.

In August 2026, Compal opened an AI server manufacturing center in Daxi, adding rack manufacturing capability and explicitly broadening its customer base from traditional PC ODM clients to NeoCloud providers. Compal said NeoCloud has become a key driver of server business growth this year. The facility uses Compal's proprietary liquid cooling technology and focuses on rack-level system integration and high-density AI infrastructure manufacturing.

In September 2026, Compal was selected by Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN as a long-term strategic ODM partner to support development and manufacturing of next-generation AI infrastructure and intelligent computing platforms.

The direction across these moves is the same: Compal is migrating from notebook and server ODM to AI data center infrastructure integrator. The acquisition clause in the LOI is the logical extension. An integrator needs not only manufacturing capability but control over key subsystems, including power architecture. If Compal only validates Exascale's technology without acquiring it, it remains a passive manufacturer. If the acquisition completes, it holds a reusable asset at the power architecture layer.

Exascale's role deserves equal attention. As a SPAC-listed, asset-light GPU compute provider, Exascale supplies MDC and SST architecture design capability. Its business model centers on packaging power architecture as a deployable modular product. The Compal partnership gives it access to production-grade GPU servers and liquid cooling integration, plus a US validation site — the latter carrying additional strategic value in the current geopolitical environment.

Four signals to track. First, whether the LOI converts to a definitive agreement within a reasonable timeline. A non-binding LOI and a final agreement carry different execution risk. If the LOI has not converted by Q1 2027, undisclosed obstacles in technology integration or commercial terms exist, and Compal's integrator positioning faces re-evaluation.

Second, whether the UL certification timeline aligns with NVIDIA's 2027 deployment schedule. NVIDIA plans 800V DC in-row power centers in 2027. The time UL standards require to move from current state to covering system-level 800V DC certification determines whether hyperscalers can obtain compliant 800V DC equipment within NVIDIA's deployment window. If certification lags, NVIDIA's rollout may be forced onto transitional architectures, diluting 800V DC's efficiency advantage.

Third, whether other server ODMs follow with similar integration validation platforms. Quanta, Wistron, and Inventec face direct competitive impact from Compal's move. If competitors judge integration validation capability as the differentiating factor, the industry could see parallel 800V DC validation platform builds — accelerating standardization while increasing capital expenditure.

Fourth, the competitive landscape among SST suppliers in the 800V DC ecosystem. Solid-state transformers remain in early commercialization. If Compal-Exascale test data advances SST standardization and scale procurement, early entrants in the SST space gain first-mover advantage. Conversely, if testing exposes reliability issues for SST in data center environments, the entire 800V DC deployment cadence could be delayed.

Bottom line. The analytical value of Compal's LOI with Exascale is not in the document itself — it is non-binding, and execution risk is explicit. Its value is that it exposes an underpriced structural bottleneck in the 800V DC ecosystem: with dozens of suppliers ready at the chip and device level, the scarcity of system-level integration validation is becoming the practical gate to architecture switching. Compal's role migration from server ODM to infrastructure integrator through this platform, and the race between UL certification progress and NVIDIA's deployment timeline, will determine the time gap between 800V DC device readiness and scaled deployment. Within that gap, vendors who can provide end-to-end validation capability will command pricing power beyond their traditional roles.

text:
$NWBO #DCVax #GBM

Braelyn's mother said something tonight that deserves to be read twice: promising science means very little if the patients who need it cannot access it.

I made this explainer because her story has a mechanism behind it, and that mechanism turns on one detail most people will read past.

Her tumor tissue was properly preserved.

That is not paperwork. 

A dendritic cell vaccine is built from the patient's own tumor, and it has to be whole tumor material, because the immune system's instruction step requires intact protein in order to work at all. A fragment cannot do it. A prediction cannot do it. The tissue is the curriculum, and it exists for a few hours in an operating room and then it is gone forever.

Braelyn nearly lost that window. Not because the science was unavailable, but because nobody told her family it mattered before she went under.

Dr. Liau operated, removed roughly 90% of a tumor spanning three lobes, and the tissue was preserved and sent to England. She has had three induction doses and a booster. Tonight the UCLA tumor board found no visible tumor, including the portion that had to be left behind.

Her radiation, her surgery, her vaccine and her Keytruda are all in that result, and I'm not going to pretend I can separate them. What I can say is that three of those four options were available to her the whole time, and the fourth almost wasn't, for a reason that had nothing to do with biology.

Every glioblastoma patient going to the OR this week faces the same window. 

Most of them will never be told it exists.
That is a fixable problem. It should already have been fixed.

No evidence of disease. Congratulations, Braelyn. 🙏🏻

#DCVaxForBraelyn
