text:
Pincher Martin (@PincherMartin8), you write:

“You don't know that the rape and murder took place there.”

No eyewitness stood inside the large machine department at the rear of the second floor of the National Pencil Company, 37–41 South Forsyth Street in Atlanta, Georgia, shortly after noon on Saturday, April 26, 1913, and watched every second of Mary Phagan’s assault and murder.

But no eyewitness to every second of the crime does not mean no evidence existed.

There was Jim Conley’s sworn testimony about Frank wanting to “be with” Mary, a euphemism for sexual intimacy, Mary refusing him, and Frank striking her. She fell backward and hit her head on the handle of the lathe, where hair was found tangled. Blood was found on the floor of the machine department. There was evidence placing Mary in the large machine department at the rear of the second floor. There was blood on her underclothing. Her drawers were cut or torn open. One stocking supporter was broken. Her outer dress was reported torn and bloodstained. Phagan family oral history has long remembered Mary’s outer dress as cut or torn up the center from the hem toward the crotch.

Dr. J. W. Hurt found blood on the drawers and genital area. Dr. Henry F. Harris later examined tissue under a microscope and found signs of violence near the hymen shortly before death.

There was also a large amount of testimony about Leo Frank’s conduct toward women and girls before Mary was killed. Some of it went before the murder jury. Some came out during the coroner’s inquest. Judge Leonard S. Roan kept some specific stories from the jury because of the rules controlling character evidence.

Hugh Dorsey later put these parts of the case together before the jury. He pointed to Mary’s damaged and bloody clothing, called her a “ravished girl,” and argued Frank had sexually attacked her.

The record becomes much clearer when the events are put back into their dates.

Recollecting back in time about two years to March 1911: Nellie Wood says Frank made an unwanted advance

Nellie Wood said she worked at the National Pencil Company for only two days around March 1911, a little more than two years before Mary Phagan was killed.

Wood told her story under oath during Coroner Paul V. Donehoo’s inquest on Thursday, May 8, 1913.

The Georgia Supreme Court record in Leo M. Frank v. State of Georgia preserves her account. Wood said Frank called her into his private office, had her sit down, became too familiar with her, and tried to touch her breast and lower limbs and dress. She said she resisted him and soon quit working at the factory.

The Atlanta Georgian reported her story the next day, Friday, May 9, 1913, in its coverage of the final session of the coroner’s jury. The newspaper gave the same basic office story.

Wood later called the encounter an “indecent proposal.”

In plain English, this meant an improper sexual offer.

Her accusation was part of the official investigation months before Frank was convicted.  

Wood returned during the murder trial on Wednesday, August 20, 1913. The Atlanta Georgian reported Dorsey tried to bring the full office incident before the jury, but Judge Roan stopped him.

Roan allowed general character evidence but would not let the State prove bad character by listing every separate claimed sexual act.

Roan ruled on what the jury was allowed to hear. He did not rule Wood’s story true or false.

More than a year before May 1913: Robert House and Druid Hills Park

Robert F. House was a special policeman for the Druid Hills Land Company.

On Saturday, May 10, 1913, House gave investigators a sworn statement about an event he said happened more than a year earlier.

The Atlanta Georgian, Sunday, May 11, 1913, published his story under the headline “Caught Frank With Girl in Park, He Says.”

House said a man he later identified as Frank had gone into Druid Hills Park with a young woman shortly after 2 o’clock in the afternoon.

House said he followed them into a secluded area and ordered the man away.

He later went to the Fulton County jail and identified Frank as the man he remembered.

This was an accusation given to investigators, not a separate criminal conviction, but it was part of the May 1913 investigation.

Summer 1912: Irene Jackson and Mamie Kitchens describe the ladies’ dressing room

Irene Jackson was called as a witness by Frank’s own defense.

She testified on Saturday, August 16, 1913.

The Atlanta Journal, Saturday, August 16, 1913, in the article “Witness, Called by Defense, Testifies Against Frank,” reported Jackson saying Frank had opened the ladies’ dressing-room door while women were changing during about summer 1912.

One of the women was Emily Mayfield, who was partly dressed.

Jackson described other times when Frank opened the dressing-room door without knocking.

Mamie Kitchens gave another account.

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence says Kitchens was in the fourth-floor dressing room with Irene Jackson while Jackson was changing. Kitchens said Frank opened the door without knocking and looked inside.

On cross-examination, Kitchens said the event happened during working hours and Frank asked why they were not working. She also said she had never met Frank for an immoral purpose.

The defense gave another reason for Frank being around the dressing room. Girls had reportedly been flirting through a window, and Frank said he was trying to stop it.

Frank directly denied an improper purpose in his statement to the jury on Monday, August 18, 1913.

The Atlanta Constitution, Tuesday, August 19, 1913, in its coverage of Frank’s statement, quoted him saying:

“I never peered into the girls’ dressing rooms.”

Frank said he was trying to stop girls from flirting through the windows.

The jury heard both sides.

February and March 1913: Dewey Hewell says Frank knew Mary and approached her often

Dewey Hewell worked at the National Pencil Company during February and March 1913.

She testified on Wednesday, August 20, 1913.

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence records Hewell saying Frank talked with Mary Phagan two or three times a day in the rear working room.

The old court record calls it the “metal department.” It was the large machine department at the rear of the second floor.

Hewell said Frank called Mary by her first name, stood close to her, leaned toward her face, and put a hand on her shoulder.

She admitted other girls were around and said she did not know what Frank and Mary were discussing.

Her testimony did not prove a sexual act, but it did show Frank knew Mary and approached her often.

Around mid-March 1913: Will Turner says Mary backed away from Frank

Will Turner, a teenage former factory worker, described another event from around mid-March 1913, about six weeks before Mary was killed.

The Atlanta Journal, Tuesday, August 19, 1913, reported Turner saying he entered the rear machine department around the noon period and saw Mary backing away from Frank.

According to the newspaper, Mary said she needed to get back to work.

Turner said Frank kept moving toward her and estimated Mary backed away several feet.

The defense argued an ordinary conversation between a superintendent and an employee was being made to look improper.

Judge Roan allowed the basic story into evidence.

The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, August 20, 1913, also reported Dorsey arguing this earlier event could have been the beginning of the chain leading to Mary’s death. Frank’s lawyers said it showed nothing more than an ordinary conversation.

March and early April 1913: Nellie Pettis and “How about it?”

Nellie Pettis was sixteen years old.

Her sister-in-law, Lillie Mae Pettis, worked at the National Pencil Company.

Nellie said she went to the factory several Saturdays to collect her sister-in-law’s wages. These visits appear to have happened during March and early April 1913.

At the coroner’s inquest on Thursday, May 8, 1913, Pettis said Frank looked at her, handled money, winked, and asked:

“How about it?”

The Atlanta Georgian, Friday, May 9, 1913, reported this testimony from the final inquest session.

Pettis also said she had seen Frank flirt with girls and women.

Her story later became disputed.

The Atlanta Journal, Sunday, March 15, 1914, printed affidavits involving Nellie Pettis and Lillie Mae Pettis.

Nellie stood by her account.

Lillie Mae challenged parts of it.

Saturday, April 26, 1913: Mary Phagan enters the National Pencil Company

Mary Phagan went to the National Pencil Company on Saturday, April 26, 1913, to collect $1.20 in wages.

She had eaten cabbage and bread at about 11:30 a.m.

Frank later placed Mary in his office at about 12:05 to 12:10 p.m.

The large machine department was at the rear of the second floor.

Mary’s machine was there.

The ladies’ dressing room was there.

The toilet area was there.

Grace Hix pointed these areas out on the factory diagram during the trial on Wednesday, July 30, 1913, as reported by The Atlanta Journal that same day.

This rear area became important because Conley later placed Mary, Frank, and Mary’s body there.

Early Sunday morning, April 27, 1913: Mary’s damaged clothing

William H. Gheesling worked for P. J. Bloomfield’s undertaking establishment.

He removed Mary’s body from the factory at about 3:50 a.m. on Sunday, April 27, 1913.

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence describes blood and urine on Mary’s underclothing and says the right leg of the drawers had been cut or torn upward along the seam.

Gheesling could not say for sure whether someone used a knife or ripped the cloth.

The garment had been opened.

W. W. “Boots” Rogers was among the men who saw Mary’s body early Sunday morning.

The Atlanta Journal, Wednesday, July 30, 1913, reported damage to Mary’s undergarments and a broken stocking supporter.

A stocking supporter was part of the clothing used to hold up a stocking.

The blood and urine on the drawers, the opened seam, the damaged undergarments, and the broken stocking supporter were separate parts of the clothing evidence.

Contemporary newspaper reports also described Mary’s lavender outer dress as torn and bloodstained.

Phagan family oral history has long remembered Mary’s outer dress as cut or torn up the center from the hem toward the crotch.

Sunday morning, April 27, 1913: Dr. J. W. Hurt examines Mary

Fulton County physician Dr. John W. Hurt examined Mary at about 9 o’clock Sunday morning, April 27, 1913, at P. J. Bloomfield’s undertaking establishment on South Pryor Street.

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence records Hurt finding blood on the drawers and genital area.

He found the hymen was not intact.

The hymen is a thin rim of tissue near the opening of the vagina.

Hurt said the condition he saw could have been caused by penetration shortly before death.

But Hurt stopped short of saying rape had been proved.

He said there were no clear outward signs from which he could say rape had happened and he could not say when the hymen had been damaged.

Wednesday, April 30 through Thursday, May 8, 1913: the coroner’s inquest

Coroner Paul V. Donehoo opened the inquest on Wednesday, April 30, 1913.

A coroner’s inquest was a legal hearing held to find out how someone died and whether anyone should be held for more investigation.

The hearings continued through Thursday, May 8, 1913.

Police officers, factory workers, doctors, Newt Lee, Leo Frank, Nellie Wood, Nellie Pettis, and others testified.

The coroner’s jury found Mary died from strangulation and recommended Frank and Lee be held for more investigation.

Monday, May 5, 1913: Dr. Henry F. Harris

Dr. Henry Frederick Harris, Secretary of the Georgia State Board of Health, examined Mary on Monday, May 5, 1913.

Harris studied tissue under a microscope.

He found no sperm cells.

He also found tissue lining the vaginal wall pulled loose and fully detached in places.

The medical word for this surface tissue is epithelium.

Harris found widened blood vessels and bleeding inside the surrounding tissue.

The medical word for bleeding into tissue is hemorrhage.

Harris believed these injuries happened while Mary was still alive.

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence records him finding evidence of violence near the hymen shortly before death.

Harris admitted a finger or another object could have caused the injury.

His finding was medical evidence of violence to Mary’s genital area shortly before she died.

Friday, August 1, 1913: Harris tells the jury

Harris testified for the State on Friday afternoon, August 1, 1913.

The Atlanta Journal, Saturday, August 2, 1913, in the article “Dr. Harris Collapses on Stand as He Gives Sensational Evidence,” reported his medical findings.

Harris said the blow to Mary’s head could have knocked her unconscious but did not kill her. In his opinion, she died from strangulation.

The newspaper and official court record both placed the genital injury shortly before death, although their time estimates were not exactly the same.

Dr. John Funke later examined Harris’s tissue samples.

The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, August 20, 1913, reported Funke agreed there were signs of violence in the tissue, although he was more careful about some of Harris’s timing claims.

Monday and Tuesday, August 4 and 5, 1913: Jim Conley

The Atlanta Journal, Monday, August 4, 1913, ran the headline “Jim Conley Tells an Amazing Story.”

Conley said Mary went upstairs and later moved toward the rear working area.

He said Frank sent him back to get Mary.

According to Conley, he found her lying on her back with a cord around her neck near the rear toilet area.

Conley said he later looked at the factory clock and saw about 12:56 p.m.

During Luther Rosser’s cross-examination on Tuesday, August 5, 1913, The Atlanta Journal reported Conley attributing these words to Frank:

“I wanted to be with her, and she refused me... I struck her and struck her too hard.”

Conley’s account gave the State a sexual purpose, Mary’s refusal, a blow, and the rear machine-department location.

Frank’s lawyers called Conley a liar. Conley admitted to lying, he said he was protecting himself and Leo Frank. He though Leo Frank would honor his promise to bond him out, but once he realized that wasn't happening he decided to reveal some of the events that occurred little by little. 

Thursday and Friday, August 7 and 8, 1913: Dalton and Hopkins

The Atlanta Journal, Thursday, August 7, 1913, reported C. B. Dalton saying he had visited the factory with Daisy Hopkins and describing women visiting Frank’s office. Dalton also said Conley was present. Dalton testified that Frank's office was used to dispatch a prostitute for him to go down to the basement. 

Daisy Hopkins testified the next day.

The Atlanta Journal, Friday, August 8, 1913, reported Hopkins denying Dalton’s story.

Conley also claimed Frank sometimes had him watch the front door while women were upstairs.

The defense called these stories lies.

Rosser later attacked both Dalton and Conley during his closing argument on Friday, August 22, 1913, as reported by The Atlanta Journal.

Wednesday, August 20, 1913: ten women and Frank’s character for lasciviousness

The old legal word used in court was lasciviousness.

In plain English, it meant a reputation for improper sexual behavior or improper sexual interest in women.

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence lists ten women together:

Myrtie Cato, Maggie Griffin, Mrs. C. D. Donegan, Mrs. H. R. Johnson, Marie Carst, Nellie Pettis, Mary Davis, Mrs. Mary E. Wallace, Estelle Winkle, and Carrie Smith.

The court record says they had worked at the factory from three days to three and one-half years.

It then says:

“Leo M. Frank’s character for lasciviousness was bad.”

The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, August 20, 1913, ran the heading:

“WOMEN ARRAIGN FRANK’S MORALS.”

The newspaper gives more detail than the short court summary.

Maggie Griffin, Myrtie Cato, Marie Karst, Nellie Pettis, and Mary E. Wallace gave bad-character testimony.

The court record gives the ten women as a group. The newspaper gives more of their individual answers.

Myrtie Cato, Maggie Griffin, and Rebecca Carson

The Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence also records Cato and Griffin saying they had seen Frank enter the fourth-floor ladies’ dressing room with forelady Rebecca Carson on several occasions.

Carson denied it.

The jury heard both versions.

The ten women were only part of the character case

The ten women were not the whole State case about Frank’s conduct toward women was relevant to his nature as a sexual predator.

Nellie Wood described the private-office incident.

Robert House gave the Druid Hills story.

Irene Jackson and Mamie Kitchens described the dressing-room incidents.

Dewey Hewell described Frank approaching Mary.

Will Turner said Mary backed away from Frank.

Nellie Pettis described the “How about it?” encounter.

Dalton and Conley made more claims about women visiting the factory.

Hopkins, Carson, and Frank denied important parts of these stories.

Friday, August 22 through Monday, August 25, 1913: Dorsey puts the case together

Hugh M. Dorsey began his closing argument at about 3:30 p.m. on Friday, August 22, 1913.

He continued on Saturday, August 23, and finished on Monday, August 25, 1913.

The Atlanta Georgian, Sunday, August 24, 1913, in “Dorsey Demands Death Penalty for Frank in Thrilling Closing Plea,” reported Dorsey arguing Mary rejected Frank’s sexual advance.

Dorsey argued Frank struck her, knocked her unconscious, sexually attacked her, and strangled her.

He held Mary’s bloody clothing before the jury.

The Georgian reported him calling Mary a:

“ravished girl.”

“Ravished” was an old word for rape or forced sexual attack.

Dorsey accused Frank directly:

“You ravished her.”

The Atlanta Journal, Saturday, August 23, 1913, in “Frank Trial Adjourned Until Monday Morning,” also reported Dorsey pointing to Mary’s torn garments and stockings as part of his rape argument.

The clothing evidence, Hurt’s findings, Harris’s tissue evidence, Conley’s testimony, and the rear machine-department location were all part of Dorsey’s final argument.

1914: later examination of Mary’s clothing

During the 1914 post-trial proceedings, detective William J. Burns examined clothing connected with Mary’s body.

The later Georgia Supreme Court appeal record described severe cuts in the drawers, including damage through the crotch area, and cuts in the knitted undershirt.

This added more detail to the earlier accounts of damaged underclothing.

Phagan family oral history has also long remembered Mary’s outer dress as ripped, cut or torn up the center from the hem toward the private parts. My ancestors were present during the trial.

Tuesday, February 17, 1914: Georgia Supreme Court

Frank challenged the verdict.

On Tuesday, February 17, 1914, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction 4–2. None of the judges stated the evidence was insufficient. They were not retrying the case, the tribunal ruled the trial evidence sufficiently sustained the conviction. 

The Atlanta Journal, Tuesday, February 17, 1914, in “Leo Frank Fails to Get New Trial, Conley’s Testimony Is Held Valid,” reported the majority held the State could answer Frank’s good-character evidence with testimony about his bad character for lasciviousness.

The court also allowed some earlier sexual-conduct evidence involving Conley and Dalton.

Chief Justice William H. Fish and Justice Marcus W. Beck disagreed with part of this evidence and believed some of it should not have gone before the jury.

June 1915: Dorsey says the women supplied motive

During the clemency hearing in June 1915, Dorsey again pointed to the women who testified about Frank’s sexual character.

The Atlanta Constitution, Tuesday, June 15, 1915, reported Dorsey arguing Frank’s lasciviousness supplied a motive for the crime.

He did not treat the women as a side issue.

He tied their evidence to motive.

Monday, June 21, 1915: Slaton reviews the evidence

Governor John M. Slaton issued his commutation decision on Monday, June 21, 1915.

Slaton did not exonerate Frank. He stated he was sustaining the jury, trial judge, and appellate courts.

The Atlanta Journal, Monday, June 21, 1915, in its coverage of Slaton’s reasons for commuting Frank’s sentence, reported the review of Mary’s damaged drawers and the blood and urine on them.

Slaton also repeated Dr. Hurt’s more careful position. 

Hurt would not say the outward signs alone proved rape or not. 

The appearance sure sounded like it. Why would the underwear be torn open over the private parts, while kept around the child's hips?

What the record shows

Pincher Martin, when you write:

“You don't know that the rape and murder took place there,”

the statement leaves out a large part of the record.

Mary entered the factory shortly after noon on Saturday, April 26, 1913.

The rear machine department contained Mary’s machine, the ladies’ dressing room, and the toilet area.

Conley placed the encounter there and told the jury Frank said:

“I wanted to be with her, and she refused me... I struck her and struck her too hard.”

Mary’s underclothing was damaged. There was blood and urine on the drawers. A stocking supporter was broken. Her outer dress was reported torn and bloodstained. Phagan family oral history remembers the outer dress as cut or torn up the center petty coat from the hem toward the private parts that piece was torn off and used to soak the blood coming out of the back of Mary's head and use to wrap around her neck partially.

Hurt found blood on the drawers and genital area but would not say rape had been proved or not because he only made an external observation. He conducted no microscopic examination of tissues. 

Only Harris performed a microscopic examination of tissues.

Harris later found tissue damage, widened blood vessels, bleeding into the tissue, and signs of violence near the hymen shortly before death.

Then there was the evidence about Frank’s conduct toward women.

Wood, House, Jackson, Kitchens, Hewell, Turner, Pettis, Dalton, Conley, Cato, Griffin, and others supplied different parts of this evidence. Some stories were denied. Some were limited by Judge Roan.

On Wednesday, August 20, 1913, the official court record listed ten women and recorded:

“Leo M. Frank’s character for lasciviousness was bad.”

Dorsey then stood before the jury, argued Mary refused Frank, pointed to the clothing and medical evidence, called Mary a sexually assaulted child and said:

“You ravished her.”

No eyewitness watched every second of the crime.

But there was clothing evidence.

There was medical evidence.

There was Conley’s testimony.

There was evidence placing the claimed attack in the rear machine department.

There was a large amount of testimony about Frank’s conduct toward women.

And there was Dorsey’s direct rape argument before the jury.

A person can reject Conley, Harris, Wood, Pettis, House, Turner, Hewell, Jackson, Kitchens, Dalton, Cato, Griffin, or any of the other witnesses.

A person can believe Hopkins, Carson, or Frank when they denied the claims made against them.

Those are arguments over who should be believed and how much weight each piece of evidence deserves.

But saying there was no evidence is something else.

There was.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.
Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

News

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Is this the part where the anti-Irish activist who has non-stop since 2025 posted distortions and negativity about this country pretends he's somehow concerned about Ireland's "international reputation"? The sheer confidence with which you lecture Irish people about Ireland would be hilarious if it weren’t so transparently tedious.

You have never even visited Ireland, yet you’ve spent roughly two years online presenting yourself as some grand authority on Irish society, culture and politics, while repeatedly trying to smear virtually any Irish person who criticises the Israeli government as an antisemite. That isn’t an analysis of Ireland. It’s an obsession dressed up as scholarship and let's be clear, you actually know fuck all about Ireland as the below screenshot reminds us. 

And then comes the truly magnificent patronising flourish about how much Irish culture and literature “has to offer the world”. How generous of you. I’m sure Ireland can finally breathe a sigh of relief now that an unsuccessful writer who doesn’t actually live here has granted our literature his seal of approval.

It's actually beyond pathetic that you invoke Irish culture only to immediately tell Irish people that their understanding of their own history is somehow a sinister “manufactured narrative”. Apparently Joyce, Yeats, Pearse, Connolly and generations of Irish historical experience are all fine until Irish people draw conclusions from that history that you dislike.

And notice what is conspicuously absent from this performance: any serious engagement whatsoever with the conduct of the Israeli state, the enormous civilian death toll, the destruction in Gaza, or the reasons that so many Irish people — including Jews — have profoundly criticised Israel. Instead, everything gets funnelled into your preferred morality play in which Irish people are either “patriotic” dissenters or dupes of some mysterious antisemitic campaign.

Criticism of Israel is not synonymous with antisemitism. Antisemitism is real, vile and deserving of condemnation. But endlessly expanding the definition of antisemitism, Humpty Dumpty- like, so that it means what you want it to mean and until it encompasses ordinary Irish opposition to Israeli government policy doesn't combat antisemitism. It trivialises it.

Perhaps before appointing yourself the foreign correspondent of Ireland, you might actually come here. Talk to people. Learn some history. And, just for variety, maybe just once engage with the substance of what Israel is doing rather than spending another year frantically searching for ways to portray Irish critics of Israel as uniquely sinister.
For someone so concerned about Ireland’s international reputation, you have an oddly spectacular lack of curiosity about the country you keep lecturing.

🚨 Brexit Supreme irony.

The Times warns Celtic nationalists about trade barriers, economic scale, fiscal pooling and the dangers of isolation ‼️ the very questions Brexit never answered and the very arguments Remainers made for staying in the EU.

“Big is beautiful,” it declares.

Apparently pooled sovereignty, frictionless trade and strength through union are indispensable in Britain, but intolerable in Europe.

🤡 You simply could not make it up.

Brexit was sold as the restoration of the UK’s sovereignty. It may yet prove to have begun the UK’s dissolution. Another remainer warning labelled scaremongering becoming reality.

Brexit had no plan before the referendum … or afterwards.

The 2016 referendum did not ask whether Britain should leave the Single Market or customs union. It offered no destination, trade settlement, border solution or constitutional plan for four nations that had voted differently. 

The vote indicated a marginal majority for the leave campaign which was full of false promises, dark money and psychops. And Boris Johnson’s particular hard Brexit we ended up with wasn’t ever mentioned by Brexit camp - and when Remainers warned about it they were labelled scaremongers.

The decision for Brexit was imposed through political choices: Johnson’s 2019 Withdrawal Agreement legislation, the refusal to extend transition, and finally the 2021 Trade and Cooperation Agreement that placed GB outside Europe’s Single Market and customs union.

🔥 BUT every devolved nation: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland withheld consent from Johnson’s Withdrawal Agreement Bill.

For the first time, all three said no together. Westminster, dominated by English MPs, passed it anyway.

Brexit was therefore not a consensual decision by four equal nations about how they should leave Europe. It exposed how little constitutional power three of those nations possessed when England’s political majority wanted something else.

Now their nationalist leaders are beginning to act collectively. They understand that their economic futures require deeper access to Europe and that cooperation among Ireland, Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland could offer an alternative to permanent domination from Westminster.

A Celtic alliance need not erase Northern Ireland’s identity or compel immediate Irish reunification. It could allow these nations to cooperate on trade, energy, food security, transport, defence and culture while respecting their different identities and constitutional position

Arteta could build on the structure used against Sunderland, with Timber added to the backline and a strong starting XI tasked with establishing control early.

The ideal plan: start with intensity, create a platform for a positive result, then use the second half to manage minutes and introduce fresh options if the game is under control.

Here is how Arsenal can create problems for Ipswich. 👇🏾

🎯 SAKA + TIMBER

Arsenal should look to overload the left side of Ipswich’s defence and create situations where Saka receives isolated against his marker. Timber’s positioning can support the attack, either through overlaps, underlaps or secure circulation that allows Saka to receive facing forward.

🧠 ØDEGAARD

Ipswich may try to limit Ødegaard’s influence by keeping the midfield compact. Arsenal can counter that with movement and rotations. Ødegaard should vary his position, combine with Saka and Rice, and look for spaces between Ipswich’s midfield and defensive lines.

⚡ TZOLIS

Tzolis can provide the outlet on the opposite flank. If Ipswich shift across to contain Saka, Arsenal should switch play quickly and give Tzolis opportunities to attack the full-back or deliver from a more advanced position.

💥 HAVERTZ

Havertz’s movement will be important. Rather than remaining fixed between the centre-backs, he can drop into linking positions, attack the channels and make late runs into the penalty area. His movement can create space for Ødegaard and the wide players.

🛡️ RICE

Rice provides the balance behind the attacking rotations. His positioning can help Arsenal control second balls, protect against counters and support the counter-press when possession is lost.

😏 CALAFIORI

Calafiori offers Arsenal another route into the final third.

He can step into midfield, carry the ball through pressure and support Tzolis on the left. When he moves inside, Arsenal gain an additional passing option centrally. When he overlaps, he can create space for Tzolis to move inside or attack the full-back directly.

🔥 Progressive carries
🔥 Underlapping runs
🔥 Quick switches of play
🔥 Aggressive pressing

Strong start.

Smart rotation if the match allows it.

SAKA + TIMBER ON ONE FLANK. CALAFIORI + TZOLIS ON THE OTHER.

Arsenal should stretch Ipswich’s defensive block, move it from side to side and attack the spaces that appear.

Ipswich have conceded nine goals in their last three matches and are still searching for their first clean sheet of the season.

text:
IGBOS MUST STOP PROTESTING AND START PRODUCING

It has been over 59 years, yet Ìgbò people do not want to be smart. You are trading in another man’s land—a land of people who do not even like you, people who blame you for all their misfortune in business, even when we know they are responsible for their own misfortune because they are not so good at business. Another nation comes to outperform you in business, and here you are protesting, expecting solidarity and sympathy from the same people who want to kick you out. Ndị Ìgbò should have some shame. You pride in calling others lazy and talking down on them because they are not so good at business. Now another nation more business-oriented than you has entered your retail business space, and here you are—protesting.

Let me be honest with you: no Yoruba person will show you sympathy. All of them want you out. It is time you changed strategy, evolved, and became production-oriented. The time for selling other nations’ products is over. Start producing. Instead of protesting in another man’s land—the land of people who do not even like you—organize yourselves and lobby your governors and senators to make laws that encourage local production.

Buhari banned rice importation and Nigerians started producing their own rice in response. Now the doors are open for China to compete with you in retail in your own space. It is another opportunity for you to evolve and produce the things you sell. The Chinese are humans like you; they do not have two heads. It is time to prove how great you claim you are—or were you making empty boasts?

To the Yorubas and other Nigerians celebrating this development: at first it is more convenient to enjoy the cheaper prices the Chinese offer, but in the long run even your own people will no longer be able to do business in their own land because most people will buy from China. Do you think your people do not do business as well? Go to Mushin Building Material Market in Lagos and see hundreds of Yoruba businessmen also trading there; these are the same people the Chinese will kick out of business with way cheaper prices.

It will affect everybody, but the survival tendency will not be the same. The Nigerian project has trained Igbos to be more resilient and survival-inclined. Igbos will find a way to navigate this and come out victorious, but what would be the fate of other Nigerians who are not so used to tough times?

text:
Dear Mike,

I hope you're doing well.

My name is Kate Walsh, and I am a Senior Commissioning Editor at Pan Macmillan. I recently came across Florida Man,  and I was drawn to the way you build a comic story around a character  whose circumstances are chaotic but whose ambitions are surprisingly  sincere.

Gary Duba immediately gives the novel its particular  energy. Living in a trailer by the swamp and dealing with everything  from a snake in his toilet to a rabid raccoon in the yard, he seems to  be surrounded by problems that would make an ordinary bad day feel  almost manageable by comparison. Yet beneath the absurdity, Gary is  someone who genuinely wants to improve his situation.

I  particularly liked the contrast between Gary’s dreams and the difficult  circumstances that continually undermine them. His attempt to raise five  hundred dollars for Krystal’s bail by selling his prized Barry Bonds  rookie card gives him a straightforward goal, but bringing his best  friend Floyd along ensures that even this simple plan has plenty of room  to go wrong.

The humor also seems to work because the characters  are treated with genuine affection rather than simply as targets of the  joke. Gary’s relationship with Floyd, his loyalty to Krystal despite the  circumstances surrounding her arrest, and his determination to keep  trying give the chaos an emotional center. The result is a story that  can be outrageous without losing sight of the people underneath it.

I  was also interested in the way the Florida setting contributes to the  novel’s personality. The swamp, trailer life, bizarre encounters, and  unpredictable turns of fate all feel inseparable from Gary’s world,  giving the story a strong sense of place while allowing the comedy to  develop naturally from its environment.

I wanted to ask whether  you are currently working on another novel or new project. If you are  represented by an agent, I would be very happy to continue the  conversation through them. If you are not currently represented, I can  also offer introductions to literary agents within my network who may be  a good fit for your work.

Warm regards,

Kate Walsh
Senior Commissioning Editor
Pan Macmillan

text:
Nellie Wood and Nellie Pettis: The Incriminating Evidence They Gave Against Leo Frank

The State’s claim that Leo Frank propositioned, assaulted, and sexually violated Mary Phagan did not stand alone. Other women and witnesses said Frank made sexual propositions, unwanted advances, and acted in a sexually aggressive way toward women and girls before Mary was murdered.

Two of the earliest women to give this kind of evidence were Nellie Wood and Nellie Pettis.

Their stories involved different women, different years, and different encounters, but both placed the alleged conduct inside Leo Frank’s office at the National Pencil Company, 37–41 South Forsyth Street in downtown Atlanta.

Frank’s office was on the second floor near the front of the building, facing South Forsyth Street. The office area had an outer office and Frank’s private inner office. Trial testimony later described the office area as roughly 30 by 38 feet. The large machine department was farther toward the rear.

Employees and other visitors went to the office over pay, work, and factory business.

Wood said Frank got her alone there, made her sit down, told her nobody was coming in, put his hands on her, tried to touch her breast, and made another advance involving her lower body and dress.

Pettis said Frank displayed an open box containing a lot of money, looked from the money to her, winked, and asked:

“How about it?”

Both women gave their first damaging evidence during the original May 1913 murder investigation, not years after Frank’s conviction.

Around March 1911: Nellie Wood’s private-office encounter

Nellie Wood said she worked at the National Pencil Company for only two days.

At the coroner’s inquest on Thursday, May 8, 1913, Wood placed her encounter with Frank “two years ago in March,” putting it around March 1911.

No exact clock time survives.

Wood’s sworn testimony is preserved in the Georgia Supreme Court case files, Leo M. Frank v. State of Georgia, Microfilm Slides 1772 and 1773.

Wood said Frank called her into his private office.

She said:

“he made me sit down.”

Wood objected:

“I asked him not to.”

According to Wood, Frank answered:

“there wasn't anybody coming in his office.”

Wood said Frank’s physical behavior toward her was “all uncalled for.”

She said he tried to touch her breast. The surviving legal record also describes an attempt involving her lower limbs and dress.

Wood said she resisted him.

She believed Frank would have touched her breast if she had not stopped him.

After only two days at the factory, she quit and returned only to collect her wages.

Asked about leaving the factory, Wood said:

“I thought he had the wrong girl.”

Her May 8 sworn testimony survives today in the Georgia Supreme Court files.

Wednesday, April 30 through Thursday, May 8, 1913: where Wood and Pettis testified

The coroner’s inquest into Mary Phagan’s death opened on Wednesday morning, April 30, 1913.

Contemporary reporting scheduled the first hearing for about 8:45 o’clock at P. J. Bloomfield’s undertaking establishment on South Pryor Street in Atlanta.

By the final day, Thursday, May 8, 1913, the proceedings were being held at Atlanta police headquarters.

The morning session resumed at about 9:30 o’clock.

The room included Coroner Paul V. Donehoo, the six members of the coroner’s jury, Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey, Frank’s attorney Luther Z. Rosser, Atlanta detectives John R. Black and John N. Starnes, Pinkerton detective Harry Scott, Fulton County physician Dr. J. W. Hurt, Mary Phagan’s stepfather John William Coleman, reporters, and stenographers.

The final two hours included testimony concerning Frank’s alleged conduct toward women. Among the witnesses were Mrs. C. D. Donegan, Tom Blackstock, Nellie Wood, and Nellie Pettis.

Wood and Pettis were therefore not giving private interviews years later. They were testifying during the official investigation, before the coroner and jury, while the Mary Phagan murder case was still being investigated.

Thursday, May 8, 1913: Nellie Pettis and the money box

Nellie Pettis had not worked regularly at the National Pencil Company.

Her sister-in-law, Lillie Mae Pettis, worked there.

Nellie went to the factory in connection with her sister-in-law’s wages. Her later affidavit said she went there four times, three times for her sister-in-law’s pay and once while looking for work.

The May 1913 newspaper reports placed the main encounter about four weeks before the inquest, putting it around early April 1913, only weeks before Mary Phagan was murdered.

No exact clock time survives.

At the May 8 inquest, Pettis said she had seen Frank once or twice in his office when she went for her sister-in-law’s pay.

According to the contemporary account, Pettis asked for her sister-in-law and Frank told her she could not see her unless Pettis “saw him first.”

Pettis said she did not want to “see him.”

She then described Frank pulling a box from his desk.

According to The Atlanta Georgian, Friday, May 9, 1913, in “Best Detective in America Now is on Case, Says Dorsey,” Pettis said the box contained a lot of money.

She said Frank looked at the money, looked at her, winked, and asked:

“How about it?”

Pettis answered:

“I instantly told him I was a nice girl.”

Coroner Donehoo asked whether she said anything else.

The Georgian reported Pettis saying she told Frank to go to hell and walked out of his office.

The newspaper put this testimony under the heading:

“Girls Testify Against Frank.”

It called the testimony concerning Frank’s treatment of female employees some of the most damaging evidence saved for the final hours of the inquest.

Friday, May 9, 1913: The Atlanta Constitution reports Pettis and Wood

The next morning, The Atlanta Constitution, Friday, May 9, 1913, ran “Frank and Lee Ordered Held by Coroner’s Jury for Mary Phagan Murder.”

The newspaper said women and young girls had testified about Frank’s alleged familiarity with female employees.

It singled out Pettis’s statement and reported her claim that Frank made an open proposal and suggested money.

The Constitution placed the encounter about four weeks earlier, when Pettis went to Frank’s office to get her sister-in-law’s pay envelope.

The same article reported Wood’s testimony.

Wood said she had worked for Frank only two days.

She complained that Frank put his hands on her without reason, called her into his office, tried to close the door, got too close, and tried further familiarities.

The Constitution reported Wood saying the conduct occurred about two years earlier, matching the period she gave in the official record.

The May 9 Constitution article therefore carried damaging accounts from both Wood and Pettis the morning after they testified.

Friday, May 9, 1913: The Atlanta Journal reports Wood’s office encounter

The Atlanta Journal, Friday, May 9, 1913, published “Here Is Testimony of Witnesses Given at the Final Session of Coroner’s Jury in Phagan Case.”

The Journal reported Wood’s account of Frank trying to close the office door while she objected.

According to the Journal, Frank reassured her:

“Don't worry. No one is coming.”

Wood was quoted saying:

“He was too familiar. I didn't like it.”

The Journal account and the official stenographic record are worded somewhat differently, but both describe the same basic accusation: Wood said Frank got her alone in his office, became too familiar with her, and made unwanted physical advances.

Friday, May 9, 1913: The Atlanta Georgian gives another version of Wood’s testimony

The Atlanta Georgian, Friday, May 9, 1913, “Best Detective in America Now is on Case, Says Dorsey,” gave its own report of Wood’s testimony.

The newspaper reported Wood saying Frank’s actions did not suit her, he put his hands on her without reason, called her into his office, tried to close the door, and became too familiar.

The Georgian printed:

“He barely touched my breast.”

It also reported Wood saying Frank tried further familiarities.

This newspaper wording is somewhat different from the official stenographic record, which says Frank tried to touch her breast and she resisted.

The records differ in wording, but both describe unwanted physical and sexual behavior.

Wood’s fuller “indecent proposal” account in the Georgia Supreme Court record

Wood’s accusation did not end with the May 8 inquest.

A fuller account survives in the Georgia Supreme Court case files on Microfilm Slides 1684, 1685, and 1686.

Wood described her encounter with Frank as an:

“indecent proposal.”

In plain English, this meant an improper sexual proposition.

Wood said Frank told her:

“You know I am not like other people.”

She said he moved his chair closer and told her:

“I don't think you will understand me.”

Wood said Frank put his hands on her.

She resisted.

She stood up and opened the office door.

Wood said nobody else was in the office.

This fuller account added several damaging points to her earlier testimony: Frank allegedly got her alone, moved closer, made a sexual proposition, put his hands on her, and continued until she got up and opened the door.

Wednesday, August 20, 1913: Dorsey tries to put Wood’s full story before the murder jury

Wood returned during Frank’s murder trial on Wednesday, August 20, 1913, at the Fulton County courthouse.

The jury was sent out while the lawyers argued over whether Wood could tell the full story.

The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, August 20, 1913, in “State Closes Frank Case Near Jury; Defense Begins Its Sur-Rebuttal,” reported Dorsey telling Judge Leonard S. Roan:

“We want to show by this witness actual specific misconduct on the part of this defendant.”

Dorsey then told the court he wanted to show Frank had made an “indecent proposal” to Wood.

Judge Roan would not allow Dorsey to prove general bad character by bringing in separate claimed sexual acts one after another.

The murder jury therefore did not hear Wood’s complete March 1911 office story.

The important point is simple. Dorsey tried to place Wood’s specific accusation before the jury, Frank’s lawyers objected, and Judge Roan excluded it under the rules controlling character evidence. Wood’s original sworn account remained in the case files.

Wednesday, August 20, 1913: Pettis testifies about Frank’s character

Pettis also appeared during the murder trial on Wednesday, August 20, 1913.

Because Judge Roan had limited the State’s use of separate claimed acts, her full money-box story was not repeated before the jury.

Pettis was allowed to testify about Frank’s character.

The Atlanta Georgian, Thursday, August 21, 1913, in “Mass of Perjuries Charged by Arnold; Centers Hot Attack on Conley,” reported the questions and answers from the previous day.

Dorsey asked whether Frank’s character was good or bad.

Pettis answered:

“Bad.”

He then asked whether she knew Frank’s character for lasciviousness.

“Lasciviousness” was an old word for improper or lustful sexual behavior.

Pettis said she did.

Asked whether it was good or bad, she again answered:

“Bad.”

Unlike her specific early-April encounter, this character evidence went before the murder jury.

Pettis in the official Georgia Supreme Court Brief of Evidence

Pettis’s trial testimony survives in the official Brief of Evidence in Leo M. Frank v. State of Georgia, pages 221–222, preserved on Georgia Supreme Court Microfilm Slides 1263 and 1264.

Pettis appears among the women called by the State concerning Frank’s sexual character.

The official summary says:

“Leo M. Frank's character for lasciviousness was bad.”

Pettis therefore supplied two separate kinds of damaging evidence.

Her May 8, 1913 inquest account described a claimed sexual proposition involving money.

Her August 20, 1913 trial testimony said Frank’s character and his character for lasciviousness were bad.

Sunday, March 15, 1914: Pettis stands by “How about it?”

Pettis later stood by the main accusation.

The Atlanta Journal, Sunday, March 15, 1914, page 1, columns 5 and 7, continuing on page 2, published “Witness Against Frank Now Accuses Sleuths.”

The article carried the heading:

“MISS NELLIE PETTIS STICKS TO ORIGINAL TESTIMONY.”

Her sworn affidavit gave her age as sixteen. The May 9, 1913 Constitution reporter had earlier guessed she appeared eighteen or nineteen. Her own 1914 sworn statement gave sixteen.

Pettis said she had gone to the factory four times.

She said Frank looked hard at her on the visits.

On one occasion, she said he stood close to her and quietly asked:

“How about it?”

Her sister-in-law, Lillie Mae Pettis, disputed her story and said Nellie normally dealt with forelady Eula Mae Flowers when collecting wages.

But Nellie Pettis stood by the central accusation.

Friday, May 1, 1914: Wood repeats her accusations

Wood’s damaging account also returned during Frank’s post-trial fight for another trial.

The Atlanta Georgian, Friday, May 1, 1914, in “Evidence Is Recorded Against Conley,” reported Wood again attacking Frank’s character.

The newspaper said Wood repeated her assertions that Frank was of bad character and gave more detail about the circumstances behind her statement.

The same article reported Wood and former factory employee R. P. Barrett making charges about offers of money for statements favorable to Frank.

This was another point in the record where Wood’s damaging view of Frank resurfaced after his conviction.

Tuesday, May 5, 1914: Wood goes back into open court

One of Wood’s strongest later statements came on Tuesday, May 5, 1914, during Frank’s extraordinary motion for a new trial before Judge Benjamin Harvey Hill.

The Atlanta Journal, Tuesday, May 5, 1914, page 1, column 7, ran “Many Sensations Sprung by Dorsey at Frank Hearing.”

Wood took the stand under oath.

Dorsey asked why she had quit the National Pencil Company after only two days.

Wood answered:

“Because I was insulted by Mr. Frank.”

Dorsey then asked what proposition Frank had made.

Wood answered:

“I think the details are unnecessary.”

Later Dorsey again asked about what occurred between Wood and Frank inside his office.

Wood said:

“I don't know that I remember every detail.”

She did not repeat every part of the old encounter in open court, but she did not clear Frank either.

Under oath, nearly a year after her first testimony, Wood still said she quit because Frank had insulted her.

Wood also gave her age as twenty-two during the May 5 hearing. This places her around eighteen or nineteen when the March 1911 encounter would have happened, depending upon her birthday.

What Wood’s evidence against Frank amounted to

Taken in date order, Wood accused Frank of the following:

She said he called her into his private office.

She said he made her sit down.

She objected.

He told her nobody was coming into the office.

She said he got too familiar.

She said he put his hands on her without reason.

She said he tried to touch her breast.

The official record also describes an effort involving her lower limbs and dress.

She said she resisted him.

She later called the encounter an “indecent proposal.”

She said Frank moved his chair closer.

She said he told her he was “not like other people.”

She said nobody else was in the office.

She stood up and opened the door.

She quit after working at the factory only two days.

In May 1914, under oath in open court, she still said:

“Because I was insulted by Mr. Frank.”

What Pettis’s evidence against Frank amounted to

Pettis said she saw Frank in his office when she went to collect her sister-in-law’s wages.

She said Frank told her she could not see her sister-in-law unless she “saw him first.”

She refused.

She said Frank pulled out a box containing a lot of money.

He looked at the money.

He looked at her.

He winked.

He asked:

“How about it?”

Pettis said she understood the meaning and told him she was a nice girl.

She then rejected him and walked out.

At Frank’s murder trial she said his character was:

“Bad.”

Asked about his character for lasciviousness, she again answered:

“Bad.”

In her March 15, 1914 sworn affidavit, Pettis stood by the core accusation and repeated Frank’s:

“How about it?”

Why Wood and Pettis are important

Wood and Pettis did not describe the same incident.

Wood placed her experience around March 1911.

Pettis placed hers only weeks before Mary Phagan’s murder in April 1913.

Wood had worked for Frank.

Pettis had not. She entered the factory in connection with picking up her sister-in-law’s wages.

Wood described unwanted physical contact and an indecent proposal inside Frank’s private office.

Pettis described money, a wink, standing close, and a sexual proposition.

Both accounts entered the record during the original murder investigation.

Both appeared in the Atlanta newspapers immediately.

Wood’s sworn inquest evidence survives in the Georgia Supreme Court files.

Pettis’s bad-character testimony survives in the official Brief of Evidence.

Wood’s accusation resurfaced during the murder trial and again under oath in May 1914.

Pettis stood by “How about it?” in her March 1914 affidavit.

Whatever weight a person chooses to give these two women, their evidence cannot fairly be described as a later invention added to the Leo Frank case decades afterward.

It was there in 1913 and 1914, in sworn testimony, court records, and the daily Atlanta newspapers.

text:
@SeaOfThieves @RareLtd  YOU MADE THE RIGHT CALL. NOW GO ALL THE WAY.

Season 21 is a start. Make it a new era.

Let me start with what Rare is getting right, because it's real and it matters.

Decoupling features from seasons was the correct call. Drew Stevens said features now ship when they're finished, not on a three month clock. He admitted the game started 2026 in a rough place. That's honest, and it's the right fix.

Shipping things broken to hit a date is what damaged the trust in the first place. Pulling out what doesn't work. Reworking what's half built. Refusing to push a feature before it's ready. All of that is the right instinct.

Moving more cosmetics onto in-game gold instead of the Emporium is a real gesture toward players. And the Parley Pennant is a lovely little idea. A flag that says "I want to talk, not fight" is exactly the kind of social tool this game needs more of.

AND SEASON 21? I'LL TAKE IT.

It owns what it is. A calendar of recurring events and some Custom Seas improvements. Tricksters and Treaters, Festival of the Damned, Fight Nights, Emissaries of Fortune, Last Ship Standing returning.

It isn't big content. Nobody is pretending it is.

But it keeps the sea alive while the real work happens elsewhere, and that is far healthier than a rushed feature shoved out to fill a slot.

It's small, but it's honest. That's called a start.

The start of a new era, if you're willing to go all the way.

Because that's where this gets decided. Taking time is only worth something if that time produces something big. If we're still on bonus weekends and Custom Seas toggles a year from now, the time wasn't taken to build. It was just taken.

Nobody will remember a Gold & Glory from September 2026. Everybody remembers the night a Galleon came out of the fog at the worst possible moment.

What's missing isn't features. It's the soul. The lore, the world, the events, and above all new ones.

So here's what I'd do with that time. Every idea below is built on things already sitting in the game.

IDEA 1: USE PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN PROPERLY

The Disney licence was negotiated, voiced, animated, paid for. It was used for exactly one thing: five scripted Tall Tales, playable once, with cosmetics at the end. We reopen the drawer once a year for an anniversary cutlass.

And the writing was good. Davy Jones assembling the Dark Brethren to replace the Ferryman. The Gold Hoarder corrupted by cursed Aztec gold. Wanda the Warsmith. Calypso as the Castaway.

A ritual meant to merge the Sea of Thieves with the Sea of the Damned, interrupted by players. The Phantoms drifting around the world today are the direct leftover of it.

There is continuity. There is causality. And all of it is asleep in a Tall Tale nobody replays.

Sea of Thieves is an emergent sandbox. Its best content has never been scripted. Davy Jones and the Flying Dutchman are world threats. They have no business living in a narrative corridor.

SO MAKE THE CORAL FORTRESS A WORLD EVENT

Go and look at it if you never have outside of Dark Brethren.

J-0, north of I-1 and J-1, literally outside the map's normal regional borders. A mountain of jagged rock encrusted with coral and shipwreck debris. Siren statues, puzzles, and the journals of a First Mate named Yenay telling a doomed love story.

And a permanent scripted storm that doesn't damage ships, doesn't scramble your compass and doesn't flood your hold. Rare wrote a bespoke weather exception for this one location.

And it serves one Tall Tale nobody replays.

That's the whole argument. The set is already paid for. The most expensive part of a world event is already on everybody's hard drive. What's left is scripting and a loot table.

Three acts. A cursed fleet that surfaces beneath your hull instead of spawning on the horizon, firing coral broadsides that encrust a hole you have to break with a shovel before you can plank it.

Then the fortress itself, on foot. Then Davy Jones.

And you need zero new enemies for that fortress fight.

The Ocean Crawlers already exist with distinct roles nobody has ever put in an interesting situation. The Eel-ectric glides and chains stunning lightning. The Hermit burrows, bursts out, drops a blinding poison cloud.

And the Crab deploys a Coral Shield that protects the other Crawlers around it. An enemy that makes other enemies invulnerable automatically creates target priority. Nobody has ever used that.

Three Crabs at different angles of a vertical room, Eel-ectrics firing down from above, Hermits erupting behind you, and on-foot combat suddenly demands real crew coordination.

The blueprint exists too. Fort of the Damned, 2019, where Shadows of Fate are only vulnerable to the Flame of Fate matching their eye colour. Still the only ground fight in this game that asks you to think instead of hold a trigger. Never reused since.

For Jones himself, three phases.

He plays the organ and the water rises in the room. You already have the rising water and bailing systems, just take them off the ship.

Then he offers a pact to one random crew member, buffing them but marking them, so every minion converges on them and the rest of the crew can see it. Five seconds of gameplay that generate an hour of arguing on voice comms afterwards.

Then he goes invulnerable and you hunt his heart through the fortress while he hunts you.

Loot: a Brethren Chest, a pile of Coral Treasure (a category that already exists and has been dead since the Sunken Kingdom was quietly abandoned), and the Heart of Davy Jones, a carryable that grants your ship one resurrection.

Sell it for a fortune or keep it as insurance. Not a gold value. A decision. And an item worth stealing.

IDEA 2: MAKE STACK DANGEROUS

Right now, hoarding treasure has no systemic consequence at all. Forty items in the hold and the world could not care less.

The only risk is another player, and on a lot of servers at a lot of hours they simply never come. Stacking has become an activity of waiting.

The game teaches you that your reward is a source of passive anxiety. That's bad for everyone. The people who want PvP can't find anyone, and the people who don't want it spend the whole session on alert for nothing.

So let the server track carried value. Past a threshold, something comes for you.

A loaded Galleon or Brigantine draws the Flying Dutchman. The sea goes flat and black, the music cuts out entirely, and he surfaces. Silence in this game is more frightening than any foghorn.

A loaded Sloop draws the Kraken. But on the horizon, you see the Dutchman pass and sail away. He clocked you, he sent the beast, he carried on.

The monster is the master's message. A two-player Sloop shouldn't have to fight him. It should have to see him.

And the Dutchman must be a chase, not a wall of HP.

Faster than you in a straight line, but unable to enter shallow water, so ducking into an archipelago becomes a real tactic and map geography finally matters.

Each hit curses a plank, so the hole takes two people to repair. He boards you instead of endlessly broadsiding, because your deck is where this game is at its most intense.

Drive him off and he leaves a mark that boosts your sell value. You survived, you get paid. Run to an outpost and sell, and he disengages, because the reason for the threat is gone.

Threat has to be an opportunity. Never a tax.

And Rare has already proven it can build this. The Burning Blade is an AI ship with its own damage state, a ten minute defeated window, a crew of Obsidian Skeletons firing autonomously with infinite supplies, and a bespoke weapon in the Ashen Roar.

The studio knows how to make a scripted ship sail, shoot, board and die.

IDEA 3: LET US DEFEND SOMETHING

Sea of Thieves never rewards defending, and that is the root of this community's permanent civil war.

You spend forty minutes on a Molten Sands Fortress. Emissary Grade V, a timed quest, killing an Eternal Guard for the key, four torches, eight waves up to an Ashen Lord, a Stronghold Key, a vault worth around 200k.

And then the objectively correct play is to load up and run.

The game made you work for forty minutes to teach you to avoid its own PvP content.

So: when the vault opens, start a ten minute timer with two options.

Leave, and it's exactly today's game, untouched. Nobody is ever forced, because the moment this becomes mandatory it becomes a tax.

Or light a brazier.

Light it and a Siege Mark appears on the map table of every player on the server with a visible countdown. Not a cloud you need a thousand hours to interpret, just an explicit icon, exactly the way the Reaper's Mark already works.

The fort's cannons come under your control. Ammo and plank barrels restock. You respawn inside the fort instead of on your ship, which is the one thing that makes on-foot defence viable at all. A bell rings when a ship enters the perimeter.

And the chests stay locked in the vault, so you can't just load the hold and camp. You defend the place, not the cargo.

Every five minutes held, the vault produces another chest.

Hold to the end and you take everything, with a sell multiplier scaling on ships driven off, plus a defence cosmetic set available no other way.

Get taken and the attackers inherit the whole stock plus a capture-exclusive item, and the fort rearms for them, so the siege restarts with them defending.

A fortress could change hands three times in one evening. That's the story the server tells the next day.

And if nobody comes at three in the morning on a Tuesday, the defenders still bank the full production. Holding is never a loss. That's the single most important balance point in the whole thing, and the one a rushed designer would miss.

Start it on the plain Skeleton Fort, not the fancy ones.

The last time Rare meaningfully touched it was Season 9, March 2023. Scaled waves and health to crew size, slowed skeletons, stopped Skeleton Lords eating bananas, cut the Captain wave down to thirteen, added a Weapon Chest.

Every one of those changes was about making it easier to finish. Not one was about making it worth finishing.

Three and a half years later the loop is still: see skull cloud, hold trigger through thirteen waves, open vault, load, leave. The Skull Cloud is the most recognisable image this game has, and what's underneath it is a queue.

A Fort of Fortune already feels like an occasion. A Skeleton Fort feels like a chore. Give the chore stakes and it stops being one.

And the numbers work. Its vault is worth a fraction of Molten Sands, so the five minute production tick isn't a rounding error there, it's most of the payout. Holding a Skeleton Fort for half an hour could genuinely out-earn rushing a Fort of Fortune.

That's how you bring players back to old content without buffing a single loot table.

A FEW SMALLER THINGS

Let the world keep scars. A fort taken three times should show it: blackened walls, torn banners, a brazier still smoking. A sunken ship should leave a wreck you can dive for twenty minutes with part of its cargo inside.

Fix the Kraken. Two to three tentacles for a Sloop, five to six for a Brigantine, seven to eight for a Galleon, an ink pool where you drown faster, gone after fifteen minutes. It has no body, no head, no face. We fight arms poking through a black wall. Give it a body under the hull, a phase where it lifts the ship, a weak point.

Make the cursed side a real faction. The Burning Blade proved playing as the monster is excellent. Scuttle your ship, pledge at the Quest Table, become a Grade 1 Reaper Emissary, run rituals worth 26k apiece, and the whole server knows you're out there. That's one of the best ideas of the last five years and it's stuck as a one-off.

Make wealth visible. A loaded ship should sit lower, run slower, show quiet signs of its cargo. Free information for everyone, and it feeds everything above.

WHAT THIS COSTS

The Contested Fortress is by far the cheapest thing here. Zero new assets, zero new enemies, zero new environments. A state, a timer, a map icon, a loot table. Systems work, not art work.

Test it on one weekend, on Skeleton Forts only, and measure how many people light the brazier. That's a Bilge Rats Weekender that actually builds toward something.

The Coral Court is mid-cost. The environment is built, the Crawlers are built, the fleet structure is built, the loot category is built. What costs money is the boss.

The full Dutchman and a Kraken rework are the expensive ones, but the Burning Blade is a foundation for the first and the second will be visible in trailers for years.

And on Disney: the approvals are real, I'm not pretending otherwise. But the licence has been negotiated once already and the content is in the game right now.

More importantly, every idea above works identically with the Dark Brethren alone. The Coral Fortress, the Ocean Crawlers, Coral Treasure, the Sea of the Damned. That's Rare content, not Disney content. The idea doesn't depend on the licence. It would just benefit from it.

SO, TO BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT I'M ASKING FOR

Keep going. Season 21 is a good start, and the fact that it's modest doesn't bother me, because it's honest about it. Keep pulling broken things out instead of shipping them. Keep reworking instead of patching over. Keep taking the time.

But make that time produce something big. Real content and real bug fixing, both, at a scale we haven't seen in years.

A start only means something if something follows it.

Give us back the soul of this game. The lore. A world that reacts to us. Real events, and new ones. A deeper Pirates of the Caribbean collaboration, or something entirely your own, I honestly don't care which.

Just make it deep, make it permanent, and make it ours.

The Coral Fortress has been asleep at J-0 since 2021. Fort of the Damned invented the best ground combat in this game and nobody ever reused it. The Ocean Crawlers have three tactical roles that have never been put in a situation worth playing. The Burning Blade proved we'll happily play the monster. Coral Treasure sells to four companies and nobody picks it up.

The potential doesn't need inventing. It's already on the table.

And Davy Jones is still sitting in the hold of the Ferry of the Damned, in Jack Sparrow's exact spot, waiting for someone to open the door. We've walked past him every time we die for five years.

Season 21 is the start of a new era. Now write what comes next.

@SeaOfThieves @RareLtd @Xbox @asha_shar @ChappersChapman 

#SeaOfThieves #BeMorePirate
