text:
This brilliantly focused piece tells a story and lays out the stakes for Canada, CUSMA, US, and Chinese relations through an analytical framework, and lays out China’s potential strategy for new capital in a G7 country. 

I highly recommend ght a key takeaway.

Here are China's 5 key objectives and what is at stake.

What should we watch in the future?

We should look forI the Form of the money. 

Is it Limited Partner-style and passive, or acquiring governance rights short of control (board seats, veto rights, information access, offtake, technology licensing) that a pure ownership test scores as clean? 

2. The sectors where China invests. Some infrastructure and energy projects are tolerable; critical minerals, ports, or grid-core assets are an alarm.

3. Signs of institutional softening. A revised SOE policy statement from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), which would amount to an investment whitelist in legal form. Reviews closed on undertakings and conditions. Perhaps we’ll see a middle state between softening and holding.

4. The American reaction. Is the US-Mexico track’s “free-riding from non-parties” language reaching Canada, or does Donald Trump execute his 100% tariff threat?

5. The trade channel. PRC economic coercionagainst Canada through canola, potash, or agricultural approvals is the earliest signal the investment relationship has turned.

Those who have studied the Belt and Road initiative understand how the CCP invests in companies in critical sectors with the long-term goal of eliminating competitors and ultimately hollowing out those industries so that as a monopoly you write the rules. We have allowed some of this investment for close to 50 years, with CITIC first investing in our mining industry.

Canada has been pushing back since 2012. 
Ottawa closed that lane for the oil sands in 2012 and for critical minerals with a screening policy in 2022. CIC’s own Canadian book of those years, 17.2% of Teck, was already passive.’

The concern for any nation is losing its evomoin gems and there  are numerous examples, including in telecommunications (Huawei), the auto industry in Europe (Volkswagen and Mercedes), and the pulp and paper industry (APP's acquisitions in Canada) — just a few. 

Next is the Canadian and North American auto industry, using Canada as the backdoor. CUSMA negotiations are as much about American reindustrialization as they are about using Canada and Mexico as a Trojan Horse to conduct their own economic war against the West and undermine every strategic industry.  Chinese capital is looking for a home and Csnada offers a stable markeylt to park that money.

One reason cited for pulling back from the trade deal was our sovereignty over who we ‘strategically partner’ with & the PM wants the flexibility to welcome these investments as their assessment of US economic strategy is well known (Davos).

The question should be: why is Canada pushing back on a continental economic security agreement & potentially welcoming a state-backed investment model that offers short-term gains but causes long-term economic, political and social issues (ask the Germans and Brits how they are doing with CCP investment).  

However, our American friends and the President need to understand we won’t be obsequious to either global hegemony that makes us a vassal state. We are Canadians, and we will fight for our sovereignty and ability to make our own decisions. 

A win-win with a democratic Beacon on the Hill should be a preferred path, but that has become increasingly difficult to sell here in Canada given the insults & attacks on our PM & country and the ever present rapture in the world order. 

While Canada does not have the intelligence treasures nor the institutional think tank apparatus to understand the CCP fully there are many who do & that too should inform our China engagement.

text:
From The 48 Laws of Power by Robert Greene.

Hiring your friend feels safe. It is often how authority dies.

Friends expect special treatment. They rarely say it. They just start resenting the rules.

People who once opposed you are often easier to manage. They know they are on probation. They perform.

Law 2/48 — Never put too much trust in friends. Learn how to use enemies.

Keep friends for friendship. Keep the competent for the work.

In the 9th century, Byzantine emperor Michael III raised a peasant horseman named Basil from the imperial stables, loaded him with gifts, and in 866 made him co-emperor. In 867, Basil had Michael murdered and took the throne as Basil I.

In 961, Song emperor Taizu, Zhao Kuangyin, did the opposite. Instead of killing the generals who had put him on the throne, he invited them to a banquet, offered them wealth and a quiet retirement, and took back their command of the army. No blood that night. The Song dynasty lasted more than 300 years.

Office version:
Don’t make your closest friend your deputy.
Make the skeptic your deputy.

The friend will assume loyalty is enough.
The skeptic will keep proving they belong.

Post 2/48.

text:
🪖💸 Sjoe! The Defence Commission That Could Cost More Than the Defence ~ 🇿🇦💰 Defence by Spreadsheet: When Ambition Runs Faster Than the Budget ~ 🪖💼 Paper Army, Real Bill: South Africa’s Defence Ambition Meets Fiscal Reality.
There is a quiet consistency in the way a constitutional democracy examines its failing institutions. When revenue collection is compromised, a commission is appointed. When a public investment vehicle is captured, a commission is appointed. When the police service shows signs of systemic infiltration, a commission is appointed. 

When intelligence structures require cleansing, a high-level panel is convened. The rhythm is almost predictable. 

And yet the one institution that holds the monopoly on organised violence—the force charged under Section 200 of the Constitution with defending the republic—has remained outside that rhythm.

That selective exception is not an administrative detail. It is the central institutional fact.

1. The Cumulative Pattern

The case for examination has never depended on any single personality. Individual proceedings have supplied illustration. Testimony concerning residual cash travel allowances—issued in foreign currency, major costs prepaid, leftovers retained—revealed a control weakness that has endured for two decades. 

Those details matter. They do not, however, exhaust the argument.

The stronger case arises from the convergence of independent indicators: readiness figures showing only a minority of personnel medically fit for deployment; multi-billion-rand discrepancies between asset registers and physical verification; command friction in which presidential instructions on foreign military participation were not fully observed; and a thirty-year force-evolution strategy whose final phase projects spending levels the fiscus cannot currently sustain.

Presidents have appointed defence-related inquiries before. The Seriti Commission into the Strategic Defence Package demonstrated that the instrument exists and can be used. Precedents, however, do not answer whether the present constellation of indicators requires a new and broader examination focused on readiness, residual controls, force design and industrial foundations.

Civil-military scholarship has long observed that professional degradation combined with incomplete civilian scrutiny does not reliably produce obedience. It can produce resentment and alternative sources of legitimacy. A force that is simultaneously under-capable in mass and still residual in specialised capacity is not a contradiction. It is a classic pathology.

The cumulative pattern therefore supplies the institutional justification: an unexamined force that holds coercive power has been left outside the accountability mechanism applied almost everywhere else. That exception itself becomes evidence.

Sjoe!
A republic that commissions inquiries into nearly everything except the institution that can apply organised violence is practising selective transparency with remarkable consistency. The silence has become its own form of policy.

Questions Stirring: 
Why has the one institution capable of applying organised violence been systematically shielded from the public, under-oath scrutiny applied to nearly every other failing organ? 
What calculation makes the political cost of illumination higher than the cost of continued opacity? 
And why does that calculation appear to treat the risk of internal reaction as more immediate than the risk of progressive erosion of civilian supremacy?

These questions matter together because they force attention onto architecture rather than episode. A single prosecution can be managed. A recurring pattern of selective exception cannot.

2. Paper Ambition, Fiscal Reality

Cabinet has endorsed a thirty-year force-evolution strategy structured in four sequential phases. The final phase, described as a “Blueprint Force,” is projected to require up to 4.6 percent of GDP. Current allocations remain near 0.7 percent. Parliamentary research has noted inconsistencies in the targets offered to the legislature, uncertainty about whether each milestone adds capability to a growing force or replaces earlier designs, and the structural reality that personnel costs already consume roughly seventy percent of the existing budget.

Early phases at lower percentages remain theoretically feasible if accompanied by personnel and capability reform. The full end-state is widely regarded as unattainable under present macroeconomic conditions. The decisive indicator is therefore not the solemn language of the planning documents but the persistent gap between those documents and the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework allocations that continue to deliver real-term decline.

That gap is more than an accounting inconvenience. It is a revealed preference. 

Long-term strategy speaks the language of limited-war capability and regional operations. Near-term budgeting speaks the language of fiscal consolidation and competing social claims. The distance between the two measures where the country currently stands on the journey and simultaneously tests the practical ranking of defence among national priorities.

Political scientists have long noted that governments under electoral pressure tend to protect symbolic planning while deferring costly execution. The pattern is familiar across middle-income democracies facing simultaneous security and fiscal stress. 

South Africa is not unique in producing ambitious force-design documents. It is distinctive in the size of the gap between the final projected percentage and the current allocation.

Sjoe!

A country that plans in decades while budgeting in real-term decline is not merely optimistic. It is describing a different republic from the one that must pay the invoices.

Questions Stirring: 
Is the force being designed around an identified strategic requirement and then costed, or is it being designed around an assumed funding envelope that the fiscus has already shown it cannot meet? 
What does it reveal when long-term planning language speaks of limited-war capability while near-term budgets continue to shrink in real terms? 
And how long can aspirational percentages substitute for capability-based costing?

These questions matter together because they convert solemn strategy into arithmetic. Planning without funded execution is not strategy. It is theatre with better stationery.

3. The Residual Vulnerability

Foreign subsistence-and-travel allowances were issued in cash in the currency of the destination country. Major costs—accommodation, often meals—were frequently prepaid by the department. Residual amounts were retained and, on occasion, converted back into rand. Once cash leaves the formal system, the distinction between legitimate leftovers and other sources becomes inherently difficult to police.

The same principal-agent gap first surfaced two decades earlier when official travel instruments were converted into personal benefit. Exposure produced guilty pleas and temporary political cost. It did not produce structural redesign—mandatory residual-surrender rules, real-time transparency thresholds, or hard competition requirements for the underlying spending. 

The vulnerability therefore persists as one visible strand within a broader pattern of weak discretionary controls.

Large residual cash does not prove illicit origin in any individual case. It does create a permanent audit shadow. Systems that routinely generate untraceable residual cash after major costs have already been covered invite precisely the difficulty of distinction that later investigations must struggle to resolve. 

Exposure without redesign simply documents the gap for another generation.

Sjoe!
A control weakness that survives its own exposure is no longer a weakness. It is a preference wearing an audit report.

Questions Stirring: 
If exposure two decades ago did not close the gap, what institutional incentive has kept residual cash practices alive? 
Does the difficulty of distinguishing legitimate leftovers from other sources after cash has left the system create a permanent audit shadow? 
And why does a control weakness first diagnosed in one era continue to function, largely unreformed, in another?

These questions matter together because they demonstrate that diagnosis without redesign is merely documentation. A vulnerability that outlives its own scandal becomes evidence of deeper institutional preference for opacity over correction.

4. The Selective Exception as Evidence

Section 84(2)(f) of the Constitution has been invoked repeatedly for high-profile crises. No equivalent public, under-oath process has been established for the force itself. Preferred instruments have remained internal boards of inquiry, ministerial statements and intermittent parliamentary questions. 

When almost every other major institutional failure received judicial scrutiny while the institution that holds coercive capacity did not, the exception ceases to look accidental.

Civil-military theory is unambiguous on the point. Forces that experience professional degradation and incomplete civilian control become more, not less, prone to political intervention when internal networks perceive existential threat. 

Authority that is never fully tested becomes authority that is quietly renegotiated.

Each delayed report, each discretionary non-publication, each internal process that substitutes for public examination adds another small renegotiation. Over time the cumulative effect is a gradual shift in the real distribution of power, even if the formal constitutional text remains unchanged.

The selective pattern is therefore not neutral administrative preference. It is independent evidence that requires explanation if claims of consistent civilian supremacy are to remain coherent.

Sjoe!
An instruction that arrives, is acknowledged, and then gently dissolves is not an order. It is a suggestion wearing a uniform. The difference is visible only when someone finally decides to measure it.

Questions Stirring: 
What does the repeated preference for contained, delayed and discretionary processes reveal about the actual distribution of authority? 
If the commander-in-chief elects not to force full illumination, is that choice an exercise of power or an admission of its limits? 
And how do external partners interpret a system in which high-level military engagements proceed with limited visible consequence for non-compliance?

These questions matter together because they move the problem from motive to capability. An authority that is never tested is an authority that is already being redefined in practice.

5. Capability Beyond the Barracks

Platforms, maintenance cycles and specialised skills appear as the visible tip of a larger industrial iceberg. Shortfalls in aircraft availability, delayed maintenance and specialist capacity register as symptoms of broader manufacturing, engineering and skills erosion rather than as purely military failures. 

Partnerships for infrastructure have been discussed not merely as building repairs but as potential instruments for rebuilding domestic capability—if structured to leave skills, suppliers and investment confidence behind.

The country is therefore doubly constrained. Fiscal limits restrict funding of force-design milestones. Industrial erosion restricts the productive base required to convert any additional funding into sustained capability. Knowledge does not return because a budget line increases. Experience cannot be imported in a shipping container. 

An engineer with three decades of hard-earned judgement cannot be replaced by a procurement contract.

Nations that developed resilient defence industries rarely began by buying finished platforms. They built engineering schools, specialist suppliers, research continuity and the expectation that difficult problems would keep arriving. 

Capability compounds. 

Once the ecosystem begins shrinking, rebuilding it becomes painfully slow. The defence force, in that sense, functions as an industrial thermometer. Its visible shortfalls register deeper trends in the productive economy long before those trends become impossible to ignore elsewhere.

Sjoe!
A nation rarely notices the day it stops building complicated things. There is no siren. One workshop closes. One apprenticeship disappears. One experienced engineer accepts an opportunity elsewhere. Years later everyone wonders why the aircraft will not fly. The aircraft is simply delivering the message.

Questions Stirring: 
Can public spending create capability instead of merely consuming it? 
Should success be measured by finished buildings or by the skills, suppliers and businesses left behind? 
And if the defence force is acting as the country’s industrial thermometer, what is the wider economy trying to tell us before the temperature rises further?

These questions matter together because they reframe sovereignty. A nation that can still design, manufacture, maintain and improve complex systems enters partnerships as a collaborator. A nation that can only purchase finished products enters them as a customer. 

The difference is measured in decades of accumulated knowledge, not in the next budget cycle.

Synthesis

The five strands interlock with unusual coherence. An unexamined force that holds the monopoly on organised violence has remained outside the accountability tool applied elsewhere. Long-term documents project ambition measured in percentages of GDP that current allocations do not approach. Residual control weaknesses persist across decades. Selective scrutiny itself has become evidence. Industrial foundations continue to erode.

Independent lines of evidence—constitutional practice, fiscal arithmetic, residual control failures, civil-military analysis and industrial capacity—converge on one testable claim: the selective exception is no longer neutral. It is diagnostic.

The claim is falsifiable. Demonstrable, funded progress on early force-design phases accompanied by structural reform, residual-cash redesign and measurable industrial recovery would weaken it. Persistence of the opposite pattern strengthens it.

The stakes are institutional rather than partisan. A constitutional order that systematically exempts the force holding coercive capacity from the examination it applies to nearly every other failing organ is gradually redefining the practical meaning of civilian supremacy, whether it intends to or not.

Objections

Some will argue that national security classification justifies the exception. Classification is real; immunity from accountability is not. The Constitution already provides mechanisms for handling sensitive evidence inside a judicial process. Opacity that shields residual cash practices and readiness shortfalls is not protection. It is the opposite.

Others will contend that underfunding alone explains the degradation. Underfunding is real and severe. It does not explain the selective application of the commission mechanism, the persistence of unreformed control weaknesses across two decades, or the gap between solemn thirty-year documents and real-term budget decline.

A third view holds that internal processes are sufficient. The cumulative record of qualified audits, non-implementation and repeated parliamentary dissatisfaction suggests that internal processes have already been tried and found wanting.

Final Resolution

An institution left deliberately unexamined cannot forever be presumed to serve the constitutional order that claims to command it. The quiet question that remains is whether the republic still possesses the will to apply to its most consequential force the same standard of public examination it has applied almost everywhere else.

The beloved country has faced harder reckonings. It can choose this one while the tools of diagnosis and redesign remain available. The pattern is not destiny. It is a choice still open.

Sjoe.
The converging evidence—from constitutional practice, fiscal allocations, residual control failures, civil-military analysis and industrial capacity—establishes that the selective exception of the force that holds the monopoly on organised violence has itself become the central institutional fact requiring explanation.

Forget the south or the sunbelt, leftists struggle to win in NYS outside of metro NYC and Buffalo).

Mole National Park, Ghana🇬🇭

Mole National Park is one of Ghana’s most remarkable wildlife destinations, stretching across the beautiful savannah landscapes of northern Ghana. It is the country’s largest national park and offers visitors an opportunity to experience wildlife in a peaceful and natural setting.

The park is especially known for its elephants, but visitors can also encounter buffalo, antelopes, warthogs, monkeys and a wide variety of birds. Walking and safari experiences make Mole a wonderful place to connect with Ghana’s wild side while enjoying the open landscapes and natural beauty of the region.

Mole is more than just a wildlife destination, it is a place where nature, adventure and the beauty of northern Ghana come together.

Okay.  So...
We probably need to establish here where you stand on the text.  Because your logic is coherent, but it isn't consistent with the Biblical text by any means, and you're making assertions the Bible never does.

Samuel never says anything even remotely approaching "animal offerings should cease until all are righteous with contrite hearts".

He says "to obey is better than sacrifice".

Contextually, that's really straightforward.  God gave Saul an instruction.  Saul disobeyed it and then used the spoil from his victory as sacrifices.

God wanted his obedience more than sacrifices.

That's quite literally all that passage tells you.

I'm assuming you're inferring "contrite heart" and not quoting - because I know that passage well enough.  It's Psalm 51.  And you're right, it says:

“For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it;
you will not be pleased with a burnt offering.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit;
a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.”

Good so far for your thesis, but the next two verses don't help your argument much:

“Do good to Zion in your good pleasure;
build up the walls of Jerusalem;
 then will you delight in right sacrifices,
in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings;
then bulls will be offered on your altar.”

Sounds like the same refrain to me. 
"To obey is better than sacrifice".

WORKING WITH TREE IS ONCE AGAIN A SPECIAL FORM OF WISDOM

The secret of a sacred tree is that it has abundant fire within it, which is not the case with other trees. Again, the fire generated by the plant kingdom is considered superior to the fire generated by the mineral kingdom, such as oil, gasoline, etc. Even meditations carried out in the shade of these trees have a great impact. The water in which the roots of these trees are placed has great healing effects.

Many people have attained initiations meditating under these trees, and even to this day, in the Shigatze cave temple, there is an enormous Ficus religiosa tree that glows golden. Members of the White Brotherhood meet there. This is just to give you an idea of ​​the need to select the type of wood needed for the ritual. 

Master Morya specifically mentions the cedar and the kapok (cotton tree) that grow in the Himalayas. We make sure the sticks are dry and also that we don't cut down the tree for fuel. We simply collect the fallen stems or twigs. That's sufficient. Ahimsa (harmlessness) is important. We can't cut down a tree to perform a fire ritual ourselves. This is how the Masters understand it.

Every tall, enormous tree is considered a great spirit in its own right. It is believed that invisible beings constantly meditate on the branches of these trees. For that reason, meditating under the shade of these trees is an added benefit that contributes to meditation. 

The tree blesses us; the beings within it bless us as well, and we are charged with the appropriate vibration for meditation. Exceptionally, tall trees transmit abundant solar energy, which is necessary for elevating consciousness. Working with trees is, once again, a special form of wisdom.

Occasionally, when we go to the forest, we can collect tree stems or twigs, or firewood from a fallen tree. In fact, the various plant materials used in the Fire Ritual are energetically related to different cosmic intelligences. The devas are pleased when the corresponding energy is offered to them as food.

They are pleased when, through Fire, we offer them food that is energetically pleasing to them. We experience the energy of each deva and recognize that same energy in the plant kingdom. Then we offer the herb or plant that corresponds to the deva's energy, invoking it with the appropriate sound. Such is the Fire ritual. 

Remember that no animal flesh or alcoholic beverages are used in the ritual. Nor are metals used. The ritual is entirely vegetarian! In black magic, meat, alcohol, liquor, kerosene, and gasoline are used, and even human flesh is used in black magic! The fire ritual associated with black magic begins at midnight, while rituals associated with white magic are performed between two lights. There are very few exceptional nights when it lasts until midnight.

Scientists of the spiritual realm have experimented with the energies of the various grains, legumes, and medicinal plants corresponding to the planetary, solar, and cosmic devas, utilizing them accordingly. For example, chickpeas have the energy of Jupiter, lentils, the energy of Saturn. 

Did you know that rice is from Venus and wheat is from Jupiter? Let's not think that everything belongs to Earth. Let's not think that everything belongs to Earth, but rather is made available on the subtle plane from other planets. Likewise, the variety of materials from the plant kingdom can be found in their planetary, solar, and cosmic energies.

PERSONALIS $PSNL OWNS ALL OF ITS BUYER'S DOWNSIDE AND NONE OF THE UPSIDE:

Personalis at $16.29, after a +$0.08 / +0.49% Monday. The Fremont, California company sells a blood test that hunts traces of cancer DNA left after treatment. Second of thirty on the Momentum Len5 watch.

Six runner-ups below, one per Len5, and no two are second for the same reason. Personalis is the strangest: what holds it back is not its business but a clause. It cannot rise on its own news any more, because the price it will be paid was fixed in July - and the market keeps paying more than that anyway.

On July 20 it agreed to be bought by Tempus AI at $61.60 (premarket), -$0.61 / -0.98% from Monday's $62.21 close, for $16.25 a share in the Chicago buyer's stock. That headline is not symmetrical:

- Above $48.42, measured as Tempus's average over the fifteen trading days before completion, holders receive however many Tempus shares are worth exactly $16.25. The buyer rising changes nothing.
- At or below $48.42 the swap locks at 0.3356 Tempus shares, and from there the payout falls with the buyer.

The upside stops at $16.25; the downside runs to $46.00, where Personalis wins the right to walk away and the locked swap is worth about $15.44. Tempus closed at $48.41 the day the deal was signed and $62.21 on Monday, +28.5%. Holders are owed the same $16.25 either way.

The market has not accepted that ceiling. Monday's close is four cents above it, and on August 21, across three days in which Tempus rose 25%, Personalis closed at $18.38 and touched $18.89 - 13% past the agreed number. Paying above a signed price is a bet the price does not hold: a raised offer, a rival, or a vote that says no. That vote has no date.

This Len5 wants a price near the top of its own one-year range, the recent climb and the longer one agreeing. Both hold: $4.955 on April 29 to $16.29 is +228.7%, the newest stretch the strongest part. Second rather than first is the range - the name ahead sits at its own high, Personalis 13.8% under its August 21 peak.

The business is doing its part and no longer setting the price. August 4, three months to June 30: revenue $22.4M, +30%, on 10,384 clinical tests, +199%, after Medicare widened what it will pay for. WATCH the buyer's shares instead - $48.42 is the only level that changes what a holder receives. CHANGE IT: a close above $18.89, now Tempus's job. WHEN: no vote date is set, and both companies expect to finish late 2026 or early 2027. RISK: if the deal breaks, this is a loss-making business again. Tempus AI fits none of the six Len5es - it loses money, leaving the value styles no earnings to discount.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Arch Capital Group at $97.42 (after hours), -$0.53 / -0.54% from Monday's $97.95 close, insures specialist risks and reinsures other insurers from Bermuda. Second of fifty-four on the Len5 hunting businesses nobody could rebuild, bought under their worth; Arch's version is the nerve to refuse business priced too thin. July 28, quarter to June 30: net income $1.0B, $3.00 a share, on a combined ratio of 83.5% - claims and costs took 83.5 cents of every premium dollar. CHANGE IT: strip out storms and old claims and that ratio was 82.5% against 80.9% a year earlier. WHEN: October 26 tentative, $1.85 carried against $2.56. VERDICT: 7.5 times profit at 1.43 times its $68.04 book value.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Broadridge Financial Solutions at $174.40 (premarket), +$0.01 / +0.01% after Monday's +$6.65 / +3.96%, prints and mails the proxy ballots your broker must send you. Second of fifty-one on the Len5 hunting settled earning power bought cheaply, and settled means billed again: recurring revenue, the fees charged every year rather than one-off work, grew 8% to $4.9B in the year to June 30, with adjusted profit of $9.60 a share, +12%, and a dividend raised 12% to $4.36. CHANGE IT: fiscal 2027 is mapped at 6% to 8% recurring growth, slower than the year just finished. WHEN: comments close September 21 on a Securities and Exchange Commission plan making email the default way investor documents reach you. VERDICT: about 18 times that $9.60, and 31.2% under the $253.36 it reached a year ago today.

GROWTH LEN5:
ServisFirst Bancshares at $42.30, after a +$0.17 / +0.40% Monday, lends to Southern businesses with almost no branches - 666 people in Birmingham, Alabama. Second of thirty on the Len5 hunting profit growth the price has not already charged for, and 14.4 times profit charges little. July 20, quarter to June 30: net income $85.8M against $61.4M, +39.7%, on a net interest margin - what a bank keeps on loans after paying its depositors - of 3.63%. CHANGE IT: that margin is the whole story and most of it came earlier, up 0.53 points on the year but only 0.10 of that last quarter. WHEN: October 19 tentative, $0.83 carried. VERDICT: the fastest grower here earned $0.79 against $0.79 expected - 40% growth, no surprise.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
AppLovin at $328.68 (premarket), -$5.56 / -1.66% from Monday's $334.24 close, runs the system that decides which advert appears inside a mobile app, with 898 people. Second of thirty on the Len5 hunting businesses early as well as fast. Fast is not arguable - August 5, quarter to June 30: revenue $1.92B, +53%; net income $1.27B, or 66 cents of every revenue dollar; money earned per app install +58% while installs fell 2%. Early is what holds it back a place, at a $111.8B company already carrying most of the advertising inside mobile games. CHANGE IT: the early piece is everything that is not games, where advertiser spending set a record in a quiet quarter. WHEN: November 4 tentative, $4.01 carried. VERDICT: 55.9% below its high of last September while growing 53%.

INCOME LEN5:
Euroseas at $74.80, after a +$0.24 / +0.32% Monday, owns containerships out of Athens and rents them to the lines that move boxes, on charters written in years. Second of thirty on the Len5 hunting cash reaching owners that the business itself funds, and funding is not close: the August 13 quarter earned $4.70 a share, and the $0.80 quarterly dividend - $3.20 a year, about 4.3% here - is paid tomorrow, covered nearly six times by that one quarter. text:
Freedom Fest Returns to Orange Beach: A Celebration of Cars, Music, and Coastal Culture

The City of Orange Beach is hosting its 6th Annual Freedom Fest at The Wharf on Saturday, September 19, and Sunday, September 20, 2026. Bringing together patriotic displays, local shopping, live entertainment, and coastal community spirit, this free, two-day celebration offers a full lineup of activities for residents and visitors alike.

The Island's Pinnacle Auto Expo

At the heart of the festival lies the Bama Coast Cruisin' Fall Car Show along Main Street and Wharf Parkway. The event has solidified its reputation as the pinnacle auto expo on the island, drawing hundreds of registered participants and thousands of spectators to admire classic hot rods, antique automobiles, custom trucks, and vintage cars from every era. Car enthusiasts can explore row after row of pristine rides, complete with VIP reserved parking spaces for entrants, door prize giveaways, and custom builds on display. The automotive showcase culminates on Sunday afternoon with a police-escorted 14-mile Beach Cruise along the scenic coastal highway.

Live Music Stages and Entertainment

Festivalgoers will find continuous live music at the Flora-Bama / CoastAL Music Stage located on the west side of The Wharf. Spanning both festival days, the stage highlights a diverse roster of regional musicians and bands, delivering energetic performances that keep the festival grounds buzzing from morning until late afternoon.

Food Vendors and Local Artisans

Alongside the musical performances, the west side of The Wharf hosts a large array of food vendors serving up fresh coastal cuisine, specialty snacks, signature festival treats, and refreshments operated in partnership with local community organizations. Visitors can stroll through rows of arts, crafts, and outdoor experience booths featuring handmade goods, woodwork, jewelry, and specialty items.

Family Activities and Community Spirit

Rounding out the event is a dedicated Kids' Zone located near the Ferris wheel, sponsored by the Orange Beach Police Department as a fundraiser for their K9 unit. Featuring inflatables, games, patriotic military booths, and family activities, Freedom Fest delivers an All-American weekend celebration of freedom, community, and Gulf Coast heritage.

Israel is fighting Hamas, the same Hamas that butchered civilians on October 7, still holds hostages, and has spent decades screaming they want every Jew gone from the river to the sea. That is not a slogan for freedom. That is a death wish for Israel.

Jews accepted a small, messy share. Arabs rejected it and invaded the second Israel declared independence. After 1967 Israel offered land for peace. The Arab League replied with three no’s: no peace, no recognition, no talks. In 2000 and 2008 Israeli leaders put real two-state deals on the table, most of the West Bank, Gaza, parts of Jerusalem. Palestinian leaders walked away both times.

While all that was happening nearly a million Jews were kicked out of Arab countries. Their communities got erased. The Arab population in Israel, the West Bank and Gaza exploded.

A ton of those viral “starving kids” photos were children with cystic fibrosis or other illnesses that nobody bothered mentioning. When celebrities slap on a keffiyeh and start yelling genocide without checking a single fact, they are not brave. They are useful idiots for people who never wanted two states. They wanted the Jewish one gone.

Britain’s 1939 White Paper slammed the door on Jews trying to escape the Holocaust. After the war they dumped tens of thousands of survivors in camps on Cyprus. Hundreds died there. Israel selling weapons years later was cold, ugly realpolitik, not some cartoon revenge plot.

As for the Irish comparing this to their history with the English, grow the fuck up. Ireland was colonised by an empire sending settlers to take the land. Jews were not an empire. They were a people with ancient roots who came back as refugees after two thousand years of exile, pogroms and near-extermination. The Arab side rejected every serious two-state offer and chose war. Hamas does not want better borders or equal rights. It wants Israel erased. That is not the same fight.

Wake the fuck up. Stop swallowing the propaganda Kool-Aid. The facts have been staring you in the face the whole time.

Palestinian leaders walked away both times.

The famine story is collapsing too. Actual surveys show child malnutrition in Gaza is among the lowest in the entire region. A ton of those viral “starving kids” photos were children with cystic fibrosis or other illnesses that nobody bothered mentioning. Hamas has been caught stockpiling and diverting aid while using civilians as human shields.

When celebrities slap on a keffiyeh and start yelling genocide without checking a single fact, they are not brave. They are useful idiots for people who never wanted two states. They wanted the Jewish one gone.

And you lot in Britain clutching your pearls over Israeli arms sales to Argentina in 1982 or some Falklands comments need a history lesson. Britain’s 1939 White Paper slammed the door on Jews trying to escape the Holocaust. After the war they dumped tens of thousands of survivors in camps on Cyprus. Hundreds died there. Israel selling weapons years later was cold, ugly realpolitik, not some cartoon revenge plot.

As for the Irish comparing this to their history with the English, grow the fuck up. Ireland was colonised by an empire sending settlers to take the land. Jews were not an empire. They were a people with ancient roots who came back as refugees after two thousand years of exile, pogroms and near-extermination. The Arab side rejected every serious two-state offer and chose war. Hamas does not want better borders or equal rights. It wants Israel erased. That is not the same fight.

Wake the fuck up. Stop swallowing the propaganda Kool-Aid. The facts have been staring you in the face the whole time.

text:
Dear God, thank You for this day.  Lord, forgive us our sins and lead us in seeking You with all of our hearts to abide in You through all we do.  Apart from You we are no good.  With You as our Guide we can do all things through Christ who strengthens us.  Establish our thoughts and direct our steps this whole day long that Your light might shine through us for the benefit of others, for Your glory alone.  Nevertheless Father, not our will but Your will be done.  In Christ we pray believing.  Amen and Amen 

Psalm 86:5

    [5] For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving,
        abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you.

"There were also with him other little ships."  Mark 4:36 

Jesus was the Lord High Admiral of the sea that night, and his presence preserved the whole convoy. It is well to sail with Jesus, even though it be in a little ship. When we sail in Christ's company, we may not make sure of fair weather, for great storms may toss the vessel which carries the Lord himself, and we must not expect to find the sea less boisterous around our little boat. 

If we go with Jesus we must be content to fare as he fares; and when the waves are rough to him, they will be rough to us. It is by tempest and tossing that we shall come to land, as he did before us.

Proverbs 16:3

    [3] 
    Commit your work to the LORD,
        and your plans will be established.

When the storm swept over Galilee's dark lake all faces gathered blackness, and all hearts dreaded shipwreck. When all creature help was useless, the slumbering Saviour arose, and with a word, transformed the riot of the tempest into the deep quiet of a calm; then were the little vessels at rest as well as that which carried the Lord. 

Jesus is the star of the sea; and though there be sorrow upon the sea, when Jesus is on it there is joy too. May our hearts make Jesus their anchor, their rudder, their lighthouse, their life-boat, and their harbour. 

Psalm 86:11

    [11] Teach me your way, O LORD,
        that I may walk in your truth;
        unite my heart to fear your name.

His Church is the Admiral's flagship, let us attend her movements, and cheer her officers with our presence. He himself is the great attraction; let us follow ever in his wake, mark his signals, steer by his chart, and never fear while he is within hail. 

Not one ship in the convoy shall suffer wreck; the great Commodore will steer every barque in safety to the desired haven. 

By faith we will slip our cable for another day's cruise, and sail forth with Jesus into a sea of tribulation. Winds and waves will not spare us, but they all obey him; and, therefore, whatever squalls may occur without, faith shall feel a blessed calm within. He is ever in the centre of the weather-beaten company: let us rejoice in him. His vessel has reached the haven, and so shall ours.

Hebrews 5:7-10

[7] In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence. [8] Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. [9] And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, [10] being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

Revelation 3:8

[8] “‘I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

text:
My friend @johnsw launched his new book today, ‘Crazy Successful’.

It offers a positive take on neurodiversity and explores the hidden advantages for entrepreneurs.

This is the book I needed as a kid.

I’m diagnosed with four conditions, including ADHD and dyslexia. I was expelled from two schools.

Today, I wake up next to the ocean and get paid to explain how exciting technology products will improve people's lives.

I wouldn’t take a ‘cure’ if you offered it to me.

👉🏻 ADHD gives me the ability to hyperfocus on certain tasks. The trick is learning how to game my brain into obsessing over useful work.

👉🏻 Dyslexia makes me a better copywriter, as I'm so sensitive to visual hierarchy.

I've always hated rules.

But now I understand that's because I prefer to design my own systems for work.

Three things changed my life:

1. Thai boxing taught me the relationship between effort and growth.

2. Sales rewarded objective results rather than obedience to a prescribed process.

3. Tech startups gave me role models: ridiculously successful entrepreneurs with brains like mine.

I had to learn these lessons the slow way.

Your kids, friends and students don't.

Buy them a copy of 'Crazy Successful'.

text:
A prayer of complete trust in Allah.

Sharing the beautiful prayer offered by the Holy Prophet (sa) during the Tahajjud prayer, Beloved Huzoor (aba) narrated:

“Tawus relates that he heard Hazrat Ibn Abbas (ra) say that when the Holy Prophet (sa) would wake up at night to offer the Tahajjud prayer [voluntary predawn prayer], he would supplicate the following. It is a lengthy prayer and its translation is as follows.

‘O Allah! All praise belongs to You. You are the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth and all that is therein and all praise belongs to You. To You belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and all that is contained within them and all praise belongs to You. You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and all therein and all praise belongs to You. You are the King of the heavens and the earth and all that is therein and all praise belongs to You. You are the Truth, Your promise is true, the final reckoning with You is true, Your word is true, Paradise is true, Hell is true, all the Prophets are true, Muhammad (sa) is true and the Hour is true.

O Allah! I have submitted myself to You, believed in You, placed my trust only in You, turned only towards You and only for your sake have I taken up this dispute (or only with Your help have I confronted my opponents) and I have sought judgement only from You. Forgive me my earlier and latter sins, as well as those that I have concealed and those that I have disclosed. You are the One Who hastens and You are the One Who delays. There is none worthy of worship but You.’ It is also narrated that he would say: ‘There is no God besides You.’ This is a narration found in Sahih al-Bukhari.”

text:
A New Book Seeks to Shame the Elites Who Caved to Trump

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 6:32 min
14SEP2026
By Michelle Goldberg
https://t.co/YkRoUuynmq
The thing I’ve found most shocking about Donald Trump’s second presidency is not the epic grift, the ICE paramilitary violence or the assaults on free speech. 

These abuses, while horrifying, are predictable. 

What has stunned me has been the capitulation of so many American elites to Trump’s vulgar authoritarianism.

I didn’t expect major law firms, some that have long boasted about their progressive pro bono work, to fold with barely a fight. 

I didn’t expect TV networks to settle bogus lawsuits by paying the president millions, or for Ivy League schools such as Columbia to relinquish autonomy over curriculum, admissions and student discipline. 

In Hungary, it took years for Viktor Orban’s government to bring most of academia, the news media and other pillars of civil society to heel. 

Why were so many powerful people in America, a country whose civic culture is steeped in resistance to tyranny, so willing to abase themselves and their institutions?

That’s the question at the heart of Jacob Weisberg’s important new book, “Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era.” 

It’s an inverted version of John F. Kennedy’s “Profiles in Courage,” offering character studies of eight people who gave in to Trump despite surely knowing better. 

Reading it made me wonder if there’s something about America today that selects for spinelessness at the highest levels.

Some of Weisberg’s choices perplexed me; a few of the figures he focuses on are less morally compromised than simply rotten. 

There’s nothing that mysterious, at least to me, in the failure of people like Mitch McConnell, Megyn Kelly or the vulture capitalist Stephen Schwarzman to display much democratic integrity. 

What’s harder to fathom is why people who presented themselves as bulwarks against Trumpism during his first term made such degrading compromises during his second.

The Amazon founder and Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos adopted the motto “Democracy Dies in Darkness” for his newspaper during the first Trump presidency, then gutted it during the second. 

As president of Barnard during the first Trump administration, Sian Beilock championed sweeping antiracism initiatives. 

In Trump’s second term, as president of Dartmouth, she has kept mostly mum about Trump’s attacks on higher education. 

These are people who once knew how dangerous Trump was, but now that he’s worse than ever, they’re pretending not to see. Why?

The answers are a little different in each case, but they usually involve intra-elite competition. 

From the outside, these people look as if they can easily afford to risk acts of bravery. 

But they’re consumed in different ways with making sure their peers don’t get ahead of them. 

Courage is contagious, but so, it turns out, is cravenness.

An emblematic example in Weisberg’s book is Brad Karp, the former chairman of the law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison, which owed its reputation to its work for civil rights. 

As Weisberg writes, Paul Weiss was the first major New York law firm to hire a Black associate, William Coleman, who would help write some of the legal briefs in Brown v. the Board of Education. 

It represented Edith Windsor in her landmark 2013 gay marriage case.

During the first Trump administration, Karp assigned 75 lawyers to fight Trump’s family separation policy. 

“Each of us needs to do what we believe is right, whatever the consequences,” Karp said in a 2024 interview.

So it’s astonishing that less than a year later, after Trump issued an executive order targeting the firm, Karp made a deal with the administration that included providing $40 million in pro bono work, which has included services for the Commerce Department. 

As Weisberg points out, Paul Weiss’s surrender helped set off “a bidding war for submission.” 

Today, the firm’s culture has changed; gone from its website are pages that once described its work on voting rights, reproductive rights and immigrant rights.

Why would anyone sell out his own ostensible values the way Karp did? 

Weisberg, who interviewed Karp for the book, attributes his decision-making to Paul Weiss’s changing financial underpinnings. 

In the 2010s, the firm became a leader in the spectacularly lucrative field of private equity law. 

Competition for star lawyers who demanded salaries in the eight figures was fierce, since clients tended to be more loyal to their attorneys than to their firms. 

Threatened by Trump, Karp feared an exodus of partners and the loss of one of the firm’s biggest clients, Apollo Global Management, whose chief executive is a powerful Republican donor. 

Karp repeatedly described Paul Weiss’s peril as “existential.”

But as Weisberg points out, the stakes were hardly as grand as that word implies. Karp and his colleagues weren’t facing prison or penury. 

“An average of $7.5 million per partner might have fallen to, who knows, $4 or $5 million for a couple of years,” writes Weisberg. 

That’s a real hit, but it’s not exactly martyrdom.

Ultimately, Trump’s return to office brought Karp down, though not in the way he feared. 

This year, he was forced to resign after the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, which revealed that Karp had socialized with the sex trafficker and offered him free legal advice. 

Karp met Epstein through one of his prized clients, Leon Black, Apollo’s billionaire co-founder. 

Given the waters Karp swam in, the idea of choosing decency over riches might have seemed foolish. 

Paul Weiss is now one of the most profitable law firms in the world; revenue is up almost 24 percent.

The philosopher Susan Neiman’s new book, “Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era,” is a useful companion to “Profiles in Cowardice.” 

Like Weisberg, Neiman wanted to explain why so many institutions caved to Trump. 

She believes it begins with an ethos that disdains virtue as hypocritical or naïve. 

“When self-interest becomes the basis of reason, evil no longer needs to justify itself,” she writes. 

“It’s already been mistaken for rationality.”

Neiman cites research showing that “the longer people study economics, the more selfish they become.” 

The reason, as she interprets it, is that they grow convinced that maximizing self-interest is normal, and that to do otherwise makes you a sucker. 

The more the logic of capitalism pervades the rest of life, the less room there is for compassion, honor or heroism. 

Maybe that’s why some of the people most financially able to defend liberal democracy have decided it’s one of the few luxuries they can live without.

A New Book Seeks to Shame the Elites Who Caved to Trump

NYT Gift Article link

14SEP2026
By Michelle Goldberg
https://t.co/YkRoUuynmq
The thing I’ve found most shocking about Donald Trump’s second presidency is not the epic grift, the ICE paramilitary violence or the assaults on free speech. 

These abuses, while horrifying, are predictable. 

What has stunned me has been the capitulation of so many American elites to Trump’s vulgar authoritarianism.

I didn’t expect major law firms, some that have long boasted about their progressive pro bono work, to fold with barely a fight. 

I didn’t expect TV networks to settle bogus lawsuits by paying the president millions, or for Ivy League schools such as Columbia to relinquish autonomy over curriculum, admissions and student discipline. 

In Hungary, it took years for Viktor Orban’s government to bring most of academia, the news media and other pillars of civil society to heel. 

Why were so many powerful people in America, a country whose civic culture is steeped in resistance to tyranny, so willing to abase themselves and their institutions?

That’s the question at the heart of Jacob Weisberg’s important new book, “Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era.” 

It’s an inverted version of John F. Kennedy’s “Profiles in Courage,” offering character studies of eight people who gave in to Trump despite surely knowing better. 

Reading it made me wonder if there’s something about America today that selects for spinelessness at the highest levels.

Some of Weisberg’s choices perplexed me; a few of the figures he focuses on are less morally compromised than simply rotten. 

There’s nothing that mysterious, at least to me, in the failure of people like Mitch McConnell, Megyn Kelly or the vulture capitalist Stephen Schwarzman to display much democratic integrity. 

What’s harder to fathom is why people who presented themselves as bulwarks against Trumpism during his first term made such degrading compromises during his second.

The Amazon founder and Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos adopted the motto “Democracy Dies in Darkness” for his newspaper during the first Trump presidency, then gutted it during the second. 

As president of Barnard during the first Trump administration, Sian Beilock championed sweeping antiracism initiatives. 

In Trump’s second term, as president of Dartmouth, she has kept mostly mum about Trump’s attacks on higher education. 

These are people who once knew how dangerous Trump was, but now that he’s worse than ever, they’re pretending not to see. Why?

The answers are a little different in each case, but they usually involve intra-elite competition. 

From the outside, these people look as if they can easily afford to risk acts of bravery. 

But they’re consumed in different ways with making sure their peers don’t get ahead of them. 

Courage is contagious, but so, it turns out, is cravenness.

An emblematic example in Weisberg’s book is Brad Karp, the former chairman of the law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison, which owed its reputation to its work for civil rights. 

As Weisberg writes, Paul Weiss was the first major New York law firm to hire a Black associate, William Coleman, who would help write some of the legal briefs in Brown v. the Board of Education. 

It represented Edith Windsor in her landmark 2013 gay marriage case.

During the first Trump administration, Karp assigned 75 lawyers to fight Trump’s family separation policy. 

“Each of us needs to do what we believe is right, whatever the consequences,” Karp said in a 2024 interview.

So it’s astonishing that less than a year later, after Trump issued an executive order targeting the firm, Karp made a deal with the administration that included providing $40 million in pro bono work, which has included services for the Commerce Department. 

As Weisberg points out, Paul Weiss’s surrender helped set off “a bidding war for submission.” 

Today, the firm’s culture has changed; gone from its website are pages that once described its work on voting rights, reproductive rights and immigrant rights.

Why would anyone sell out his own ostensible values the way Karp did? 

Weisberg, who interviewed Karp for the book, attributes his decision-making to Paul Weiss’s changing financial underpinnings. 

In the 2010s, the firm became a leader in the spectacularly lucrative field of private equity law. 

Competition for star lawyers who demanded salaries in the eight figures was fierce, since clients tended to be more loyal to their attorneys than to their firms. 

Threatened by Trump, Karp feared an exodus of partners and the loss of one of the firm’s biggest clients, Apollo Global Management, whose chief executive is a powerful Republican donor. 

Karp repeatedly described Paul Weiss’s peril as “existential.”

But as Weisberg points out, the stakes were hardly as grand as that word implies. Karp and his colleagues weren’t facing prison or penury. 

“An average of $7.5 million per partner might have fallen to, who knows, $4 or $5 million for a couple of years,” writes Weisberg. 

That’s a real hit, but it’s not exactly martyrdom.

Ultimately, Trump’s return to office brought Karp down, though not in the way he feared. 

This year, he was forced to resign after the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, which revealed that Karp had socialized with the sex trafficker and offered him free legal advice. 

Karp met Epstein through one of his prized clients, Leon Black, Apollo’s billionaire co-founder. 

Given the waters Karp swam in, the idea of choosing decency over riches might have seemed foolish. 

Paul Weiss is now one of the most profitable law firms in the world; revenue is up almost 24 percent.

The philosopher Susan Neiman’s new book, “Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era,” is a useful companion to “Profiles in Cowardice.” 

Like Weisberg, Neiman wanted to explain why so many institutions caved to Trump. 

She believes it begins with an ethos that disdains virtue as hypocritical or naïve. 

“When self-interest becomes the basis of reason, evil no longer needs to justify itself,” she writes. 

“It’s already been mistaken for rationality.”

Neiman cites research showing that “the longer people study economics, the more selfish they become.” 

The reason, as she interprets it, is that they grow convinced that maximizing self-interest is normal, and that to do otherwise makes you a sucker. 

The more the logic of capitalism pervades the rest of life, the less room there is for compassion, honor or heroism. 

Maybe that’s why some of the people most financially able to defend liberal democracy have decided it’s one of the few luxuries they can live without.

If the Clarity Act fails to advance today, I think many people are underestimating the significance of that outcome.

The consequence would extend far beyond another failed vote in Washington. It could mean years of continued regulatory ambiguity for one of the most important technological and financial transformations of our generation.

That would be a profound strategic mistake for the United States.

Blockchain infrastructure, stablecoins, tokenized assets and digital markets are not dependent on congressional approval to continue evolving. The innovation will move forward regardless. The real question is whether the companies, capital, talent and infrastructure behind that transition remain anchored in the United States or migrate to jurisdictions willing to provide clearer rules.

The SEC and CFTC may be able to offer temporary regulatory relief and greater clarity through rulemaking, but administrative policy is not a substitute for durable legislation. Businesses making decade-long investments cannot responsibly operate under a framework that may shift with every election cycle or change in agency leadership.

This debate is therefore much larger than crypto prices, partisan politics or the interests of a single industry.

It is ultimately about whether the United States intends to lead the development of the financial infrastructure that may define the next several decades, or concede that leadership through institutional paralysis.

Senators on both sides should recognize the scale of the decision in front of them.

The Clarity Act advancing today matters far more than most people realize.

MY 2 CENTS | THE CLARITY ACT: FROM FIT21 TO TODAY

WHY THIS MAY BE THE MOST IMPORTANT U.S. CRYPTO MARKET-STRUCTURE BATTLE YET

1️⃣ The CLARITY Act did not appear from nowhere. Its political and legislative roots go directly back to FIT21, the Financial Innovation and Technology for the 21st Century Act, which passed the House in May 2024 by 279–136, including support from 71 Democrats, but never became law. FIT21 was the first serious congressional attempt to answer a question that had dominated U.S. crypto regulation for years: when should a digital asset be treated as a security, when should it be treated as a commodity, and which federal regulator should supervise the market around it?

The new Congress essentially restarted that project. On May 29, 2025, lawmakers introduced H.R. 3633, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. The objective was never simply to “legalize crypto”, because crypto was already legal. The real objective was to replace years of regulation through enforcement, court cases and agency interpretation with an actual statutory market structure. That distinction matters enormously. A functioning capital market requires participants to understand the rules before deploying capital, not after receiving an enforcement notice.

2️⃣ The House moved surprisingly quickly. After committee work during the spring and early summer of 2025, the House passed CLARITY on July 17 by a bipartisan 294–134 vote. That was a significant political signal because comprehensive crypto regulation had moved beyond being an issue supported exclusively by one party or by the industry itself.

The timing is equally important. One day later, President Trump signed the GENIUS Act, creating the first dedicated federal framework for payment stablecoins. The two pieces of legislation are often discussed together, but they address different layers of the digital-asset economy. GENIUS primarily addresses who can issue payment stablecoins, how reserves must be managed and what regulatory standards apply to those issuers. CLARITY is much broader. It attempts to determine how digital assets are classified, how spot markets operate, which intermediaries must register, what disclosures are required and where the SEC’s jurisdiction ends and the CFTC’s begins. GENIUS built one important room. CLARITY is trying to design the architecture of the entire house.

3️⃣ At the heart of CLARITY is the division of regulatory authority between the SEC and the CFTC. The legislation creates a clearer statutory framework for “digital commodities” and substantially expands the CFTC’s role in supervising their spot markets, while assets and transactions that remain securities stay inside the SEC perimeter.

This sounds like bureaucratic plumbing, but economically it is one of the most important parts of the bill. The CFTC already regulates derivatives markets and has anti-fraud powers in commodity spot markets, but the United States has historically lacked a comprehensive federal licensing framework for ordinary crypto spot exchanges trading non-security digital assets. CLARITY attempts to fill that gap by creating registration, customer-protection, disclosure, segregation and market-integrity requirements for digital-commodity exchanges, brokers and dealers.

For issuers and projects, the broader objective is equally important: provide a legal pathway that allows the market to know in advance which regulatory regime applies. If successful, that would be a major departure from the years in which the legal status of a token could effectively depend on which enforcement action arrived first.

4️⃣ The Senate, however, did not simply receive the House bill and rubber-stamp it. During late 2025 and throughout 2026, the market-structure framework was rebuilt through both the Senate Agriculture Committee and the Senate Banking Committee because digital assets cut across commodities law and securities law simultaneously.

In January 2026, the Agriculture Committee advanced the Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act, creating a proposed CFTC framework for digital commodities with requirements covering customer-fund segregation, conflicts of interest, disclosures, exchange registration and protections for software developers. Then, on May 14, the Banking Committee advanced H.R. 3633 by 15–9 after months of bipartisan negotiation.

This means the CLARITY Act being debated today is not simply the House bill that passed in July 2025. The Senate process has changed important provisions involving DeFi, banking, AML, public-official ethics, stablecoin rewards, customer protection and the division of power between regulators. If the Senate ultimately passes an amended version, the House will still have to accept those changes or Congress will need to reconcile the two texts before a final bill can reach the President.

5️⃣ For me, DeFi and self-custody are among the most important parts of the entire debate because this is where regulation can either recognize the technological difference between decentralized software and a financial intermediary or erase that distinction completely.

The current framework attempts to protect genuinely non-custodial developers, software providers and distributed-ledger infrastructure from automatically being regulated as traditional financial institutions simply because they publish code or participate in network operation. At the same time, lawmakers are trying to ensure that businesses cannot escape regulation merely by attaching the word “DeFi” to an architecture in which a small group still controls customer assets, transaction policy or the economic outcome.

That distinction is fundamental. Writing open-source software is not economically equivalent to holding customer deposits. Validating a decentralized network is not the same activity as operating a custodial exchange. Regulation should follow control, custody and intermediation.

The danger is that an overly broad interpretation of “control” could gradually push decentralized infrastructure into the same identity, surveillance and compliance perimeter as centralized banking. If that happens, America may succeed in regulating crypto while simultaneously eliminating some of the characteristics that made decentralized networks worth building in the first place.

6️⃣ This is also why calling CLARITY a simple “deregulation bill” is inaccurate. The Senate framework expands federal oversight of digital-asset intermediaries, including anti-money-laundering obligations, customer protections, registration requirements, sanctions tools and information-sharing mechanisms. Registered exchanges, brokers and dealers would operate much more like regulated financial institutions than many crypto platforms did during the early years of the industry.

Supporters argue that this is precisely the point: bring major activity onshore, give legitimate companies a pathway to compliance, create stronger protections for consumers and give law enforcement clearer tools against fraud and illicit finance.

Critics, including Democratic members of the Senate Banking Committee, have argued that some versions of the legislation still leave vulnerabilities involving sanctions evasion, national-security threats and parts of DeFi. That criticism should not simply be dismissed as “anti-crypto”. A durable framework needs to solve both sides of the equation: enough freedom for decentralized technology to function, but enough accountability that centralized actors cannot hide behind blockchain terminology while performing traditional financial activities.

My concern is therefore not whether crypto should have rules. It obviously needs rules where intermediaries hold other people’s assets. The real question is how far those rules should extend into peer-to-peer software and non-custodial activity.

7️⃣ One of the most revealing battles around CLARITY is not actually about Bitcoin, Ethereum or token classification. It is about stablecoin rewards and the banking system.

Banks are worried that crypto platforms could offer rewards on stablecoin balances in ways that make tokenized dollars increasingly attractive substitutes for conventional bank deposits. The crypto industry argues that competition should be allowed and that digital-dollar products can deliver more efficient financial services. Community banks respond that they use deposits to fund loans to households and businesses and that large-scale migration of deposits into stablecoins could increase their funding costs or reduce their lending capacity.

This is where a seemingly narrow crypto bill begins affecting the architecture of the broader financial system. If trillions of dollars eventually migrate from deposits into tokenized cash instruments, the impact will not stop at Coinbase or stablecoin issuers. It could change bank funding, credit creation, deposit pricing and even the transmission mechanism of monetary policy.

The latest compromise attempts to address the issue through a regulatory circuit breaker rather than an outright prohibition. That is politically understandable, but it illustrates the deeper point: crypto legislation is no longer about regulating a niche technology. It is increasingly about deciding who controls the economics of digital money.

8️⃣ Ethics became another major obstacle because lawmakers were being asked to write the rules for an industry in which elected officials and their families can themselves have significant financial interests.

Democratic negotiators argued that comprehensive crypto legislation could not credibly move forward without stronger restrictions preventing senior public officials from directly profiting from businesses affected by the regulatory framework they help create. The debate became particularly intense around President Trump’s family crypto interests, but the principle should apply far beyond any individual administration.

The revised Senate text released ahead of today’s vote contains a large number of changes negotiated with Democrats, including stronger ethics provisions and additional enforcement mechanisms. Reuters reports that Republicans incorporated 126 substantive Democratic changes in an attempt to build the coalition necessary for passage.

Whether those provisions are sufficient remains politically contested. My position is simpler: crypto market structure should be written so that it remains credible regardless of whether the White House is controlled by Republicans or Democrats. A regulatory system that appears designed to benefit or punish whichever political faction is currently in power would not create regulatory certainty. It would merely replace agency uncertainty with political uncertainty.

9️⃣ Today, September 15, 2026, is therefore important, but the process needs to be described accurately. The Senate is not yet voting on final enactment of the CLARITY Act. The immediate test is procedural: whether the Senate can obtain the 60 votes needed to move the legislation forward.

That threshold is crucial because Republicans cannot reach 60 votes alone. Democratic support is therefore not optional; it is mathematically necessary. The 15–9 bipartisan Banking Committee vote showed that some cross-party support exists, but committee cooperation does not automatically translate into 60 votes on the Senate floor.

If the procedural vote succeeds, the legislation still has to survive debate, amendments and eventual final passage. Because the Senate text has changed materially from the version passed by the House, reconciliation between the two chambers would still be required before the legislation could reach the President.

If the vote fails, the political calendar becomes a major problem. Congress is moving toward the November midterms, legislative time is limited and failure to enact the bill before the end of the congressional term could force lawmakers to restart significant parts of the process.

This is why today matters even though it is not the final vote. It determines whether almost two years of market-structure work moves into the final legislative phase or risks being pushed back into another political cycle.

🔟 MY 2 CENTS: I am broadly supportive of what CLARITY is trying to achieve because the United States cannot build a serious digital-asset industry indefinitely through enforcement actions, contradictory agency interpretations and court decisions. Markets need rules that participants can understand before they invest capital, build infrastructure or launch products.

But the quality of those rules matters much more than simply passing something with “clarity” in the title.

A good framework should give the CFTC meaningful authority over genuine digital-commodity spot markets while preserving SEC jurisdiction where there is actually a security or investment contract. It should require strong customer protections from custodial exchanges because anyone holding other people’s assets creates genuine counterparty risk. It should preserve self-custody, peer-to-peer transfers and open-source development because those activities are fundamentally different from operating a financial intermediary. It should prevent companies from using fake decentralization as a regulatory loophole, but it should also prevent regulators from treating every decentralized protocol as if it were JPMorgan with a blockchain interface.

For Bitcoin specifically, CLARITY does not suddenly create a new legal identity. BTC already occupies the commodity side of the U.S. regulatory spectrum. The benefit is broader: clearer rules for spot markets, intermediaries, custody and institutional participation reduce the regulatory uncertainty surrounding the infrastructure through which Bitcoin is traded and held.

For the broader crypto market, the consequences could be much larger. Clear token-classification rules could reduce the probability that a project spends years building in the United States only to discover later that regulators consider its token an unregistered security. Exchanges could know what they are legally permitted to list. Banks, brokers and asset managers could allocate capital with a clearer understanding of the regulatory perimeter. Tokenization projects could move from legal experimentation toward scalable financial infrastructure.

My BASE CASE is therefore not that passage of CLARITY automatically sends every altcoin higher. Regulation does not create product-market fit, decentralization or useful technology. What it can create is a lower regulatory risk premium for legitimate U.S. crypto businesses.

My BULL CASE is much more important over a five-to-ten-year horizon: legal certainty encourages banks, exchanges, brokers, asset managers, technology companies and institutional investors to build digital-asset infrastructure inside the United States rather than offshore. That could make America one of the central jurisdictions for tokenized finance, digital commodities and blockchain-based capital markets.

My BEAR CASE is that political compromise produces a framework so complex, expensive and identity-heavy that only the largest exchanges, banks and asset managers can comply economically. That outcome would be ironic: legislation designed to legitimize decentralized finance could accelerate concentration in the hands of the same large intermediaries crypto was originally designed to reduce dependence on.

My BEAR CASE is that political compromise ultimately produces a framework so complex, expensive and identity-heavy that compliance becomes economically sustainable only for the largest exchanges, banks and asset managers. Such an outcome would create an uncomfortable contradiction: legislation designed to give decentralized finance greater legitimacy could unintentionally accelerate concentration in the hands of the same large intermediaries whose role crypto originally sought to reduce.

This is the regulatory balance Congress still has to find. The United States clearly needs a more predictable legal framework for digital assets, particularly where custodial businesses hold customer funds, operate centralized markets or expose investors to counterparty risk. Stronger standards for segregation of assets, disclosure, fraud prevention and accountability are therefore not incompatible with the principles of crypto; in many cases they are necessary if institutional participation is expected to grow.

The difficulty begins when rules designed for companies that control customer assets are extended too broadly to genuinely decentralized protocols, non-custodial software and self-custody. Open-source developers and users interacting directly with permissionless networks do not perform the same economic function as exchanges, brokers or banks, and regulation should preserve that distinction. A successful CLARITY framework would therefore protect investors where identifiable intermediaries create identifiable risks, while avoiding the reconstruction of the traditional financial architecture — including unnecessary identity collection and centralized gatekeeping — on top of networks that were specifically designed to operate differently. 

But genuine decentralization, self-custody and open-source software should not be forced into a regulatory architecture created for institutions that control other people’s money.

The best CLARITY Act would regulate intermediaries because they intermediate, not networks merely because they exist.

Today’s vote will not finish the American crypto-regulation debate.

It will tell us whether Washington is finally prepared to move that debate from enforcement actions and courtroom interpretations into actual law.

And if it succeeds, the long-term impact may be considerably more important than whatever BTC does in the first five minutes after the vote.

• Somaliland’s case is not one of secession, but the restoration of its sovereign statehood within the internationally recognised borders of 26 June 1960.
