text:
Our research has been published in the inaugural issue of the peer-reviewed journal The Digital Hate Review.

We analysed 1,378 articles published between February and May 2024 by eight major news outlets: The Guardian, The New York Times, BBC, CNN, The Washington Post, Reuters, Associated Press, and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

The study examines a gap in journalistic standards in reporting on military conflict, specifically, the reporting of casualty figures in Gaza.

During the most heavily covered war in Gaza’s history, we found a striking asymmetry in the use of sources. 

Both principal sources offered incomplete information:

• Gaza’s Hamas-run Ministry of Health reported total deaths, without distinguishing between civilians and combatants.

• Israel reported figures for killed combatants.

Comparing these two sets of data is essential for assessing one of the central questions of the war: the proportion of civilian and combatant casualties.

Yet Israeli figures appeared in only 3% of the articles we analysed. This systematic omission led to removing Hamas combatants from the public picture and reinforced a narrative in which Israel is fighting Gaza’s civilian population alone.

News outlets also increasingly failed to identify primary sources. The Guardian was the clear outlier: in 43% of the articles in which it cited casualty figures from Gaza’s Hamas-run Ministry of Health, it did not identify the source at all.

While the UN sources put disclaimers saying that the data from Gaza still hasn’t been independently verified, this disclaimer is almost absent in the media.

Instead, the figures were presented as self-evident or generally known information. This was the highest rate among all the outlets we analysed. 

This imbalance also matters beyond the media. International institutions often treat press reporting as an epistemic authority. For example, when citing the number of killed militants, the UN commission referred to a Guardian article rather than to IDF data.

The Guardian article relied on a database of individually named militants, a figure nearly twice lower than the IDF’s reported total number of killed militants.

Our article examines how these reporting choices can shape an “authoritative version of reality”, and why standards of sourcing, attribution, and context are so important in conflict reporting.

text:
AND THEY HAD ALREADY SENT THOSE CHEMISTS TO THAT EXACT ADDRESS.

February 26, 1993. A truck bomb detonates in the parking garage under the North Tower.

The Justice Department's own review of the FBI Laboratory records what happened next. The Laboratory's chemists specializing in explosives residue analysis went to New York City immediately to conduct examinations at the blast scene. Doing so, the report notes, "left no chemists specializing in explosives residue analysis at the laboratory in Washington."

Read that again.

The FBI sent every chemist it had specializing in explosives-residue analysis to the World Trade Center. Headquarters had no residue specialists left.

Now here is the part that matters most, and I want to be precise about it, because it cuts against the lazy version of my own argument.

Those chemists did not find residue identifying the main charge.

The OIG says so directly. The 1,200-pound urea nitrate figure everyone remembers did not come from residue recovered at the scene. It came from blast reconstruction and from chemicals traced to the defendants. The OIG spent an entire section criticizing an FBI examiner for blurring exactly that distinction in court.

And when a different FBI chemist did report detecting urea nitrate on a tire fragment from the scene, the two residue specialists fought it. They argued the instrument had only shown urea and nitric acid, which can come from urine, fertilizer, car exhaust or ice melter. They ran a blind test on their own unit chief using one of their own urine samples and a urea-fertilizer mix. The original report was amended.

Sit with what that tells you.

The agency the conspiracists insist would bury explosive residue is an agency whose own residue chemists went to that building, found nothing that identified the explosive, put that negative in writing, and then went to war with their own colleagues to stop an overstated positive from standing.

That is not a laboratory that manufactures findings to fit a narrative. That is a laboratory that had a screaming internal fight over whether a single tire fragment was good enough.

Eight years later, the FBI Laboratory and its explosives experts worked that same complex again.

So the proposition on offer is this: the lab that had already sent every residue chemist it had to the World Trade Center, and that had already demonstrated it would report a negative and defend that negative against internal disagreement, suddenly could not or would not look.

2/4

text:
Snapchat Camera for Chrome now public

If you’ve ever wanted to spice up your video calls with some digital flair, this might just be the ticket.
Snapchat Camera for Chrome now public

So what exactly is this all about? The Snapchat Camera for Chrome extension lets users apply augmented reality (AR) lenses during live streams or video chats on platforms like Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and more. It’s essentially a way to bring the fun of Snapchat filters into your professional life—or any other setting where a webcam might be involved.
Why Does This Matter?

But why does this matter? For starters, it’s a clever workaround for hardware limitations. The extension bypasses local processing by offloading all the heavy lifting to Snap’s cloud infrastructure. This means you can use Snapchat Lenses even if your laptop isn’t exactly cutting-edge tech. So if you’re stuck with an underpowered machine but still want to look like a superhero in your next meeting, this might be the solution.
How Does It Work?

Here’s how it works: install the extension from the Chrome Web Store, sign in with your Snapchat account, and select “Snapchat Camera” as your camera source in supported web apps. Then, click the Snapchat Camera icon to open the extension pane, choose a lens, and voilà—your video calls are now AR-enhanced.
What Is Stored?

When you use Snapchat Camera for Chrome, your video stream is sent to Snap’s servers for processing. This means that while the extension itself doesn’t store any data locally on your device, Snap has access to your footage during the session. The company claims it won't collect or use this data outside of providing the core functionality of the AR lenses.
What Is Excluded?

It's worth noting that Snapchat Camera for Chrome does not work with Discord (Web) due to limitations in how Discord handles custom camera sources. If you’re a frequent Discord user, you might need to look elsewhere for similar features.
User Controls

You have control over whether or not to use the extension and which lenses you apply during your video calls. Additionally, Snap provides an option to disable the extension entirely from within Chrome’s settings if you decide it's no longer needed.
Availability

The Snapchat Camera for Chrome is currently available as a public preview in the Chrome Web Store. While it supports numerous platforms like Google Meet, Microsoft Teams (Web), Zoom (Web), Amazon Chime (Web), StreamYard, Restream, Loom, Canva, WeVideo, Facebook, Vimeo, Instagram, and Veed, Discord (Web) is notably excluded.
What This Does Not Prove

While Snapchat Camera for Chrome offers an innovative way to enhance video calls with AR lenses, it doesn’t prove that all webcams will suddenly become cutting-edge devices overnight. It’s a workaround rather than a hardware upgrade.
Practical Takeaway

Is this a game-changer or just another tech trend? If you’re looking to add some fun and creativity to your video calls without worrying about the limitations of your device, Snapchat Camera for Chrome might be worth trying out. However, if privacy concerns are paramount or you find the cost prohibitive, it might not be the right fit.

So what changes for you? If you’ve ever wished you could use Snapchat filters during video calls but were held back by hardware limitations, this might be the ticket. But if you’re concerned about privacy or skeptical of the value proposition, it’s worth thinking twice before jumping in.
What Do You Think?

text:
I built my entire tech stack from the ground up: I create all my indicators from scratch, and I designed my own engine exporters, terminal, console, and automated reporting systems that run cross-instrument volatility analysis. Yet, despite building all this infrastructure, I refuse to write crypto code in the United States out of genuine fear of going to prison, which makes relocating to Dubai an increasingly attractive reality.

The threat of criminal prosecution for software creators cuts right to the heart of the current legislative fight on Capitol Hill. In my second article, I focused heavily on macro architecture, T-bill reserves, and stablecoin asset backing, but the threat of developer imprisonment remains the most dangerous unresolved issue in the final text of the CLARITY Act. Under the current enforcement environment and precursor legislation like the GENIUS Act, operating an unlicensed money transmission business carries severe criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. 1960. The core fear for developers like me has always been that simply writing, publishing, or maintaining open-source smart contracts could be legally conflated with running an unlicensed financial institution.

The latest legislative draft attempts to address this concern by incorporating a control-based framework. Under this compromise, if I publish open-source code or maintain a decentralized protocol without holding custody of customer funds or possessing centralized execution rights, I am not classified as a financial intermediary. However, while non-custodial developers retained an administrative exemption from registration, lawmakers stripped out an explicit, ironclad criminal liability shield. That omission leaves open a dangerous loophole where overzealous prosecutors can still target software creators under broad anti-money-laundering statutes if third parties misuse the open-source protocol.

My foundational thesis is that software code is protected expression under the First Amendment. Protecting non-custodial developers from prison sentences for the downstream actions of anonymous users is vital for keeping technological innovation inside the United States. Until the law guarantees absolute, explicit immunity for writing non-custodial code, builders like me will continue looking toward jurisdictions like Dubai that offer regulatory certainty without the threat of incarceration.

Meanwhile, markets are reacting aggressively to the broader legislative push. Bitcoin is moving higher this morning as the market prices in the end of existential regulatory uncertainty, with stock index futures holding steady and Treasury yields remaining sensitive to long-end liquidity support. The passage of Treasury-backed stablecoin rules effectively creates a perpetual institutional buyer for U.S. Treasury bills, synthesizing national debt strategy with crypto adoption. As legal clarity unlocks institutional capital, liquidity is surging directly into digital assets, driving Bitcoin's current outperformance just as my previous analysis anticipated.

text:
Stop counting certificates as capacity.

Singapore already ran this experiment. We called it data science.

For years the message was: shortage, convert, SkillsFuture, become a data engineer. Bootcamps filled. Titles inflated. Dashboards shipped. Then the middle of the market cooled. Pay for data engineers and analysts stalled or fell. Four in five tech workers faced thinner options. The top 10–20% still got offers. That is not a shortage. That is a barbell.

The state did not invent a fake need. Banks still cannot fill a real production data scientist. What failed was the unit of measurement. Course completions are not operators. A 12-week Spark certificate is not a person who has owned a warehouse, an SLA, and a messy estate.

Now the slogan is AI. Postings with “AI skills” jumped. Look closer. Most of that jump is AI user roles — people who should use Copilot in the job they already have. The builder seats are a thin slice. Policy is aiming at 100,000 “AI-bilingual” workers. That is literacy. It is not a private GPU cage, a fine-tune, or a PDPA-safe perimeter.

If we copy the data episode, the sequence is already written: intake surge, salary headlines, a mass of GenAI CVs, then a quiet split in 2028 between a small paid core and everyone told to upskill again.

Attitude change for the AI era is not “study AI harder.” It is:
1. Treat a four-year degree as foundations — systems, security, stats, judgement. Do not pretend it mints this year’s agent stack.
2. Finish people on live systems. Apprenticeship is the last mile. Certificates are not.
3. Hire pods, not unicorns. Weights, integration, security, privacy are four jobs. One posting will sit open.
4. Separate fluency from capacity. Teach the country to use AI. Do not confuse that with the few who can own models inside a regulated firm.
5. Stop moving the slogan every time the middle of the last pipeline cools.

AI will matter here. Counting diplomas as if they were megawatts will not. We already tasted that pill. Don’t swallow it twice.

Understanding SDRAM Synchronous Dynamic Random Access Memory

SDRAM is one of the most important components for modern computing technology - without SDRAM, modern computing hardware would be very different to what it is today.

SDRAM enables computing hardware of all types to handle data in real-time. Its mode of operation lies in word "Synchronous" which is part of its acronym.

Why "Synchronous" Changed Everything
Before SDRAM, memory was asynchronous, meaning it responded to the CPU whenever it was ready.

This approach created massive bottlenecks. However SDRAM revolutionized this by synchronizing with the system clock.

Think of it like a perfectly timed dance: the CPU knows exactly when the data will be ready, allowing for "pipelining." The memory can start processing a second command before the first one is even finished.

From SDRAM to DDR5: Where We Are Now
While the original SDR (Single Data Rate) SDRAM is now a legacy technology, its descendants—DDR4 and DDR5—are currently the stars of the show:
🔹 DDR4: The reliable workhorse. Still dominant in many industrial applications, but production is currently being phased down to make room for newer tech.
🔹 DDR5: The new standard. It offers double the bandwidth of DDR4 and introduces On-die ECC (Error Correction Code) for enhanced reliability, making it essential for AI and high-performance servers.
🔹 LPDDR5X: The mobile champion. Found in the latest smartphones and ultrabooks, it prioritizes "Performance per Watt" to keep your devices fast without killing the battery.

The Market Landscape
The memory industry is currently facing a fascinating (and challenging) "DRAM Drought." Because of the explosive demand for High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in AI data centers, manufacturers like Samsung and SK Hynix are reallocating their production lines.

This has led to:
✅ Accelerated EOL: Legacy DDR4 components are being retired faster than expected.
✅ Pricing Shifts: Memory prices have seen significant volatility as AI infrastructure consumes global wafer capacity.
✅ Innovation: We are already seeing the first glimpses of LPDDR6 and CAMM2 form factors, designed to make laptops even thinner and more efficient.

Whether you are a hobbyist building a project or an engineer designing a next-gen system, understanding the timing and architecture of SDRAM is critical.

[Weekly Crypto] 2026.09.14

1️⃣ Senate Republicans Unveil Revised 630-Page Clarity Act Ahead of First Procedural Vote Senate Republicans led by Sen. Cynthia Lummis released a revised 630-page version of the Clarity Act on September 10, setting up the bill's first procedural vote on September 15. The new draft adds rulemaking requirements for "non-DeFi trading protocols" that would have to register with the CFTC, narrows the DeFi provisions so they apply only to spot and cash digital commodity transactions, and clarifies how credit unions can conduct crypto activities. Republicans say they incorporated more than 114 provisions from Democratic colleagues, while the ethics section — which keeps Justice Department enforcement authority — is largely unchanged. "Unlike rulemaking, legislation gives this industry a lasting solution that shields it from the whiplash of changes in the White House," Lummis said, though the bill still needs Democratic votes to clear the floor. The Block

2️⃣ PayPal Opens PYUSDx, Letting Any Business Issue Its Own PYUSD-Backed Stablecoin PayPal went live in early September with PYUSDx, a developer platform that lets businesses launch custom stablecoins backed by PayPal USD, built with token infrastructure specialist M0 and crypto payments firm MoonPay handling issuance and distribution. First announced in February 2026, the platform launched with tokens from crypto-native issuers Saturn, Concrete and Cap, which together bring over $100 million in processed volume, with https://t.co/CSJdFpSxRj and Fairblock also joining. "As more financial institutions are getting involved, this creates fragmentation — we abstract away the complexity and create a layer that facilitates integrations," said M0 CEO Luca Prosperi. The move turns PYUSD from a single product into issuance rails other companies build on, giving PayPal a distribution angle against Tether and Circle that it can extend through Venmo. CoinDesk

3️⃣ Circle Buys Singapore's Tazapay for $400 Million to Push USDC into Emerging Markets Circle is acquiring Singapore-based payments company Tazapay for $400 million, buying payout rails across more than 100 markets plus banking and fintech relationships spanning Asia, the Middle East and Latin America. Tazapay holds local licenses and already performs regulated work Circle cannot do on its own in much of the world — customer verification, collecting funds and paying out recipients — which is what lets stablecoin settlement actually touch local currency on local rails. "Stablecoin settlement is becoming core infrastructure for global commerce," said Circle SVP of Payments Irfan Ganchi, who framed the deal as buying banking relationships that take years to build. With USDC at roughly $74 billion in circulation, the purchase targets exactly the emerging markets where USDT has long dominated. CoinDesk

4️⃣ Coinbase and Moov Bring Stablecoin Payments to More Than 1,000 Community Banks Coinbase and payments infrastructure provider Moov announced a partnership on September 10 that will give over 1,000 community banks and credit unions stablecoin payment acceptance, settlement, real-time funding and payouts. The integration embeds Coinbase's Payments API and custodial wallets directly into Moov's existing platform, so participating institutions — Citizens Bank of Edmond among them — can offer merchant acceptance and consumer payments without building crypto infrastructure themselves. "Modern tech should meet local institutions where they are, giving them tools to compete with largest players," said Coinbase head of corporate affairs Ryan VanGrack, while Citizens Bank of Edmond CEO Jill Castilla noted small business customers want lower interchange costs and faster settlement. It continues Coinbase's shift from bank custodian to embedded infrastructure provider, following earlier work with PNC, Citi and JPMorgan. The Block

5️⃣ Solana's Transaction V1 Goes Live, Tripling the Size of a Single Transaction Solana's Transaction V1 format activated on September 15 at roughly 01:00 UTC, raising the maximum data a single transaction can carry from 1,232 bytes to 4,096 bytes. The bigger envelope lets developers pack multiple steps into one all-or-nothing transaction instead of splitting them across several, which matters for multisignature company wallet approvals and zero-knowledge proofs that previously did not fit under the old hard cap. Ethereum has no equivalent protocol-level size limit, relying on a flexible block gas limit instead, so the upgrade narrows a structural gap Solana had carried alongside its speed and cost advantages. Older transaction formats still work, but the Solana Foundation warned that "services that feed blockchain data to wallets, trading apps and analytics platforms must be able to recognize V1 transactions" or see requests fail. CLARITY Act cloture vote starts 2:15 PM ET today.

It needs 60 votes to open debate. Odds of 2026 passage have whipsawed over the last 48 hours as both support and opposition from various parties landed in the same window.

We had a round of optimism on Sunday night as Senate Republicans released what they called their final draft, and President Trump agreed to the tougher ethics package. Odds jumped to 35%.

That optimism quickly dissipated as 18 attorney generals urged a no vote. Eight bank groups demanded tighter stablecoin-reward limits on Monday morning.

Treasury Secretary Bessent and SEC Chair Atkins have publicly endorsed the bill, citing the importance of it in order to maintain supporting US tech leadership.

Senate Democrats have sent a counter offer to the Republicans, just hours ahead of the vote. Odds have now dropped to 19%.

This bill is the crypto industry’s number 1️⃣ priority — it would finally settle the years-long question of who regulates crypto, the SEC or the CFTC. But it’s been stuck for months on one sticking point: ethics rules meant to stop Trump profiting from his own crypto empire, which reportedly earned him $1.4bn last year.

Republicans released what they called their final offer late Sunday, with the White House’s blessing. The Democrats were unimpressed. 😐

Elizabeth Warren called it “a weak fig leaf 🍂 that will do nothing to stop him from making his next $1.4 billion in crypto profits.” Her two objections: 
❌it lets Trump’s own appointees switch off enforcement, and 
❌it leaves his existing ventures — including World Liberty Financial — untouched.

🔻Mark Warner told Semafor the provision was “not near enough,” and confirmed the Democrats are sending back a counteroffer.

🗳️So this is literally on a knife-edge. 🔪
The cloture vote is still set for 2:15pm ET today, and it needs 60 votes to advance and even if it clears, the ethics fight rolls straight on into the debate itself to one awkward question nobody’s cracked: what to do about the sitting president’s personal crypto fortune? 

🔮 Watch 2:15. Everything after it depends on the count. 🗳️

Britney Spears Says She Wants to Grow Closer to God

Britney Spears has been speaking more openly about faith, prayer and her desire for a deeper relationship with God.

In a personal social media reflection, Spears expressed belief in the Holy Spirit, spoke about prayer and shared her desire to become closer to God.

After decades of extraordinary fame and intense public scrutiny, her words offer a glimpse into the spiritual questions that appear to be important to her today.

Her comments should not automatically be interpreted as announcing a new Christian conversion, nor should anyone assume where her spiritual journey will ultimately lead. What can be taken from her own words is that prayer and seeking God have become meaningful parts of her reflections.

For Christians, moments like this are an opportunity for prayer rather than speculation.

Pray that Britney continues seeking truth, finds genuine peace and grows deeper in her understanding of God. Above all, pray that her search leads her closer to Jesus Christ and a lasting relationship with Him.

“Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.” — James 4:8

Sometimes a spiritual journey begins with something remarkably simple: the desire to know God more deeply.

text:
Happy birthday former Clinton, University of Oklahoma and NFL tight end Trent Smith, born on this day in 1979 in Norman.

Smith was an All-State selection and PrepStar All-American as a senior in 1997 after catching 35 passes for 601 yards and eight touchdowns in helping the Red Tornadoes to a second straight state championship.

He also had 100 tackles from his defensive end spot.

Considered a top five tight end recruit nationally, Smith selected OU over several other offers and caught 18 passes for 175 yards and two touchdowns as a redshirt freshman in 1999.

In 2000, he was a member of the Sooners' national championship team, making 29 catches for 310 yards and three touchdowns, including eight catches for 96 yards and a touchdown in OU's Big 12 Championship game win over Kansas State.

His best season with the Sooners came in 2001 when he caught 61 passes for 564 yards and six touchdowns, earning second-team All-Big 12 honors. He earned first-team honors a year later with 46 receptions, 396 yards and five touchdowns.

In four seasons with OU, Smith had 154 receptions for 1,445 yards and 16 touchdowns.

Smith was a seventh-round pick of the Baltimore Ravens in the 2003 NFL Draft. Injuries derailed both his first two professional seasons and he signed with the San Francisco 49ers in 2005, playing in five games and making three catches for seven yards.

In 2006, he appeared in ten games for the Cologne Centurions of NFL Europe. He made 23 catches for 249 yards and three touchdowns.

Following his playing career, Smith worked for the Oklahoma Employment Security Commission and later served on the Oklahoma State Board of Education. Today, he owns Sooner Medical Staffing and last December he was named General Manager of Football by the Yukon Millers.

TALKING POINTS BRIEF | Tuesday Morning Football Edition

DENVER DIDN’T JUST LOSE A GAME.

It lost every argument its fans planned to make this week.

Kansas City 31. Denver 10.

Here are the 7 talking points everyone will be discussing:

1. DENVER’S REIGN LASTED UNTIL KICKOFF.

The Broncos entered the season as defending AFC West champions.

Three hours later, Kansas City looked like it had merely loaned Denver the division for a year.

2. THE GAME WAS TIED 7–7.

Denver fans may want to screenshot that sentence.

It was the last comforting development of the evening.

3. KENNETH WALKER III RAN THROUGH DENVER’S DEFENSE AND ITS SELF-ESTEEM.

In his Kansas City debut, Walker rushed 23 times for 173 yards, caught three passes for 18 yards and scored twice.

His 60-yard touchdown came on fourth-and-one.

Denver needed one yard.

Walker took sixty.

4. DENVER’S OFFENSE PRODUCED 177 TOTAL YARDS.

Not in the first half.

Not before halftime.

For the entire game.

There are people who accidentally walk farther than that while looking for their car after the game.

5. THIRD DOWN BECAME “PLEASE LEAVE THE FIELD” DOWN.

Denver converted only 2 of 12 third downs.

Kansas City converted 9 of 17.

One team sustained drives. The other sustained emotional damage.

6. BO NIX’S RETURN STARTED WITH AN INTERCEPTION.

Nix recovered long enough to throw a 19-yard touchdown pass to Evan Engram.

Unfortunately, that was less the beginning of a comeback and more the final sign of offensive life.

7. THE MOST PAINFUL PART WASN’T MAHOMES.

Denver knew Patrick Mahomes was returning.

What it apparently did not expect was Kansas City to dominate on the ground, control the line of scrimmage and make Denver look unprepared for the most predictable game plan imaginable.

Kansas City spent last season hearing that its run was over.

Denver spent the offseason hearing that it had arrived.

On Monday night, only one team appeared to believe what it heard.

The season is only one game old.

But if you are a Denver fan, it already feels much older.

OVERREACTION OR WARNING SIGN?

Is Denver still a contender, or did Kansas City expose something the rest of the league will now copy?

text:
Florida State fired its athletic director.

I want to be careful here, because I would hate for anyone to think we are gloating.

WE DID THAT!

From Dallas. Eight hundred miles away. On a Monday night in somebody else's stadium, with a kicker and a backup plan.

Michael Alford is out, effective September 14. Bruce Warwick is the interim. The next guy inherits a head coach he didn't hire, a stadium he didn't build, and a pile of debt he didn't sign for.

Here is the detail that should keep somebody in Florida up at night.

SMU turned the ball over four times in that game.

Four. And still won 27-24. In their building. On national television. While their own fans chanted for their head coach to be fired, in real time, in front of the recruits.

A man lost his career to a team that spent the evening handing him the football, and he still could not get it done.

Now. About that debt.

You know my position. Florida State is carrying four hundred and thirty-seven million dollars, and I have argued that SMU boosters should quietly buy every dollar of that paper and become the lienholder.

People told me that was a bit. It was never a bit.

Understand our situation. SMU took zero television revenue to join the ACC. Nine years, twenty-four million a year, gone. We do not get a media check.

But nothing in that agreement says we cannot earn interest.

We cannot collect from the league. We can absolutely collect from Tallahassee. Every month. On time. With a late fee.

And today we are pleased to announce an expansion of services.

SMU Structured Finance is now underwriting head coaching buyouts.

Mike Norvell is carrying roughly forty-six million in guaranteed money. A large number for a department in your shape. A very manageable number for thirty guys from Highland Park who covered a hundred-million-dollar shortfall in a week because somebody asked nicely at lunch.

So let us help. Competitive rate. Flexible terms. We will even structure it so the first payment comes due after the coaching search, which we understand is a sensitive time for cash flow.

Need the ACC exit fee financed down the road? Seventy-five million after 2029-30? Come talk to us. We are full service.

Your board chairman said this morning that more restructuring is needed and that the president and the board are in lockstep on what the results must be.

Sir, we agree completely. We have reviewed your capital structure, and we see significant opportunities.

Now, I have heard the whispers about going independent again, or about the SEC coming to rescue you.

Let me be gentle.

You are not getting into the SEC.

Florida is already in the SEC. You bring the conference no new state, no new territory, and no new anything. Tallahassee is the 105th television market in America, which puts it comfortably behind Fort Wayne.

You also sued your last conference. Whatever room decides these things, somebody is going to say that sentence out loud, and the vote will end right there.

If the SEC expands, it expands into markets it does not own. That means Miami, at number eighteen, with a national brand and the richest recruiting ground in the country.

And it means SMU.

Dallas-Fort Worth is the fourth-largest television market in the United States. We passed Philadelphia. And we bring something no other candidate in America can offer.

We have already proven we will join a conference for free.

Nine years, no media money, covered by our own donors in a week. We are the only program in the country with a documented track record of paying to be somewhere. Put that in a presentation and watch how fast a room of commissioners stops talking.

Now think about where that sentence would have landed in 1987.

The lights went out in Tallahassee two weeks ago. The man who turned them on got walked out.

And somewhere on Mockingbird Lane, a very patient gentleman in a golf shirt is updating a spreadsheet.

Pony Up. Ask about our rates.

★★★★★

text:
Carnage Of a Throwaway Society
by Greg Allen
Published Jun 1, 2017 

President Lyndon Baines Johnson initiated subsidies to eradicate poverty and social injustice in 1964 that were labeled “The Great Society.”  Instead of being a blessing they actually have been a curse for those who’ve come in contact with them.  The fatherless rate in Afro-American families has skyrocketed.  Some scholars claim many black mothers are married to the government.

Studies have found that the poverty rate, since 1964, has virtually been the same even with the billions that have been spent by the government.  The initiatives LBJ introduced have had devastating effects on the black community.

Crime hasn’t subsided with “The Great Society” experiment either.

Bob Cole, Executive Director of ReBuild in Indianapolis, helped add some insight.

In 2004, he began working with Ex-Offenders coming home from Prison.  5 years later he started a non-profit called “Rebuild.”  Bob said he chose to expand his horizons and assist people needing to return to Independently Self Sustainable – his favorite 3 words.

His primary goal is not helping criminals, but to prevent future victims. “With helping those in need to become Independent, it drastically reduces them re-offending by committing another crime and returning to Prison.  I have been blessed to help over 3,000 over the years.  I’m able to sit down one-on-one and guide.” Bob said.

He once met a young lady in nursing school.  While doing the practical part of her training she lifted a patient and injured her back.  A doctor put her on pain medication, and she became addicted.  She stole medications from a cart while passing them out to patients.  She got caught and served a year, followed by probation, substance abuse classes, random drug testing, etc.  She stated she wanted to complete her nursing training and become the RN she always wanted to be.  Bob told her “It would never happen.”

The young lady was eventually able to return to her studies and became a respectable RN and no longer on public assistance.

Bob vowed to never use the words “It will never happen” again.

Bob added, “When I chose to concentrate primarily on assisting those in need of employment, a wise local business owner gave one sentence that completely changed my life.  He said, ‘Assisting people with jobs is a piece of cake, a turtle could do it.  The challenge is Job Retention.’  He was right and I learned anyone will do anything for about 2 weeks.”

“It became my destiny to assist individuals with actual employment, but the type of work he or she will actually enjoy getting up in the morning to go do.  What a concept!  Unfortunately, it just cannot be done in massive groups.  Employers don’t want a professional like me asking them to hire 50 criminals, but they will absolutely talk to me about one.”

Bob added, “Grant dependent organizations aren’t afforded my method.  If they don’t show massive numbers, they won’t receive funding to continue operating.  Of course, the funding entity expects not only massive numbers, but they demand an increase in those numbers every year.  What is an organization to do, pray they were able to help enough?”

It’s not unrealistic to say government fails people.  For decades, 7 out of 10 men and women re-offend and return to prison every year.

Mr. Cole’s sobering confession is: “We live in an advocate world.  If you’re an Ex-Offender I can put on a crisp white shirt and tie and assist you all day long, but you’ll have a 90% chance of failing on your own.”

“If a person is able to secure real employment and make enough money to set a budget and stick to it, and I mean real employment where they enjoy getting up in the morning and going in every day.  Then all the rest will fall in place, housing, transportation, no more public assistance and no more prison time at a rate of twenty some thousand dollars a year per inmate.  I know, because I’m an Ex-Offender.”

I appreciate Bob Cole’s intuitive insight.  It was a voluntary offering of which I’m quite thankful.  I still lay hold to the thought, as Ronald Reagan did, that government isn’t the answer, oftentimes it’s the problem.  Individuals who offer to get their hands dirty in the trenches are often the Samaritans who make a difference in the lives of the ordinary.

Greg Allen’s column, Thinkin’ Out Loud, was published bi-monthly from 2009 to 2017.  He’s an author, a former nationally syndicated columnist and the founder of Builder of the Spirit Ministries in Jamestown, Indiana.  He can be reached at https://t.co/9QdchPfdBy.

Israel is fighting Hamas, the same Hamas that butchered civilians on October 7, still holds hostages, and has spent decades screaming they want every Jew gone from the river to the sea. That is not a slogan for freedom. That is a death wish for Israel.

This shit did not start in 2023. In 1937 the British offered to split the land. Jews said yes even though they got the short end. Arabs said fuck no. In 1947 the UN voted for two states. Jews accepted a small, messy share. Arabs rejected it and invaded the second Israel declared independence. After 1967 Israel offered land for peace. The Arab League replied with three no’s: no peace, no recognition, no talks. In 2000 and 2008 Israeli leaders put real two-state deals on the table, most of the West Bank, Gaza, parts of Jerusalem. Palestinian leaders walked away both times.

While all that was happening nearly a million Jews were kicked out of Arab countries. Their communities got erased. The Arab population in Israel, the West Bank and Gaza exploded.

The famine story is collapsing too. Actual surveys show child malnutrition in Gaza is among the lowest in the entire region. A ton of those viral “starving kids” photos were children with cystic fibrosis or other illnesses that nobody bothered mentioning. When celebrities slap on a keffiyeh and start yelling genocide without checking a single fact, they are not brave. They are useful idiots for people who never wanted two states. They wanted the Jewish one gone.

And you lot in Britain clutching your pearls over Israeli arms sales to Argentina in 1982 or some Falklands comments need a history lesson. Britain’s 1939 White Paper slammed the door on Jews trying to escape the Holocaust. After the war they dumped tens of thousands of survivors in camps on Cyprus. Hundreds died there. As for the Irish comparing this to their history with the English, grow the fuck up. Ireland was colonised by an empire sending settlers to take the land. Jews were not an empire. text:
You do not walk into No One Lives looking for a sermon and you leave with one anyway because the film is not interested in comforting you. It is interested in the second you realize the room you thought you owned was never yours. A gang of highway thieves pulls a couple off the road because the couple looks like money and the night looks empty and the last job already went sideways and Flynn wants to feel like a man again. That is the setup the world understands. That is also the last moment the world still belongs to them. What you are supposed to learn starts right there. Things are not always what they seem. The pretty couple in the diner is not a couple. The quiet man at the table is not prey. The girl in the trunk is not a prize. The title is not a threat painted on a poster. It is a law the movie intends to enforce.

This is why the picture stands apart from the rest of its field. Home invasion cinema usually asks you to suffer with the innocent. Backwoods slasher cinema usually asks you to watch animals hunt tourists. Wrong place wrong time cinema usually asks you to wait for the sheriff. No One Lives refuses the contract. It hands the night to two kinds of predator and then asks which one you are willing to breathe with. Derek Magyar, who plays the hot blooded thief Flynn, said the story is evil versus evil and the audience has to decide which side of itself it is gripping. That is the film’s real engine. You are not here to crown a hero. You are here to watch people discover, too late, that they selected the one man on the highway who treats murder the way an accountant treats a ledger. He calls himself a numbers guy. He does not rant. He does not monologue to feel large. He counts. He closes accounts.

Betty looks like a girlfriend until the knife is at her throat and she chooses the blade herself rather than remain inside the life he built around her. That death is not decoration. It is the first lesson written in blood. Control is a costume. Devotion can be a cage. The man they zip tied in a gas station basement is not a husband having a bad night. He is the architect of a massacre at a party where fourteen people died and one heiress vanished. Emma Ward is in the hidden compartment of his car because he decided she was his. The gang opens that compartment and thinks they have found two million dollars of luck. What they have found is a witness who already knows the truth they are too greedy to hear. She tells them he will come. She tells them they should call the law. They hear reward money instead. That is the moment the movie stops being a kidnapping picture and becomes a parable about appetite. You F’ed up is not slang here. It is the plot.

Consequences follow because the film believes they must. It does not lecture with speeches. It lectures with bodies. Ethan, the giant with the knife, learns that size is not a philosophy. The Driver does not outmuscle the room so much as he outthinks the room and then uses the room against itself. Hoag wants to keep a low profile and not shit where he eats and still ends up paying the bill for everyone else’s hunger. Amber recognizes Emma from the news and still treats a human being like a lottery ticket. Denny tries to fix a Jeep as if machinery can outrun a man who has already decided the night’s arithmetic. Flynn keeps choosing violence the way some men choose a drink, as if the next pour will finally make him the person he imagines. Each choice is small. Each choice is fatal. The gore is not there to wink at you. The gore is the receipt. Ryuhei Kitamura wanted the blood of the nineteen eighties, the wet kind, the kind that sticks in heat and refuses to look like a screensaver. Nearly all of it is practical. You are meant to feel the weight of a decision after it can no longer be unmade.

What makes the film unique is the inversion that never quite lets you stand up. Most revenge stories hand the blade to the wronged innocent. Here the hunter was already hunting before the gang ever saw him. Betty’s suicide does not redeem him. Emma’s terror does not redeem him. The slaughter of a family at the start of the night does not redeem the gang. Everybody arrived stained. That is why the picture feels like a cultural oddity rather than another weekend slasher. It is a twisted love story wearing a slaughterhouse coat. Kitamura said that is why he took the script. Not because everybody dies, which the title already promised, but because Driver loves in an extreme and broken way and the movie is willing to stare at that love without blinking. Luke Evans built the man by reading about psychopaths, about faces that cannot tell joy from grief, about calm that is not mercy. He understood that a true predator does not need to scream while he works. The quiet is the weapon. That performance is why people who dismissed the movie on paper still remember the man in the car years later. He looks like he could buy you dinner. He looks like he belongs in the world. That is the horror that outlives the set pieces. Monsters who announce themselves are easier to survive than monsters who pass for ordinary until the count begins.

You are supposed to take away a colder kind of caution than the usual don’t go in the woods warning. Do not assume the victim in front of you is the weakest person in the room. Do not assume the score in front of you is clean. Do not assume the story you walked into is the story that will walk out with you. The gang’s first crime that night is already a massacre of a family that came home too early. They think they can wash it off with a richer job. The universe of this film does not wash. It compounds. Emma is not a damsel waiting for rescue. She is a person who has already survived the man now hunting her captors, and her will to be the one who ends him is the closest thing the movie offers to agency. When the shotgun fails in her hands the Driver does something the rest of the picture has trained you not to expect. He cuts the tracker out of her and lets her live. Not because he has grown a conscience. Because she impressed the only code he has, and because a numbers guy can close every other account and still keep one name off the page. Then he finishes the work. The motel owner who learned his real name does not get to keep that knowledge. The last wounded thief in a hospital bed does not get to keep the morning. Even mercy here is a kind of possession. Even freedom here is granted by the same hand that built the cage.

That is why it is a must watch if you care about what genre cinema can do when it stops begging to be respectable. Critics split on it because respectability was never the point. Rotten Tomatoes sat in the low forties. Metacritic sat even colder. The limited theatrical run in May of twenty thirteen opened in a handful of cities and did not print money. WWE Studios put it into the world beside other tough guy titles and the marketplace shrugged. None of that is the measure that matters for a film like this. The measure is whether the inversion stays in your mouth. The measure is whether you still flinch at the idea that the most dangerous person on a dark road might be the one who did not raise his voice at dinner. The measure is whether you understand, after eighty six minutes, that consequence is not a twist. It is gravity. Genre crowds found it, the way they find the mean little pictures that play fair with their own nastiness. They found a slasher that behaves like a nasty seventies thriller in modern clothes. They found cinematography from Daniel Pearl, the same eye that once made Texas look like a wound, shooting Louisiana night as if the dark itself had a pulse. They found a movie that moves fast enough to feel like a dare and strange enough that you keep saying you did not see that coming even after you know the premise.

It is a legend in the small fierce way cult films become legend. Not because the world agreed. Because a certain kind of viewer cannot shake the joke at the center. The thieves thought they were the storm. They were weather. The man they boxed in was climate. That joke is ancient and the film tells it without mercy and without a speech at the end to tell you how to feel. You F’ed up. Things were never what they seemed. The wrong guy was sitting there the whole time, drinking coffee, waiting for the night to confess what it really was. Watch it to learn how quickly a room changes owners. Watch it to learn that appetite without attention is a suicide note written on other people’s skin. Watch it because the title keeps its promise and because very few films have the nerve to keep a promise that ugly and still find a warped tenderness inside the wreckage.

The last thing the picture wants from you is a play by play. It wants the bruise. A girl runs through trees before you even know her name and carves proof that she lived into bark because she already understands that being alive is not the same as being free. A family comes home at the wrong hour and pays for a stranger’s panic. A woman at a table looks at her companion as if the real danger is the man flirting with her, and she is right and she is wrong at the same time. A trunk opens and the reward becomes a curse. A body is moved and the curse rides inside it. A wood chipper, a scythe, an engine, a shower, a hospital bed. Each one is less a stunt than a sentence served. By the time Emma is wheeled past him in white light and he touches her arm like a man visiting a life he refuses to release, you should understand the full thesis. Obsession can wear the face of rescue. Survival can wear the face of damnation. The person who lets you live may be the person who decided you were never going to live without him.

Behind the camera the legend gets even stranger and that strangeness explains the texture. Kitamura came from Versus and Godzilla Final Wars and The Midnight Meat Train, a Japanese stylist hired to put a stamp on an American exploitation machine. He fought for wide masters and long pushes because he believed you remember the iconic shot after you forget the dialogue. He told producers he would not drown the film in digital blood. Robert Hall and the Almost Human shop poured gallons of the old analog stuff until Louisiana heat cooked it onto skin. They shot in June and July on a schedule of about twenty five days, ninety percent nights, during the shortest nights of the year, in weather that made every prosthetic a punishment. Evans climbed out of a body cavity built around Brodus Clay, the WWE performer who played Ethan, and Clay later joked he had given the first male caesarean in a movie and delivered a five foot ten Englishman. Evans said the blood went in his armpit hair and dried fast and the shell smelled and the first time the corpse shook it was an accident they kept because it looked like the dead man was still arguing. Lee Tergesen hung upside down over a chipper for takes that went on long enough for the blood to pool in his head. Jerome Dillon, once the drummer for Nine Inch Nails, scored the dread instead of decorating it. Pathé partnered with WWE Studios. The budget numbers wander depending on who is talking, somewhere in the low millions, never enough for comfort, always enough for nerve. They premiered it at Toronto in the Midnight Madness slot on September eighth of twenty twelve, which is exactly the church this kind of picture belongs to. Then it went out into a marketplace that wanted either respectability or a wrestler joke and did not know what to do with a calm Welsh actor playing a love struck calculator in a field of corpses.

That production story is not trivia pasted on the end. It is the reason the movie feels handmade and slightly unholy. You can see the heat. You can see the stubbornness. You can see a director and a lead actor who both admitted they were more interested in the twisted romance than in the body count, and who then made the body count so excessive that the romance had no place to hide. Luke Evans was not yet the franchise face he would become. Adelaide Clemens held the film’s only real moral voltage, the refusal to be only a trophy. The supporting thieves are written as appetites with names and that is enough, because the lesson does not require their biographies. It requires their error.

So the film remains what it was on that first night in Toronto. A compact, vicious, oddly sincere machine about the moment a person learns the mask across the table is thinner than the one they are wearing themselves. It is gory because the bill is gory. It is special because it will not let you pick a clean jersey. It is a classic of the mean little shelf, the shelf where people keep the movies that told them the truth without asking permission. You watch it to feel the second the hunters become inventory. You watch it to remember that the world is full of people who think they are the exception. You watch it because no one lives is not a slogan. It is what happens when you grab the wrong wrist in the dark and the dark closes its hand back.

text:
NATO Confirms Lithuania Shot Down Russian Military Geese After They Flew in a V and Released a Chemical Substance

VILNIUS — NATO and Lithuanian officials said allied fighters had “neutralized a formation of hostile waterfowl” over central Lithuania after the birds displayed what one briefing called “unmistakable tactical signatures”: a V-formation and the release of a chemical substance.

The intercept came two days after a radar track over Vilnius — later identified as ordinary birds — closed the airport for 38 minutes and scrambled an Italian Eurofighter from Šiauliai. Officials said this time there was no confusion.

“They were flying in a V,” a Lithuanian Air Force spokesman said. “That is not recreational migration. That is a command-and-control geometry. You do not accidentally form a V. A V is a decision.”

Other indicators, according to the briefing: several birds “dispensed an unidentified chemical substance” over farmland, parked cars, and a bicycle path; the lead goose “honked with unusual confidence”; and the flock refused to squawk in Lithuanian when challenged on Guard frequency.

“The payload was viscous, off-white to green, and biologically active,” a National Crisis Management Centre official said. “It burned slightly on contact with paint. That is not breadcrumbs. That is a capability.” Lab results remain classified as goose.

Italian Eurofighters on NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission achieved visual ID and engaged. Debris included feathers, webbed feet, and grain “consistent with Kaliningrad feed stocks.”

Moscow denied operating military geese, calling them “ordinary migratory citizens of the sky” and the chemical-warfare charge “Russophobic ornithology.” If anything fell on Lithuania, a spokeswoman said, it was “a natural process and also Lithuania’s problem.”

A NATO planner, speaking on background, was less dismissive. “A goose is cheap, deniable, and already pre-trained to fly in formation,” he said. Asked whether the alliance keeps a goose threat matrix, he replied: “We maintain a goose threat matrix.”

Draft rules of engagement would treat a V plus “visible payload release” as hostile intent. A single goose flying straight remains “a monitoring problem.” Canada offered advisors. France offered a chef. Neither offer has been accepted.

Asked whether NATO had simply shot down regular geese, the spokesman did not blink. “If they were regular geese, they would not have been in a V, and they would not have been dropping things on a NATO country. The V is the tell. The chemical is the confirmation. The rest is just feathers.”

Lithuania has not invoked Article 5. One soiled windshield, officials said, does not yet meet the threshold. They reserved the right to revisit that if the next flock arrives in a diamond.

ROBOTAXI
Updated 2026-09-15
Sources: Robotaxi + Owning Robotaxi Fleet bookmark folders (224 unique). Not Cybercab.

NEW TODAY
- Testers (MelvinInvests): Tesla robotaxi army vs Uber — owns vehicles/software/charging/customer stack; Uber marketplace only…
- Testers (TeslaNewswire): Slovenia Ministry tested FSD Supervised; working toward Robotaxi approval (safe/efficient/doesn’t tire)…
- Testers (RobotaxiRadar): Confirmed fleet past 1,000 — 996→1,001 in service; unsupervised 300→305 (all new unsupervised)…
- Testers (TeslaZoa): Austin visitor — 5 rides (2 Model Y / 3 Cybercab); downtown ~every 30s; Model Y wait ~5m; Cybercab waits…
- Folder totals: Robotaxi 220 (+4) + Fleet 4 (0 new) → 224 unique

WHAT IT IS
- Tesla’s paid autonomous ride service. You book a car in the Robotaxi app. The car drives. There is no human driver on unsupervised rides.
- Live cars today are mostly Model Y. The purpose-built Cybercab is the volume vehicle testers say Tesla is prioritizing.
- Camera-only vision. Tesla VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy: no lidar, radar, or HD maps required for safe operation on this stack.
- This how-to merges the public Robotaxi service folder with Owning Robotaxi Fleet (owner / private-fleet economics). Not Cybercab-only bookmarks.

HOW IT WORKS
- Download the Tesla Robotaxi app and join the waitlist. Official robotaxi (Sep 2025): app is available to all; access expands over time.
- Book the ride in Tesla’s app. Elon: Tesla will not partner with Uber or Lyft. “We will have enough demand.”
- Unsupervised means no safety driver. Supervised cities still have a person in the car.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): service hours are 6am to 10pm, 7 days/week. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger. Upgraded vehicle distribution and routing so you wait less.
- Testers: you can change destination and keep the same trip for multiple stops.
- Cars return to a depot or homebase and park themselves (Houston footage).
- Ashok: FSD v15 is already running on Model Y robotaxis and will run on Cybercab.
- Testers: Tesla is limiting Model Y conversions to prioritize Cybercab, built with an unboxed modular process.
- Testers (Aug 24): Tesla expects Cybercab to replace Model Ys in the Robotaxi fleet over time and become the highest-volume vehicle there. Testers flag Sept 3 / 9/3 as the Cybercab strategy moment. Austin public Cybercab rides described as “imminent.”
- Testers (Sep 7): Cybercab expected to be actively deployed across Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet soon; Austin Cybercab wait times described as going parabolic on demand.
- Testers (Sep 7): Tesla hiring Robotaxi Fleet Support Supervisors night shift across 21 cities (Cybercabs incoming signal).
- Testers (Sep 7): Waymo Q3 2025 occupancy — 90% of trips have 2 or fewer people (two-seater Cybercab justification resurfaced).
- Testers (Sep 8): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 969 after +59 vehicles; 31 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 8): Houston hub still holding ~100 Cybercabs waiting on orders plus Model Y robotaxis; little lot growth since last check — FSD v15 brain called out as the unlock.
- Testers (Sep 8): Texas Robotaxi fleet momentum — Jeff Lutz cited 432 registered autonomous vehicles incl. 45 Cybercabs; software quality cited as why Tesla can keep adding cars.
- Testers (Sep 11 TeslaZoa): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 994 after +14 vehicles; 6 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 11 AIScottAdams): sleep-through long-haul thesis — lie-flat Robotaxi rides could cannibalize short- and long-haul flights (tester/AI channel, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 11 CernBasher): “Tesla Just Opened The Floodgates In Austin!” ($TSLA video/title post).
- Testers (Sep 11 teslayoda): “Robotaxis incoming to California.” Still Testers — signal, not a new Official city launch.

- Testers (Sep 12 Alexs_jame): “BREAKING” clip framed as Elon Musk and Tesla AI celebrating a Robotaxi service launch day — tester/media claim, not Official robotaxi.
- Testers (Sep 13 gailalfaratx): Austin UT campus — Robotaxis ferrying football fans fully unsupervised (no safety supervisor); emotional “how far Tesla has come” note.
- Testers (Sep 13 niccruzpatane): Austin ride comparison — 21 Robotaxi vs 2 human Uber rides; claims Robotaxi comfort next-level (smooth turning, less heavy braking).
- Testers (Sep 13 TeslaZoa): Nashville spot — 26 Cybercabs + 7 Robotaxi validation Model Ys (33 AVs total) on public roads (signal, not a new Official city launch).
- Testers (Sep 13 herbertong / TeslaLarry): peak-demand surge capacity may matter more for profits than steady-state fleet count; Tesla need not own that surge capacity.
- Testers (Sep 13 herbertong / TeslaLarry): network efficiency (charging, cleaning, maintenance, depots, coverage) may beat raw Robotaxi count as the competitive edge.
- Testers (Sep 13 SERobinsonJr): MSM late to a 720-unit figure — tester says more are coming / already on site (fleet/Cybercab count chatter, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 14 MelvinInvests): stack thesis — Tesla owns vehicles/software/charging/customer vs Uber marketplace (tester/investor take, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 14 TeslaNewswire): Slovenia Ministry of Transport tested FSD Supervised; working toward Robotaxi approval (tester/news signal, not Official launch).
- Testers (Sep 14 RobotaxiRadar): fleet officially past 1,000 — 1,001 in service; unsupervised 305; all latest adds unsupervised (tester tracking site).
- Testers (Sep 14 TeslaZoa): Austin density — downtown Robotaxi ~every 30s; Model Y waits ~5m; visitor mix of Model Y + Cybercab rides.
HOW TO USE
- Official robotaxi: download the app, join the waitlist.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): rides run 6am to 10pm every day. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; routing upgrade is meant to cut wait time.
- Testers: booking is in the app. One Orlando rider paid with an X Money card.
- Tesla site (as quoted): app in 29 languages; service animals; space for some wheelchairs and assistive devices.
- Testers: vehicles in Nevada must be marked “Robotaxi.”
- After the Aug 20 Nevada approval, testers say Tesla still has to finish vehicle inspections, insurance, and published rates before paid rides start there.

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)
- Elon (Feb 2026, also in Robotaxi folder): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Fleet testers frame the network like Airbnb for cars: owner adds vehicle; Tesla handles software, routing, payments, rider experience; platform fee often modeled ~25–35%; owner keeps the rest after operating costs (tester).
- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.
- Fleet / Teslaconomics: Cybercab cost chatter ~$25k–$30k; Elon told that tester production was starting in ~1 month (Mar 2026 context — treat as dated tester claim). Rough capital for a ~$1M/yr fleet ~$850k–$1M in vehicles (tester arithmetic).
- Fleet / chamath: intends to buy and deploy large fleets nationally when possible; expects payback and positive FCF in under 2 years (tester / investor claim, not Official Tesla).
- Fleet / BrianRoemmele: “all in” on buying into the owning-fleet thesis now; separate Optimus ownership program mentioned but not published in this dump.
- Fleet / tslaming (Mar 2026): then only 8 unsupervised Austin robotaxis — historical; do not use as current fleet size (Robotaxi dump Aug 23 tester: 908 total).
- Testers / Teslaconomics (Aug 25, Robotaxi folder): “owning your own Tesla Robotaxi fleet can one day make you financially free.” Still a tester slogan — no Official owner-earnings number in this dump.
- CONFLICT / caution: owner earnings, Cybercab sticker, ROI, and payback are tester models. Dump explicitly says none of it is guaranteed. Do not treat as Official Tesla guidance.

SERVICE AREA / CITIES
- Unsupervised (no safety driver), as listed May 2026: Austin, TX (launched Jun 22, 2025); Dallas, TX and Houston, TX (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Supervised (safety driver), as listed May 2026: SF Bay Area, CA (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Testers: Bay Area rides to and from SFO. Earlier: San Jose Airport pickup.
- Testers: an Orlando rider reviewed a live Robotaxi trip (Jul 2026). Aug 21 testers also list Orlando and Tampa as live; that is not on the May 2026 official city list.
- Testers (Aug 25 Teslaconomics): 7 metro areas live. Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa ramping unsupervised; Bay Area still safety-driver. Treat as tester city list, not Official May 2026 list.
- Testers (Aug 27 travel_invest): recap of Official hours post lists 6 target cities — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa. Tester translation, not a new Official city list.
- Nevada (Aug 20, 2026): full network permit for paid public service. Start small in Clark County / Las Vegas; Tesla can expand elsewhere in the state after notifying the commission.
- Testers (Aug 23): Nevada approved Tesla for up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles, up from a 10-car interim limit. Tesla said it would be “extremely happy” to have around 2,500 running within a year.
- Testers (May 2026) said Tesla was also aiming at Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa.
- Hiring and test-vehicle posts (treat as signals, not live service): Arizona, Florida, Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, California, D.C., plus a Germany Arzfeld pilot with a safety driver and Japan Kanagawa job listings.
- Ashok: expanding to a new city is getting cheaper; the end state is operating whole states, not city by city.

ACCESS AND PLANS
- Official: Robotaxi app waitlist. Access expands as cities open.
- Testers (Aug 27 WorldlyReviewer): received an email from Tesla advertising Robotaxi. Tester report of Tesla marketing, not a new Official service announcement.
- Elon (Feb 2026): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Testers (JPMorgan via folder posts): robotaxi operating cost about $0.50–$0.60 per mile vs $2.50–$3.00 for typical ride-hail; long-term platform goal $0.30 per mile. Older Morgan Stanley note used $0.81 per mile vs Waymo $1.36–$1.43.
- Folder testers argue Tesla scales on existing Model Y / Cybercab manufacturing and Superchargers, vs lidar-heavy custom cars.
- Testers (Aug 23): Waymo’s latest self-driving hardware reportedly costs around $20K.
- See OWNING / FLEET for private-owner economics from the Owning Robotaxi Fleet folder.

SAFETY
- Elon: scale as fast as possible, but do not harm anyone. One injury becomes a worldwide headline and a regulatory clampdown.
- Ashok (Jul 2026): zero notable incidents over 380,000 unsupervised miles, across six cities in two states. Cameras only.
- Testers on NHTSA ADS data (Jun 16, 2025–Jul 15, 2026): zero collisions initiated by the Model Y ADS. Two new incidents were other drivers hitting a stopped or parked Robotaxi (Austin red-arrow stop; Dallas parked). No passengers, no injuries, no tow.
- Austin: testers said 100% of tracked robotaxi rides in that NHTSA window were unsupervised.
- Testers: 7x safer than the average human driver is an FSD claim in this folder, not a Robotaxi-only official stat.

FLEET AND INFRASTRUCTURE
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; upgraded intelligence in vehicle distribution and routing. Testers (tslaming) say that gain is backend ops (demand forecasting, fleet placement), not a self-driving software change.
- Testers (Aug 23): 908 robotaxis in the total fleet (dated). Newer tester tracking-site counts: 969 (Sep 8), 994 (Sep 11 TeslaZoa) — still Testers, not Official.
- Testers (Aug 19): about 97 Cybercabs at the Houston Robotaxi lot. Model Ys and Cybercabs still rotating in the geofence.
- Testers: Tesla plans 80 wireless chargers in Austin as Phase 2 of a Robotaxi charging hub.
- Testers: private (not public) V4 Supercharger depots, including 56 stalls in Chandler / Phoenix East Valley; a Dallas-area fleet depot; a Las Vegas Cybercab wash/service site.
- Testers: scale needs charging, cleaning, and maintenance automated, not only FSD.
- Fleet-size tweets in this folder are days-to-months apart and disagree. Do not treat an old 500–600 car count (or the Mar 2026 “8 unsupervised in Austin” fleet-folder snapshot) as current.

USEFUL WORKFLOWS
- New city: download the Robotaxi app, join the waitlist, ride when your city opens.
- Live city: book in the Tesla app. Try a multi-stop trip if the app offers it.
- Airport: testers already used SFO and SJC where those pickups were live.
- Watch Nevada: paid Las Vegas service after the Aug 20 permit plus leftover admin steps; testers now cite a 5,000-vehicle cap.
- Watch Austin: testers say public Cybercab rides are “imminent.”
- Owning a fleet: not open as a turnkey product in this dump. Watch Elon’s owner-network comments + Tesla fee structure; treat $30k/yr and <2yr payback as tester models only.

text:
They didn’t make matching silver.

They made a king’s banquet that never repeats itself.

Reed & Barton’s Francis I pattern — patented 1907 — carries 15 different clusters of grapes, pineapples, lemons, and scrolls. No two standard pieces in a service are identical. 

A French silversmith named Ernest Meyer spent three years drawing it after King Francis I of France, the monarch who brought Leonardo da Vinci across the Alps.

Sterling versions cost a fortune. So the company launched the silver-plated twin: King Francis hollowware. Mid-century America put the punch bowl, twelve footed cups, tray, and ladle on wedding tables and holiday sideboards. Same high-relief fruit. A fraction of the price.

The Taunton, Massachusetts factory that made it for 191 years went bankrupt in 2015. 

The line is discontinued. What’s left are vault pieces — American-made, already heirlooms.

Would you rather own the plated punch set that actually got used… or the sterling one that sat in a chest?

#ReedAndBarton
#HeirloomSilver #VintageSilver

Historical composite for education. Marks, pattern dates, and company history verified. Not an appraisal or offer to sell.

text:
IGBOS MUST STOP PROTESTING AND START PRODUCING

It has been over 59 years, yet Ìgbò people do not want to be smart. You are trading in another man’s land—a land of people who do not even like you, people who blame you for all their misfortune in business, even when we know they are responsible for their own misfortune because they are not so good at business. Another nation comes to outperform you in business, and here you are protesting, expecting solidarity and sympathy from the same people who want to kick you out. Ndị Ìgbò should have some shame. You pride in calling others lazy and talking down on them because they are not so good at business. Now another nation more business-oriented than you has entered your retail business space, and here you are—protesting.

Let me be honest with you: no Yoruba person will show you sympathy. All of them want you out. It is time you changed strategy, evolved, and became production-oriented. The time for selling other nations’ products is over. Start producing. Instead of protesting in another man’s land—the land of people who do not even like you—organize yourselves and lobby your governors and senators to make laws that encourage local production.

Buhari banned rice importation and Nigerians started producing their own rice in response. Now the doors are open for China to compete with you in retail in your own space. It is another opportunity for you to evolve and produce the things you sell. The Chinese are humans like you; they do not have two heads. It is time to prove how great you claim you are—or were you making empty boasts?

To the Yorubas and other Nigerians celebrating this development: at first it is more convenient to enjoy the cheaper prices the Chinese offer, but in the long run even your own people will no longer be able to do business in their own land because most people will buy from China. Do you think your people do not do business as well? Go to Mushin Building Material Market in Lagos and see hundreds of Yoruba businessmen also trading there; these are the same people the Chinese will kick out of business with way cheaper prices.

It will affect everybody, but the survival tendency will not be the same. The Nigerian project has trained Igbos to be more resilient and survival-inclined. Igbos will find a way to navigate this and come out victorious, but what would be the fate of other Nigerians who are not so used to tough times?

text:
Every evening at dusk, at Phrom Sampov near Battambang in Cambodia, a black plume forms in the sky. A storm of bats, millions of them together, spiral out from a cave inside Phnom Sampov mountain, forming a continuous, swirling ribbon of black against the sunset. The limestone cave's cool, humid darkness makes it a perfect roost, safely tucked away from predators, while the surrounding rice fields and farmland offer an endless insect buffet each night. Together, they have given rise to one of the region's largest bat colonies. The exodus lasts up to half an hour before they scatter to hunt. Locals set up chairs and cold drinks at the base of the mountain, turning it into a nightly open-air show. 

See one of Southeast Asia's most mesmerising sights on the #AngkorAndMore tour of Cambodia with Khaki Tours from 21-28 Nov, '26, walk along a bank of the Sangker river to see city buildings like the Governor’s residence, museum, railway station and more and go “Ooh-la-la.”

from Deep Seek:
The September 2026 updates to X's Terms of Service will significantly affect New Zealand users by, in practice, making it much harder to hold the platform accountable in a New Zealand court. The key changes involve moving legal disputes to Texas, limiting your ability to join class actions, and shifting responsibility for AI actions onto you.

Here is a breakdown of the key changes and what they mean for you in New Zealand.

### ⚖️ Legal Disputes Move to Texas
*   **What the terms say**: Any legal dispute between you and X will be resolved in Texas courts under Texas law, rather than in New Zealand.
*   **What it means for you**: This creates a major practical barrier. To sue X, you would likely need to engage a US lawyer and travel to Texas, which is prohibitively expensive for most individuals.

### 🚫 Waiving Your Right to a Class Action
*   **What the terms say**: You agree to waive your right to a jury trial and to participate in any class, collective, or representative action against X.
*   **What it means for you**: This prevents New Zealand users from banding together to share the costs and resources of a lawsuit. You would have to pursue any claim individually, making it economically unviable for smaller disputes.

### 🤖 You Are Responsible for AI Actions
*   **What the terms say**: You are responsible for your use of the services, "including features that perform autonomous actions on your behalf".
*   **What it means for you**: If you use an AI feature on X (like Grok) and it posts something defamatory, breaks a law, or causes harm, you—not X—will be held liable for those consequences.

### 🔍 AI Content and Privacy
*   **What the terms say**: The definition of "Content" now includes your AI prompts, inputs, and outputs, granting X a broad license to use them. You are also responsible for ensuring this content complies with all laws.
*   **What it means for you**: Be extremely cautious with what you type into AI features. Anything you input can be treated as public content that X can use and share, and you bear the legal responsibility for it.

### 🛡️ New Zealand Consumer Law Might Offer Some Protection
While X's terms are designed to make legal action difficult, New Zealand law may push back on some of these clauses.
*   **Unfair Contract Terms**: The **Fair Trading Act 1986** allows New Zealand courts to declare "unfair contract terms" in standard form consumer contracts unenforceable. A clause that forces disputes into a foreign court and effectively denies a consumer their day in a local court could be challenged as unfair. A precedent exists in *Viagogo*, where a clause mandating Swiss law and courts was declared unfair under the FTA.
*   **Consumer Arbitration Agreements**: The **Arbitration Act 1996** has specific protections for consumers. An arbitration clause in a standard contract is not enforceable against a consumer unless both parties agree to it in writing *after* the dispute arises. This could render X's arbitration clause inoperative for New Zealand consumers.

### 📝 Your Options as a New Zealand User
You are not without options, but they require careful consideration.
1.  **Accept the Terms**: You can continue using X, accepting these new legal risks and limitations on your rights.
2.  **Deactivate Your Account**: If you do not agree with the new terms, you can deactivate your account and stop using the service.
3.  **Seek Legal Advice**: If you have a specific dispute with X, it is crucial to consult with a New Zealand lawyer who specializes in consumer law to understand your specific rights and options.

If you have a specific concern about how these changes might affect you, it may be helpful to consult a local legal professional.
